#4779. James Gray on Paper Tiger, Adam Driver, and Why Great Leading Men Need Danger and Vulnerability

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The filmmaker talks ambition, masculinity, and why he’s always trying to mine his own life for the truth.

ONCE YOU’VE GONE to outer space with Brad Pitt and almost gotten eaten in the Amazon, where else is there to head but home? That’s the question filmmaker James Gray asked himself after wrapping the World War I-era adventure epic The Lost City of Z and the celestial adventure Ad Astra. His answer: “I guess the conscious desire was to go back to what I know.”

That resulted, first, in 2022’s Armageddon Time, a largely autobiographical story of a young Gray growing up in Queens with his imperfect parents (Anne Hathaway and Jeremy Strong) and loving grandfather (Anthony Hopkins). His latest film, Paper Tiger, was originally conceived as a sequel to that one, but eventually settled into a separate mostly autobiographical and intimate tale of the director’s youth.

The new film once again features characters explicitly based on his parents, this time with the bespectacled father, Irwin, played by Miles Teller and the expressive mother, Hester, played by Scarlett Johansson. Naive Irwin gets drawn into a sketchy business plan by his brash brother Gary, a former cop and ambitious entrepreneur played by Adam Driver—and things only go south when Irwin proudly decides to show his new venture off to his sons and sees something he should not have.

Paper Tiger also marks a return to Gray’s roots as a teller of crime stories that will stop you in your tracks. (Longtime fans will remember he made his directorial debut with the Tim Roth-led hitman thriller Little Odessa in 1994.) But what could be just another crime drama in the hands of a lesser filmmaker becomes a grounded human story about the downside of ambition with Gray. His films are arresting because they feel like they could happen to you, too.

This new film, then, allowed the 57-year-old director to continue doing what he’s done his whole career: tell stories that, while lightly fictionalized, are still, at their core, true—regardless of genre. “I don’t see the movies as ‘crime dramas,’ even though clearly that’s what they are, because that’s part of the fabric of my young life growing up,” he says. “In my father’s case, and in my family’s case, it’s in our DNA. And so, for me, what is simply a memory of some sort, becomes quantifiable as a crime drama. Really, what you’re seeing is me trying to be very sincere with you about my own experience.”

It’s a story that’s been deep within him for a long time—and one he’s glad to have finally purged. “Now that I’ve gotten out of my system a little, I’m ready to expand the palette again,” he says.

As Paper Tiger expands to a nationwide release in theaters, Gray spoke with Men’s Health about finding great leading men, mining his life for stories, and the key to making everything personal.

Plus—read Gray’s take on his former Lost City of Z star Robert Pattinson as James Bond, from just a couple of days before the casting became official.

MEN’S HEALTH: You’ve worked with stars like Brad Pitt, Joaquin Phoenix, and Charlie Hunnam, and now Paper Tiger adds Adam Driver and Miles Teller to that list. So, what makes a great leading man?

JAMES GRAY: To be completely candid, some aspect of what you’re asking is unknowable until you see it on screen. It’s funny, I was reading about the casting of Peter O’Toole in Lawrence of Arabia. He had never done anything on screen, and all of a sudden they put him in the movie, and there’s magic. There are other people who you try to put in movies over and over again, and it never really clicks, for whatever reason. There’s an intangible quality to a great actor that we almost never can put our finger on.

That said, I’m looking for an ability to convey two things at once: danger and vulnerability. A sensitivity. Often, what you find is it comes from intelligence. I’ve never worked with a great dumb actor. It does not exist. If the actor is marvelous—and I’ve been lucky enough to work with almost exclusively great actors—they are all brilliant in an emotional way. Does it mean they can quote Proust? No, but that doesn’t matter. They have an emotional awareness, and they can read a room, and they have a shrewdness. All of this stuff goes into the work, because if you have a close-up of an actor, you can immediately see what they’re thinking, if they are thinking. I’m looking for both danger and vulnerability, in kind of equal measure. And you see it over and over in great performances. In fact, I can only think of one performance in all of cinema history, really only one, that is both great and has no danger in it, and that would be what Jeff Bridges does in The Big Lebowski. It has no danger at all, but it’s still a great performance. I’m not exactly sure how he pulled it off—it’s a real achievement. Maybe because he’s so sensitive and lovable in it that you fall for him, you know? But almost always, you have to have that aspect.

MH: When you’re casting for movies like Paper Tiger and Armageddon Time, which are ostensibly based on your own life, do you feel more of a pressure to make sure you get it right, as opposed to a story you’re perhaps a layer removed from, like The Lost City of Z?

JG: It’s funny, I’m not sure how much difference there is. I know Lost City of Z is about a guy in Edwardian England going into Amazonia, but when I was conceiving of that movie, I never tried to distance myself from Percy Fawcett at all. I tried to, in fact, invest myself in him. He was a dreamer, someone who felt slighted by the system, and he wanted to prove himself over and over again. He didn’t have medals. He wanted to be celebrated, and he finally gets celebrated, and he needs more. All of that is in us.

So, your question is a very good one, but in all truth, I’m trying—and maybe you don’t succeed, of course—in all cases to put myself into the work. That’s what I would say is making something personal. That’s very different from making something autobiographical. Autobiographical adheres to the facts of your life, and it is true—these last two pictures have been quite autobiographical. But that’s just so that hopefully I have an easier time in getting at what it is that I’m thinking about. They’re different modes, but you’re still trying to do the same thing, which is to get at your interiority.

MH: Miles Teller plays a character based on your father. I’ve never seen him do anything like what he does in Paper Tiger. What sold you on him?

JG: I had seen a bunch of his work, and I’d also spoken to my esteemed assistant director, a wonderful, beautiful man named Doug Torres, who’d worked on a movie with Miles Teller. I knew about him through him, and also the people that had worked with him. I had seen a film called Bleed for This, where he plays Vinny Pazienza, and his performance has what we were just talking about. He’s a boxer, he has a toughness, but it’s a very vulnerable performance. I didn’t want to lean into the nebbish, schlub aspect to the character at all. I wanted the character to have a certain fortitude, because then the vulnerability can really come through. In other words, if you’re just casting a movie and the guy is a nerd or whatever, and you’re watching a nerd be nerdy, it’s not that interesting. What I found was that Miles has an alpha quality, but to see a tenderness inside of that was the thing that really interested me. And I saw it in that film.

MH: Adam Driver is a sensational actor too. What was the appeal and experience of working with Adam?

JG: Adam has a very powerful onscreen dark quality, but he’s also open. He does completely different things from take to take. He’s always trying to find something new, something inventive. And he has tremendous craft. You can tell he’s really studied, and so you have both the craft and also he’s not in a rut. It’s just small things sometimes that you fall in love with. You’ve seen the film—he comes into the house, he brings Peter Luger’s, and he grabs the lamp, you know? A piece of set dressing. And he holds it under his face, and he says, “Tonight, Luger’s is coming to us.” So, all of a sudden, he’s like a showman. It’s these little touches, where he understands character. And again, I know I’m repeating myself—this comes from intelligence. He’s incredibly intelligent. He sees bullshit a mile away. That is a very good thing for an actor. He is a truth-teller. Great actors are truth machines. They will not let you lie in a scene. They are always open to the moment.

MH: That character is fascinating to me, because in other movies like this, he might turn into a villain. But your story plays with such shades of gray, and it really stands out.

JG: The idea was to set up a scenario where you see the guy and your immediate impression might be “Oh, he’s a cop, he’s bringing food over. He must be a jerk, or he’s trying to scheme, or something.” But in fact it turns out the exact opposite; he had nothing but very pure intentions, and winds up sacrificing himself. That was very much part of taking the audience’s expectations and subverting them. Now, when you do something like that, you’re going to have, hopefully, a small percentage of the audience, whining and complaining, telling you What are you doing there? How could he be naive? But you’re also going to have a large percentage of the audience that’s going to embrace the fact that it’s not a cliché. I was leaning into the sense Adam has as an actor, saying, “Yes, but we’re going to trick you.” And in the end, he’s going to have a generosity and a nobility to his character.

MH: Adam’s character is really brash and confident—it seems like he’s used to getting what he wants and isn’t afraid to kick some ass. Miles’s character, on the other hand, is a lot more reserved and sometimes naive. How did you go about designing the story around these two guys who each carry a very different brand of masculinity and see the world in different ways?

JG: It’s interesting you bring that up, because the operating principle of the movie… I was up very late one night, and I was watching—as one would—C-SPAN, I guess to try to put myself to sleep. And sometimes they televise the speeches that CEOs give at Davos, or that kind of thing. And I saw the CEO of a large corporation, and he was giving a speech, and he said “95% of people don’t know there’s a game.” He said, “Of the remaining 5%, 4% know there’s a game and don’t know how to play it, and then the top 1% know how to play it, and will win.”

I think his percentages are off—I think there are a lot more people who know there’s a game but don’t know how to play it, and that’s why we have a lot of anger in the world. But I thought of the story this way. You have Gary, a character who knows there’s a game, and knows how to play it, but he won’t make the ethical and moral compromises to win. You’ve got Irwin, who knows there’s a game, but has no idea how to play it. He’s smart—he’s an engineer. But he’s not shrewd. It’s a very different intelligence. And then you’ve got Scarlett, who probably knows there’s a game and maybe even knows how to play it, but fate has a different plan for her. So, the movie was organized along these principles. That this idea that our society always rewards the smartest and best, that it’s a meritocracy, is not really true. It rewards a certain kind of smarts, along with a certain kind of willingness to compromise. I saw Adam and Miles in this framework.

MH: Do you often find the germ of an idea in mundane places like watching C-SPAN in the middle of the night?

JG: One of the horrible things about creativity, and it’s also one of the truths, is that it is a very mercurial, impatient, sometimes too patient, thing, and sometimes ideas come to you in the most random of ways. The biggest obligation you have to your imagination is your willingness to make the random idea connect. In other words, the essence of creativity is your ability to make connections. So, sometimes, you get inspiration from totally bizarre sources that you’d never imagine. It’s up to your imagination to be open to the randomness of these connections, and to try and pull from them the source of your idea. It can sometimes be totally different, like, you’re in nature, you get an idea, or you hear someone, a homeless man, say something—that’s an idea. It can come from anywhere. And then we have the idea, of course, of myth, to give it some kind of structure. But the random idea is of tremendous value. It can come from C-SPAN, or it can come from a baby crying. It’s all part of the soup.

MH: With this movie, as you have so often throughout your career, you’re mining from your own life. I’m sure many of these memories are painful, so how do you protect yourself emotionally and mentally to avoid falling into a dark and difficult place?

JG: It’s an excellent question, and the answer is that you kind of can’t. I wish I could give you a glib response—the way that I protect myself is X—but what I owe you, really, is something that is honest, that is sincere. And I don’t owe you the idea that I should make myself look good, and that you should like me. I owe you my own version of the truth. So, if I’m working, it’s not fun all the time. Sometimes, you have to do things that are uncomfortable, that are unflinching, that are honest. And it’s not always pleasant. We recreated a fight between my parents, when my mother hit my father. Scarlett and Miles created it almost exactly as I recall it. This is my job. That’s why I do it. I do it to give it to you. And through that, you find the air of compassion and sympathy for a collective experience.

In other words, you’re not presenting a fantasy that has no relationship to honest emotion. And, by the way, when I say ‘fantasy,’ I don’t mean Star Wars can’t do it. Star Wars can do that. When he says, “No, Luke, I am your father,” that is actually connecting to something real, in the guise of a fantasy. When I say ‘fantasy,’ what I really mean is the filmmaker is trying to get you to like him or her or them, and that’s not my job. Sometimes you go to these unpleasant places, and it’s my job to cope.

MH: You’ve mentioned expanding your palette now that you’ve gotten these stories out of your system—do you have anything specific in mind? Is there anything you haven’t done yet that you want to try to tackle?

JG: I would love to do a Western. I would love to do a horror movie. I can’t believe I’m going to say this—I would love to do a musical. I don’t know what kind of shape the musical would take, but all of these genres are different forms of expression of the same ideas. I find the Westerns of John Ford unbelievably powerful to this day, because they’re always expressing something that’s inside Ford. Especially the films he made after World War II, which have such a thread of loss in them. And they’re very powerful to this day. You see John Wayne struggling with moral and ethical catastrophes in The Searchers, and you see a kind of post-war reckoning with what was a catastrophe of moral proportions in World War II, and you see it in John Wayne. You see the person of Ford coming out in that way, and using it in that canvas, the American West. That’s beautiful, and a way into the dark side of our personalities. Really, it becomes about me trying to find a story that will accommodate that, and that’s the difficult thing.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#4777. The Simple Guide to Finding a Weighted Vest You’ll Actually Use

Expert-tested picks that feel secure, balanced, and comfortable enough for all kinds of workouts.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Slip on a weighted vest, and suddenly your regular walk, chores, or bodyweight exercises feel a little more rewarding—the extra weight offering a simple boost in effort and making us more aware of the way our bodies maintain balance and stability.

I’m a certified personal trainer, and I sometimes recommend weighted vests to older adult clients as a way to add extra challenge to walking, cardio, and bodyweight exercises. While recent research suggests that weighted vests may not have a dramatic impact on bone density, they’re still a safe and convenient way to increase the load on your muscles and joints, helping you push yourself a little harder than usual.

Weighted vests let you add extra resistance to walking, stair climbing, jumping, push-ups, and pull-ups without needing to grip dumbbells or barbells. Some clients even wear them during everyday activities like cleaning, yard work, or mowing the lawn—making fitness a little more functional and, yes, a bit more fun.

That said, if you’ve been diagnosed with osteoporosis, consult your doctor before adding a weighted vest to your exercise routine, while folks who are pregnant or experience back, neck, or joint pain should also avoid them.

Before you take the plunge on purchasing a weighted vest, you should consider the resistance level, workouts such as walking or HIIT, and whether materials are sweat-resistant to determine which one is best for you. Ready to get vested?

After testing a handful of weighted vests for weeks, the trophy goes to the Omorpho G-Vest for its remarkable comfort, ideal weight, and sleek design. I spent a week wearing it for my regular lifting sessions and hour-long walks. It’s easy to wear for my normal gym routine, which includes moves such as walking lunges, Copenhagen planks, pull-ups, and push-ups.

However, I found it to be challenging when worn for heavier compound lifts like front squats, deadlifts, and barbell rows. Other than walking lunges, I wouldn’t normally add load to those exercises because of the logistics of holding or hanging weight, but the vest makes it possible to add resistance without gripping anything.

The fit is another reason the G-Vest earns the top spot. This vest is surprisingly comfortable considering it weighs just over five pounds from stainless steel balls. While the back panels have more weight—226 stainless steel balls on the back and 122 on the front—the weight distribution feels uniform when wearing.

It’s also compact—from the shoulder straps to the bottom of the vest is about 17 inches, which, for me, is great since I have a very short torso. It also doesn't dig into the top of my hip bone when I move around.

Even if you don’t have a short torso, you’ll still appreciate the soft-to-the-touch polyester fabric, despite it feeling like neoprene (synthetic rubber). I use adjustable cords at the sides for a customized fit. There are also straps on the shoulders to accommodate a wider frame, or if you want the vest to sit a little lower on your torso. For reference, I have mine on the shortest setting.

One downside of the G-Vest is its limited size options. There are only two: S/M or L/XL. I highly recommend using the size chart to determine which fit is best for you. I’m typically a medium when shopping for athletic tops, but I chose the L/XL because my chest circumference is on the cusp of both options. It’s also worth mentioning that the weight of the S/M vest is four pounds and 12 ounces, while the L/XL is five pounds and six ounces.

You can shell out up to $300 for a weighted vest, but not everyone needs all the extra features that come with that higher price tag. The ApexUp weighted vest is a popular option thanks to its low price point, but it offers more than just savings.

This vest is built from neoprene (which is the durable synthetic rubber you’ll find in wetsuits) and filled with iron sand, a material that’s denser than natural sand and absorbs less moisture. As a result, it won’t stick to you or clump up when you sweat.

It has a smooth, comfortable feel, with seams that are stitched over with fabric to prevent rubbing and chafing. Wide armholes and an adjustable strap across the chest mean you can get a comfortable fit, no matter your chest size.

The solo strap in ApexUp’s 10-pound version means it’s more likely to shift around during dynamic movements like burpees, making this vest a better choice for things like walking. A lot of the weight in the vest is in the front straps, so just be aware of your posture while you use this. But the mesh storage pocket in back is secure and roomy enough for your phone, which is a nice feature if you want to free up your hands.

A common complaint with this vest is the smell, which may be due to that neoprene cover. If you notice it and it bothers you, just let the vest air out a little before using it. Also, be aware that the ApexUp vest doesn’t allow you to tack on extra weight. But at this low price, you can simply buy a new one when you’re ready for more resistance and still come out on top, price-wise.

The best weighted vest is one you’ll actually wear, and the Stakt Adjustable Weighted Vest makes that part easy. Instead of looking like tactical gear, its streamlined neoprene construction fits close to the body and feels more like a weighted garment.

One way WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT likes to use weighted vests in her own training and with her training clients is to increase proprioception, or awareness of the body’s position in space. Because the Stakt vest distributes weight around the torso instead of loading only the shoulders, it can provide helpful feedback for connecting with the core and postural muscles during movement.

The Stakt weighted vest starts at six pounds and a two-pound zip-on extension brings it up to eight pounds. Grief tested both configurations while walking, doing chores around her apartment, doing pushups, and adding it to a functional training workout. It delivered comfortable, evenly distributed weight that fits and feels more like an additional clothing layer than a traditional weighted vest.

The aluminum front buckles feel sturdy. The shoulder straps use a hook-and-loop adjustment system, so once Grief found the right adjustment, it was a set-it-and-forget-it situation, and the straps stayed put. “I didn’t have to interrupt any workout to readjust them,” she said.

A porous mesh liner creates a comfortable buffer between the body and the neoprene, which adds some breathability. It also zips out for washing, which is a helpful feature, especially considering that this vest is worn close to the body. The vest also has a mesh pocket for small essentials. Its reflective detailing is minimal though, so you’ll want additional visibility gear when walking in low-light conditions.

If you’re looking for an adjustable-weight option ideal for specific functional training exercises and rucking, the Hyper Vest Elite from Hyperwear is highly customizable. I tested the 10-pound model, which is weighted with 66 individual 2.25-ounce stainless steel bars, each with its own little pocket.

If you prefer heavier weights, 15- and 20-pound options are available. Plus, you can purchase a box of individual weights to load up your vest (each pocket can fit two 2.25-ounce weights).

I wore it during multiple 60-minute walks, squats, pull-ups, push-ups, and back extensions. With the full 10 pounds loaded on my body, I found it really difficult to do pull-ups and push-ups. However, when I removed some of the weights from the individual pockets, it made for a more manageable load.

That said, I’m not sure how realistic it is to load up these tiny weights into individual pouches when switching between exercises. I think it’s a great feature, but personally, I’d design my workouts to ensure I didn’t have to adjust the weights more than once.

There are adjustable cords on each side to cinch or loosen for your preferred fit, but you won’t find shoulder strap adjustments like on the Omorpho vests. I also noticed the Hyperwear vest sits nearly five inches lower on my torso than the Omorpho vest. It doesn’t dig into my hips, but I notice it grazes my lower back when walking. It’s not a deal breaker, but I prefer shorter styles. Four size options are available: small, medium, large, and extra large.

As for material, I appreciate the heavy-duty construction of this vest, which is made with Cordura, a synthetic, tear-resistant fabric popular for backpacks and military clothing. It will hold up for years, even if you plan to go hiking or wear it in the elements. I also like the reflective strips at the zipper and across the chest for increased visibility outdoors.

If you’re looking for a weighted vest with resistance that pushes your limits while not disrupting your range of motion, this one by Vivitory checks the box. Despite the non-cropped fit, it still stays in place with only two adjustable straps and distributes weight evenly (11 pounds for the medium size and 18 pounds for the large size).

WH art director Christine Giordano was pleasantly surprised by how light it felt compared to holding it. “I was nervous it was going to be too heavy for me or cause pain in my lower back, but I was wrong,” says Giordano. “It didn’t bounce up and down or move all over—it stayed snug to my body while not being too hot and bulky.”

She loves wearing it during easy walks when waiting around for her kids’ sporting events or for more intense workouts, such as CrossFit or burpees. “I’m not a huge fan of dumbbell step-ups, so I tried it with the vest for the added weight without leaning forward,” she says.

As for the material, it’s made with neoprene, a synthetic rubber resistant to sweat that Giordano says she found to be breathable. There are also reflective strips on the vest for visibility during dawn or dusk, and a small pouch at the back for holding essentials.

If you get seriously sweaty during cardio or weightlifting, this 12-pound Reebok weighted vest is an option in hot summer temps. The back has a breathable ventilation panel that allows air to circulate.

WH contributor Korin Miller has recently added it to her workout gear lineup. “I like to go hard with my workouts, and I get really sweaty as a result—I appreciate the open-air design of this vest so I can cool off,” says Miller. “That, combined with the airy fabric, means I won’t end up with the vest sticking against my skin during workouts.”

Aside from its sweat-wicking properties, its two adjustable straps allow for a customized fit during a variety of workouts. For Miller, specifically walking, cycling, rowing, and bodyweight movements, such as planks and squats.

But, it’s important to note this model isn’t ideal for jumping. “Those extra weights can flap around during bigger movements like running and HIIT workouts—basically anything that has you jumping up and down,” says Miller.

The Omorpho G-Vest Icon is a quality choice for runners and HIIT workouts, given its snug fit and moderate weight that doesn’t feel like too much. The design is really similar to Omorpho’s OG model, with soft neoprene-style fabric, stainless steel ball bearings embedded into the fabric, and waist and shoulder adjustments for a custom fit.

The main difference is the adjustable weight and reflective strips throughout for extra visibility during night runs. The adjustable weight system is genius. It involves “G-Packs” of varying weights that snap in and out, allowing you to tack on additional, evenly distributed weight fast. (Just a heads up: A set of three G-Packs that brings the weight up to 12 pounds costs an extra $129.)

We also like that the encased stainless steel weights are not featured through the chest area. If you want to wear the G-Vest Icon with just a sports bra, you won’t have any irritation from high-impact movements.

For reference, the weights go up the entirety of the front panels on the men’s version. While the vest’s fitted style is ideal for runs, its six-pound weight means it’s better suited for things like short runs and sprints.

One downside is that the neoprene-style fabric made our tester sweat a ton when worn with layers. “My first experience with the vest was under my winter jacket on a 10-degree day during an hour-long walk,” WH contributor Korin Miller says. “I sweat my butt off despite the cold temperatures, compared to having sweat evaporate from my skin at the gym.”

Besides being a WH Fitness Awards 2025 winner, the Empower Weighted Vest is the only vest we’ve seen with a cross-style fit. It’s designed specifically to fit women’s curves while offering supreme support for the shoulder blades. The fit is compact with less material at the sides, while the straps are fully adjustable.

While its main highlight is being a custom fit for women, another unique feature is six removable one-pound bags (three in the front and three in the back pockets). In the 10-pound model (weight ranges from eight to 16 pounds), the vest can go as low as four pounds when the weights are removed if you’re seeking only light resistance.

WH health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, uses it for taking her workouts to the next level. “It elevates my walks, helps my core activate more, and makes my bodyweight exercises harder,” she says. Her only complaint is that the removable weights can make it feel bulky and interfere with hitting the full range of motion with a handful of exercises. “If I wanted to do crunches, I couldn’t lie on my back without it arching, and I couldn’t do supermans from my stomach because the bags in the front made it so I couldn’t lie flat,” she says. “During other strength exercises like squats, it hit the top of my thigh and prevented me from moving down further.” Perhaps it’s best to use the added pocket weights only during walks.

As for material, it’s neoprene for optimal sweat resistance, like the Vivitory and Prodigen weighted vests.

Not everyone wants or needs the 20-pound resistance TRX’s Hexgrip Weighted Vest can offer. But this vest is adjustable, allowing you to tweak the weight in one-pound increments, giving you room to grow up to that 20 pounds. So, if you want to use it as a 10-pound vest to start, more power to you.

This sturdy vest helps you get a secure fit with the help of three wide Velcro straps, making it a solid option for dynamic movements, some cardio workouts, and general strength training. The neoprene inner is comfortable against your skin, while the snug fit and smartly positioned weights mean you don’t have to stress about the vest moving around on you while you work out.

While it’s on the heavier end, it’s not bulky. As a result, you can still feel comfortable doing your usual range of motion. Just a heads up: Some of the weights are positioned across the chest, which may feel more noticeable if you have larger breasts. But those adjustable straps mean you can lower or raise the shoulder straps to find a position that’s more comfortable for you.

The weights slip into individual pockets to prevent them from shifting around, but make sure they’re secured well before you start your workout. (Some people have reported them sliding out.) Because the adjustment process takes some time, this isn’t a vest you’ll want to adjust mid-workout. This vest also comes in a 40-pound version, although most exercisers will do best with the 20-pounder as a heavy option.

If you have broader shoulders, the RITFIT has fully adjustable straps. They're spaced further apart—one sits higher on your chest and the other closer to your waist.

It can be more comfortable if you have a larger chest, while it may run bigger on smaller frames. It also has mesh pockets to store your keys and phone.

The load on a weighted vest can range from 3 to over 30 pounds, depending on the style and brand. If you’ve never used a weighted vest or are new to resistance training, I recommend starting with a lighter option between 3 and 10 pounds. Our best overall pick is optimal for newbies since it’s five pounds.

Heavier vests are ideal for loading bodyweight exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, squats, and walking lunges. They can also be used for walking, hiking, or rucking, depending on your fitness level. Lighter vests are ideal for speed training like sprinting, interval training, and plyometric exercises like box jumps, burpees, or jump roping.

Durable materials such as Cordura, nylon, and polyester are less likely to tear from constant wear during intense movement. All of the picks on this list are made from either of these three fabrics, and I found they perform well during explosive workouts and cardio. They also wick away sweat, which is a must for ultimate comfort. As for fit, I love an adjustable closure system with a zipper or buckles at the front, waist, and shoulders for customizing the fit.

Since 2020, we’ve updated this story and tested every major weighted vest on the market. I’m a certified personal trainer with the National Strength and Conditioning Association. I’ve worked in the health and fitness industry for nine years and have six years of hands-on experience working with clients one-on-one and in small group settings. With experience testing and reviewing hundreds of fitness products over the years, I wore select weighted vests for multiple hour-long walks and workouts, including exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, lunges, planks, and box jumps. I paid close attention to the material to see how it held up against sweat, fit for comfort, and weight for resistance levels. I also kept notes of my likes and dislikes.

WH editors, including associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, art director Christine Giordano, and contributor Korin Miller, also tested a few options and provided extensive notes on their experiences with them. Read on for our thoughts on the best weighted vests for women, as well as some other recommendations we like but haven't tested personally.

Lauren Strong is a NSCA-Certified Personal Trainer who has worked in the health and fitness industry for almost a decade. She coaches clients on the fundamentals of dumbbell and barbell training in one-on-one and group settings. She has also tested and reviewed over 200 fitness products and supplements for Garage Gym Reviews.

Jacqueline Andriakos, CPT, is the executive health and fitness director at Women’s Health, where she oversees all health and fitness content across WomensHealthMag.com and the print magazine. She has more than a decade of experience covering the wellness space and has edited ASME-nominated health features, spearheaded brand packages such as Fitness Awards, and represented the brand on the TODAY show, podcasts, and more. Before Women's Health, Jacqueline was the deputy health features editor at Self.com, and previously worked as the senior editor at Health magazine. As a writer-reporter, she has contributed to print and online publications including TIME, Real Simple, and People, among others. A dancer throughout her youth, Jacqueline went on to study journalism at the Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern University and stoked her passion for health and fitness during her college years, ultimately inspiring her to make women’s health content the focus of her media career. She is constantly researching the latest health and wellness trends, trying a buzzy new workout class, hiking and snowboarding, or browsing athleisure. Her friends would describe her as the confidant to turn to for fitness and wellness advice, not to mention answers to any weird body questions. Jacqueline is also a former group exercise instructor and is a certified personal trainer via the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM).

Natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

#4775. The 6 Best Gym Shorts for Men, Worn and Tested by Certified Trainers

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

We put a ton of shorts to the test, but options from Rhone, Vuori, and Ten Thousand came out on top.

FINDING THE PERFECT gym shorts shouldn’t feel harder than your workout. You know the struggle—shorts that ride up, cling in all the wrong places, or leave you chafed before you’ve even finished your warm-up. Truth is, you and those hard-earned leg muscles deserve better. Way better.

Whether you’re a gym veteran who can’t stop talking about leg day or a newbie figuring out the difference between a dumbbell and a kettlebell, it’s time to upgrade. According to Michael Hamlin, NSCA, CSCS, your athletic shorts should "allow you to perform basic workouts without too much hassle," from treadmill intervals to back squatting in the gym. Translation: You need shorts that stay put, don’t bunch up, and definitely don’t shout, "I just rolled out of bed."

So, we did the work for you—literally. We tested a whole locker’s worth of gym shorts, got insights from fitness pros, influencers, and even the designers behind them, and narrowed it down to the best six pairs for you. The right gym shorts should enhance, not hinder, your workout—just like the best workout shirts, the best joggers, and the best workout clothes in general. They should fit securely, wick sweat effectively, and allow full mobility for any exercise. The best gym shorts will have you feeling like a gym rock star, looking like you stepped off the cover of a fitness mag, and—most importantly—keeping your thighs cool and your glutes wedgie-free. Now that’s worth showing off.

The Ten Thousand Interval Short with Liner is the gritty MVP of gym shorts—versatile, durable, and ready for anything. Loved by athletes and editors alike, we use the Interval Short for everything from grueling lifting sessions to intense conditioning work to cooldown and recovery.

Men’s Health Senior Editor Brett Williams, NASM, is also a fan: "These are my go-to for just about every activity, from strength workouts to walking the dog. The fit, stretchy-yet-solid materials, and bountiful pockets stand out above the other shorts in my drawer."

Available in lined or unlined versions and three inseam lengths, the Interval Short checks every box. Its four-way stretch fabric offers a full range of motion, quick-drying capabilities, and an athletic fit that feels snug but breathable. Whether you’re crushing a WOD, running sprints, or chilling in the sauna, these shorts can handle it.

For years, Rhone has been cranking out workout gear so good it’ll make you wonder why you ever settled for anything less. The Pursuit Short takes things to the next level, building on the success of Rhone's Mako Short. Thanks to a durable polyester-spandex blend, these shorts give you enough stretch to handle everything from Netflix marathons on the couch to actual marathons on the pavement.

With three inseam lengths (5", 7", and 9") and the choice of lined or unlined, there’s a pair for every activity and every guy. Need support for leg day? Go lined. Prefer a lighter feel for a casual jog or coffee run? Unlined has you covered. The stretch fabric moves with you without giving up on durability. And the zippered pockets? Game-changer. No more chasing your phone mid-burpee.

Whether you’re crushing your workout or just crushing avocado toast, the Pursuit Short does it all—and looks great doing it.

The Vuori Kore Short is a great multitasker—soft, stretchy, and ready to handle whatever your day throws at you. Made with a blend of recycled polyester and elastane, they’re eco-friendly and feel like a dream. Plus, the built-in boxer-brief liner keeps you supported and sweat-free, so you can focus on your workout instead of readjusting your twig and berries every five seconds.

With 5", 7", and 9" inseam options, there’s a fit for everyone, whether you’re squatting, stretching, or just sitting on the couch pretending you worked out. Two hand pockets and a back pocket are great for storage, but let’s be real—if you’re carrying your keys while running, you’re playing with fire.

Now, the price—$78. Yeah, it’s an investment. But you’re getting shorts that look good at the gym and the smoothie bar afterward. These shorts are so versatile, you can smash your workout, then crash on the couch—because let’s be honest, they double as comfy pajamas.

The Lululemon Pace Breaker Linerless Short might just be the unicorn of gym shorts—lightweight, comfortable, and fresh even after the sweatiest leg day. After two years of putting them through the wringer, I’m still amazed by how cool they feel mid-workout and how they bounce back like nothing happened. Credit Lululemon’s brilliant design: no liner, four-way stretch that moves with you, and a back mesh panel that’s basically AC for your glutes. Redesigned low-bounce hand pockets and a zippered compartment keep essentials secure, so you’re not scrambling for your locker key mid-burpee.

"I’ve run dozens of miles wearing this short," says Senior Editor Brett Williams. They’re made of super light material, but the waistband’s fit is solid. The pockets aren’t too deep, and a zipper compartment is perfect for storing keys on the go.

Bottom line: These shorts make you feel like you’re gliding through your workout—and they’ve got enough stretch to handle those extra post-workout tacos, too.

The Nike Form Men’s Dri-FIT 7" Unlined Versatile Shorts are basically the Swiss Army knife of gym shorts—flexible, comfy, and sustainable to boot. They offer an unbeatable combination of comfort and flexibility, making them perfect for everything from jogging to lifting weights. You’ll like how these shorts will keep up with your workout without turning you into a sweaty mess.

Thanks to Nike’s Dri-FIT technology, they wick sweat faster than you can say "leg day." The unlined design is so lightweight and free-moving, you might forget you’re wearing them (don’t worry, they’re still on). Unlined, lightweight, moisture-wicking, and the capacity for complete freedom of movement—that’s exactly what you need in great gym shorts, and these deliver on that.

The 7-inch inseam is perfect for squats, lunges, or making a fashion statement without looking like you borrowed your dad’s basketball shorts. Bonus? They’re made from sustainable materials, so you can feel good about saving the planet while crushing PRs. At just $35, these shorts do it all without breaking the bank—or your stride.

The Alo Circuit Short blends comfort, style, and performance so effortlessly you might forget you’re wearing them—don’t worry, you are. With a minimal, relaxed fit and a stretchy drawstring waist, these shorts are as comfortable as they are functional. The 7-inch inseam hits the sweet spot—enough coverage for confidence, but still letting your legs breathe.

And let’s talk about those deep zippered side pockets—they’ve got room for your phone, keys, and wallet without anything flying out mid-jumping jack. The fabric? It’s that happy blend of 86 percent polyester and 14 percent elastane, softly swishy and sweat-wicking to keep you cool, even if the guy next to you in spin class is not.

Sizing is true to fit, with inseams ranging from 5 inches for size small to 7 inches for 2XL. At $68, they’re not the cheapest, but they’re versatile enough to justify it. Throw on a hoodie, and you’re smoothie-bar ready. Functional, stylish, and just flashy enough to make you the coolest guy in the gym—just don’t get caught doing arm curls in the squat rack.

Skip the cotton—it’s a sweat sponge. Synthetic fabrics like polyester blends are moisture-wicking and dry quickly, while nylon blends are more breathable for hot weather. Look for spandex or elastane for that four-way stretch, so you can move freely without restriction. Bonus: Some materials, like merino wool, are naturally anti-stink, while others feature built-in odor-fighting technology to keep you smelling fresh, no matter how hard you go.

Lined shorts offer built-in support, making them ideal for high-impact activities. "Unlined shorts offer more versatility for layering, while lined shorts provide additional support and comfort for high-impact activities," says Hamlin. If you’re lifting heavy or going ape on the air bike, the liner is a win. For casual workouts or layering over tights, unlined shorts let you move freely and stay cool.

The inseam is the length of the shorts from your nether region to the inside hem, and getting it right can make or break your workout. If you’re doing moves like squats, lunges, or anything that’s got you moving deep and low, shorter inseams (think 5 to 7 inches) are your best bet for keeping things smooth and unrestricted. While shorter inseams offer better mobility, longer inseams of 9 to 11 inches are great for taller athletes or anyone who wants extra coverage. Just keep in mind, if you’re on the shorter side, too much fabric can feel bulky and might even slow you down.

Functional storage is a must. "I say pockets are a must for me, and an extra bonus if they zip. Not a pocket in the back of my waist that I can barely reach, but pockets on the front sides," says Andy Stern from Rumble Boxing. Side pockets keep your essentials handy, and zippers keep you from chasing keys mid-jog.

Your gym shorts should feel as good as they look. Elastic waistbands with drawstrings keep you secure, while lightweight, breathable fabrics keep you comfortable and focused. Gym shorts should fit snugly around your waist—no squeezing, no sliding down mid-squat. Think "secure but free to move," like your gym buddy who knows when to spot you and when to back off. If you’re lunging and your shorts are riding up, it’s time to re-evaluate.

When it comes to picking gym shorts, it’s all about matching your moves. If you’re running, go for shorter inseams and split hems—you want freedom of movement, not fabric flapping around like you’re in a wind tunnel. Plus, reflective details keep you visible, because dodging traffic shouldn’t be part of your cardio. For lifting, you’ll need durable fabrics and compression liners to keep everything secure while you chase your personal best—nobody needs a wardrobe malfunction mid-squat. And for yoga? Think soft, stretchy, and unlined, so you can nail that downward dog without feeling like your shorts are plotting against you.

Flattering shorts come down to fit, proportion, and the right inseam for your build. If you’ve got beefy legs, short shorts will always work in your favor. Show them off with a 5-inch inseam (or less), which hits mid-thigh for most guys. For a touch more coverage, go with a 7-inch inseam, the most popular length for a casual, everyday look. Aim for a slight taper through the leg so it holds its shape without clinging. Bonus points for a smooth waistband that won’t dig in.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to try and test all kinds of gym shorts. I also enlisted help from our team of style and fitness editors, including members of our Men's Health advisory board. For months, we personally tested dozens of workout shorts. These weren’t casual try-ons; we put them through their paces in real training sessions.

Our evaluation focused on four key areas: comfort, performance (think moisture-wicking, quick-drying, and breathability), type (lined or unlined), and durability. Comfort and functionality are non-negotiable, especially for guys tackling intense training. Our mission? To find gym shorts that not only look great but also withstand tough workouts and the test of time.

We weren’t interested in trendy or fad-driven designs. Instead, we prioritized gym shorts that work for athletic guys who train hard, offer exceptional value at reasonable price points, and maintain a timeless style. The result? A curated list of six gym shorts that feel great, perform even better, and will look sharp for years to come.

#4773. Inside a Brooklyn Apartment That Feels Like an English Country Estate

Set in a wide Brooklyn Heights brownstone, photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment, though modest in scale, gives the impression of a breakfast room in some well-appointed Cornish estate. Hulking Victorian, Arts and Crafts, and Jacobean furniture dominates the space, Art Nouveau lamps aglow. The home draws an interesting contrast to the work for which he is best known—whether his black-and-white shoot with Kate Moss for Dazed or his recent Vanity Fair cover story with Carlos Alcaraz. Green’s apartment is, by comparison, more indicative of a bygone era, but it still reflects the irreverent, empathetic spirit at the heart of his practice.

The view from the bedroom into the living room

Paintings by Raphael Soyer flank a portrait by Thomas Hart Benton in the living room; armchairs by George Mann Niedecken.

Just under 1,000 square feet, the one-bedroom unit serves dual purposes: to provide space to converge with his cherished friends and to house other faces that inspire him. Covering walls are the many 20th-century figurative paintings Green has gathered over the years, among them Social Realist portraits by Raphael Soyer, nudes both bold and tentative, and myriad depictions of introspective souls—images that captured Green in a spiritual grip.

He displays the varied mix in interiors conceived with his friend Dylan Bailey, the New York–based artist and set designer, whom he met years ago on a shoot. Their collaboration was informal. Green would come home and find paint swatches left by Bailey, who might pop by and hang up a work while Green was shooting. The furniture they found at auction. “I wanted to have matching couches so when a friend comes over we can both take one, sink in, and talk,” says Green. The vintage sofas’ peach upholstery fits right in. “I didn’t realize until after getting them that the color showed up in several of the paintings,” Green says, referring to a portrait of an ironworker by Joseph Paul Vorst and a double nude by George Valentine Dureau.

A Victorian Renaissance Revival bed mingles with works by Maurice Grosser, Raphael Soyer, and Moses Soyer.

Green in the kitchen, surrounded by photographs

Green grew up outside Grand Rapids, Michigan, surrounded by, as he recalls, “cornfields and dairy farms.” With missionary parents, unstructured days, and endless skies, he had the space and time to imagine a different life. “I knew I wanted to be a fashion photographer when I was 14 or 15, then found out I could model at 16,” he recalls. “I won the lottery. Modeling was a better way to learn than art school.” He moved to New York City at 17, the first student to graduate from his high school online. “I had to be here,” he says simply. “My first year in New York I shot with David Armstrong. He took me under his wing.”

Now in his mid-30s, Green splits his time between the Big Apple and Los Angeles with his boyfriend. On the East Coast, between shoots, he runs New York Life Gallery, opened in 2022 and named after the Chinatown insurance company across the street. His first show, dedicated to Baltimore-based photographer Steven Cuffie’s tender portraits of Black women, reflected Green’s devotion to his own medium and enduring interest in the variance of human faces. The 2023 exhibition “Sleeping Beauties” would blur the lines between Green’s life and work: Many of the paintings shown have come to reside in his apartment.

Green kneels before a bookshelf by Renzo Mongiardino in the bedroom, which is painted in a custom Benjamin Moore blue.

Portraits by Raphael Soyer and Leroy E. Mitchell Jr. flank The bedroom’s 19th-century French armoire, which reflects a view of another Soyer painting.

An Austrian Art Nouveau chandelier hangs in the living room, which displays paintings by (from left) Raphael Soyer, Joseph Paul Vorst, Raphael Soyer, and Hermann Grom-Rottmayer. The walls are painted in a custom Benjamin Moore color.

A 1949 self-portrait by Leroy E. Mitchell Jr., for instance, hangs in the bedroom. This was the first painting Green bought at auction, prior to which it had been found in a dumpster. Green’s research led him to Mitchell’s early life in Detroit, his community of peers, and his time as a teacher in Ghana. Meanwhile, one of Green’s most pedigreed finds, a painting by Thomas Hart Benton, whose 1931 mural of industrial workers hangs in The Met, stoked another uncovering. “I had gotten multiple paintings and then realized many of the artists knew each other or were friends,” he says, noting that Benton and Vorst were studio mates. It is like Green is uncovering a parallel life of creatives finding true kinship.

Green Crowned the kitchen cabinet with art, including works by Raphael Soyer, Robert Philipp, and David Armstrong. To its right hang photographs by (from top) Nan Goldin, David Armstrong, and Richard Avedon.

Framed family snapshots fill the hallway shelves

It is these serendipitous journeys into the lives of other artists that Green cherishes as much as the art itself. “I love paintings,” he says. Perhaps a bit too much? Bailey would tease him that every time he arrived there was yet another portrait to place. “The reason there’s one hanging on the mirror over the mantel is because I had no more wall space,” Green says. As he explains, his collection, like his life and work, is ultimately about affection. “You cannot be a good photographer without being empathetic,” Green observes. “I love people. I love faces.” He’s made sure that love is hard to miss.

#4771. Cycling Taught Me How to Suffer—a Lesson That Helped Me Lose 140 Pounds and Find Recovery

“Riding a bike taught me that I could suffer now in benefit of tomorrow,” says actor Ethan Suplee.

SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles. On most corners, a new pack of amateur cyclists gathered. Bixi—Montreal’s bike share program—was represented, but as a garnish to the inundation of mountain, beach, fixie, and road bikes, along with their riders from around the world, taking over the city. I watched all this in awe. Cycling changed me because it taught me how to suffer. The sport familiarized me with the type of suffering that wrecks you, but you put yourself through it on purpose. You suffer to emerge resilient and better.

I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more. I wanted to know if they saw the power of suffering in the same way I did.

IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict. Checking into rehab that year put a number to my weight: 536 pounds. I’d been diagnosed with congestive heart failure, drugs were quickly killing me, and I was motivated to change. Once I’d been sober for a year, I was able to see that my weight was causing me suffering.

Standing was a herculean effort, placing my feet in the right spot to support me, calculating the angle my knees would be in at the apex of my shifting mass, deep breath, locked core, and a hope and a prayer that I didn’t topple. Tying my shoes was done in bursts of held breath and near-blackouts. I slept sitting up, because the pressure of my chest caused me to choke and gasp. I could once soothe that suffering with food and drugs and kick that discomfort down the road a bit, but in sobriety I needed healthy outlets.

I’d successfully managed lose 100 pounds before my wife tricked me into going to the gym. When she’d ask that I go, I’d tell her that the gym was a place for fit people. So she bought me a package with a personal trainer, said I could flake on the appointments, but I’d be flushing money down the toilet if I did. I went, but I was geared towards avoidance, and whenever something in the gym got hard, I’d just tell the trainer I couldn’t do it.

Riding a bike was something I did during outings with my wife and little kids maybe a few times a year. We’d cram our minivan full of bikes, find the flattest part of the Venice bike path, and slowly cruise for ten minutes at a time. Getting them back into the car was the hardest thing I had to work through.

Little did I know that someday cycling would be the key to changing my life.

ROUND AND ROUND I went losing and regaining weight. In 2009, after getting down to 300 pounds and ballooning back up to over 400, faced with having to start over once again, I turned my sights to running.

I tried running on a desolate stretch of the LA river near my house in Studio City. Not only was I unbearably slow, running hurt. My flat feet sent electric jolts of white-hot pain cascading up and through my body. That first day, I’d wrapped my ankles so tightly with ace bandages that my toes went numb. My feet were no better off and my nipples bled. The next day I could barely stand. The suffering didn’t stop when I stopped running. My feet, ankles, knees, and hips hurt long after—and I had no control over it.

With running out, but I turned to an old beach cruiser in our shed. The street we lived on was relatively flat, but every street branching off it was a steep climb. After a few rounds on my street, I decided to be ballsy and see how long I could last going uphill.

My legs were screaming, but there was no electric jolt of pain in my pedal stroke. My heart thundered, my mind told me I had to stop. But without the jarring jolt I got when my feet hit the ground while running, I knew I could go further.

Despite never riding my bike uphill as a kid, despite weighing 400 pounds, despite every physical and mental signal in me telling me to quit, I made it up to the top of that hill, up to Mulholland and Laurel Canyon, and it was glorious. Fighting through that urge to stop was incredible; getting to the top even more so. The pain while running was a warning that stayed with me after I stopped. The pain of cycling uphill was legs, lungs, and heart. I could push through it, and it stopped when I stopped.

I asked Tour de France cyclist Mike Woods about this distinction of suffering when I was in Montreal. “Suffering is a bit of a misnomer for endurance events. Are you really suffering? It’s elected, you know?” he told me. “You choose the pain, you choose when to stop, you choose when to keep going. I don’t truly suffer. Suffering is when you don’t choose for that pain to be inflicted on you”

And then he said something that really resonated with me: “But it does prepare you for real suffering, when you have something bad happen to you in life. Doing endurance events, I find—it’s fake suffering, but when you have those bad moments in your life, you’re better prepared to manage them.”

AFTER THAT HILL climb, I started riding my bike regularly, eventually graduated to a mountain bike, and then to a road bike. I rode to the top of every mountain in Los Angeles. I discovered I was capable of so much more than my mind or body allowed me to believe. Legs screaming, heart pounding, mind numbing, this was suffering, and I found that I loved it. And, like Woods said, I found that the more I suffered on a bicycle, the less I suffered off it.

“One day at a time, one pedal stroke at a time. Just move forward,” Toms Skujins, a two-time Latvian road race champion, told me in Montreal. “When you’re racing, you can stop at any point. You’re the one doing the damage, you know? That’s very voluntary suffering, because there’s, obviously, things in the world that happen where you don’t choose to suffer, and you have no choice there. Here… if your legs are screaming too much, you can just stop. For me, that kind of suffering is definitely easier to take.”

Within my first year of cycling, I was riding every day. There was a loop that took me from Studio City over the hill to West Hollywood. I’d cross Los Angeles, ride up PCH, cross the Santa Monica Mountains, and ride back to Studio City along Ventura Boulevard. It got me 100 miles and 8,000 feet of climbing, and I did it a few times a week. I’d do shorter 30- to 50-mile rides on the remaining days.

Sean Quinn, a US pro cyclist, gets it: “It sounds easy when you’re sitting on the couch, but when you’re actually in that moment suffering, your body’s basically sending you all the signals it can to make you just do anything else, just stop, stop the suffering,” he told me. “There’s no instant fix to a lot of your suffering. You have to be patient, accept that it’s gonna be shitty for a while, and wait it out, and keep a cool head, and eventually it does get better. Of course, you have to take action.”

When I was riding every day, I got down to 213 pounds. I’d like to say I stayed there. But I went back to work, stopped riding, my diet unraveled, and over the next few years, I gained nearly all of it back.

In 2016, 400 pounds again, I ruptured the biceps tendon in my right arm and had to have surgery to repair it. As a sober guy, I turned down the post-op painkillers. I was up all night in pain and had to work the following day. On set, with the motion of production buzzing around me, the pain was dull, but it was unrelenting, just like a ride up Angeles Crest Highway, more than 120 miles out-and-back, with over 13,000 feet of elevation gain. I hadn’t chosen the injury, but I had chosen to go without the pills, and that reminded me of the pain on the bike, something I picked and something I knew would come to an end. I’d remind myself of that and go back to learning my lines and preparing for the scene.

That day reminded me that I knew how to do this. So I got back on a diet, and by 2018 I was down to 260, and I’ve held steady there ever since.

Riding a bike taught me that I could suffer now in benefit of tomorrow. It’s been the most powerful lesson I’ve learned about myself.

ON THE DAY of the elite men’s road race, we fans lined the streets. There was dedicated bike parking near the finish line—Fans Village Bonjour Montreal—with thousands of bikes in neat rows. We all lined up to watch the attacks, riders going solo for that long and treacherous circuit. An American, Brandon McNulty, went off the front with about three laps to go and won the World Championship this year. It was thrilling to see. At the press conference afterward he said, “I was just dying, but I kept pushing.”

Leaving Canada, I couldn’t help but think that I shared something with everyone else there for the races. A secret membership, dues paid in sweat, and a code, to respect and revel in my voluntary suffering.

I’d gone to Montreal to ask the riders if they saw suffering the way I did, and in different words, all three told me that what you do on the bike carries over into the rest of your life. I’d thought cycling taught me how to suffer, but what it did was give me a place where I was in control of it, where I could make it a practice, so that when the suffering of life came along, the suffering I had no control over, I was better equipped to deal with it.

#4770. Puma Speedcat OG Review: A Style Writer’s Honest Opinion After 2 Months of Testing

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

After years of chunky dad sneakers and super-technical running shoes taking over the fashion scene, we're seeing a return to slimmer sneaks. And few shoes have made a bigger impression on that front than the Puma Speedcat OG. First launched in 1999, its streamlined fit and lower platform take cues from Formula 1 footwear. Now it’s found a second life as a street-style favorite. I see it constantly on the streets of NYC, and it’s become just as much of a fixture during my travels to fashion capitals like London and Paris. So I finally got my hands on the cute, comfortable sneaker, and after more than two months of testing, I understand the obsession.

The slender sneaker sits very low to the ground, giving it that ballet-flat silhouette which makes it feel much more like a fashion shoe than an athletic sneaker. Ballet-inspired shoes and “sneakerinas” are increasingly popular these days, styled with streetwear fits by celebs like Dua Lipa and Emily Ratajkowski. The buttery suede upper and lithe shape give similar kicks—like the Adidas Samba—a run for their money with a more luxe feel, separating the Speedcat from court sneakers and tennis shoes. I wear mine constantly with a simple straight-leg jean and sweater outfit formula or mix things up with something like a linen pant and leather jacket. I love how the Speedcat adds an edgy, cool-girl feel to my outfits without much styling effort. It’s also a nice change of pace from the chunkier running shoes I typically gravitate toward.

The pliable upper and sturdy heel collar make it easy to slip on and go when I’m in a rush. And darting around to catch a train is also not a problem for the Speedcat: There's very little bulk between your foot and the ground, so the shoe moves naturally with you rather than feeling like you're lugging around a chunky sneaker. One unexpected perk? I'm obviously not navigating an F1 track anytime soon, but I love driving in this shoe. I spend a lot of time behind the wheel on Long Island, and the Speedcat is one of my favorite shoes to wear for endless errands and longer drives. The thin sole doesn't get in the way of the pedals, and I can actually feel what I'm doing with my feet.

That said, this doesn’t provide the same level of comfort and cushioning you’d find in one of our favorite walking shoes, the Hoka Clifton 11. There's minimal shock absorption underfoot, so I wouldn't choose it for a day involving miles of walking or when I’ll be on my feet from morning ‘til night. I find it comfortable for my everyday routine, particularly when I'm driving, running errands, commuting to work, or heading out for a casual day. The fit is also on the snug side, especially through the toe box. If you have wider feet or prefer a roomier sneaker, I'd keep that in mind before buying and probably size up.

One thing I have been impressed with is how well the Speedcat OG has held up. Most suede uppers are tough to clean, but this one still looks great after more than two months of regular wear (including getting caught in the rain), and the outsole has a grippy feel even on wet sidewalks. Despite its lighter weight, my feet feel locked in during everyday activities. It’s not a sneaker I'd choose for a workout or any activity that requires a lot of lateral movement and support, but that's not really what it's designed for.

The Puma Speedcat OG has earned a permanent spot in my shoe rotation, and I’m already thinking about which colorways I’ll be adding to my collection next. It's not the most cushioned sneaker I own, but as someone who loves a good fashion sneaker, it’s become my capsule wardrobe holy grail. So if you're willing to trade a little underfoot cushioning for a seriously good-looking, lightweight sneaker, I think the Speedcat OG lives up to the hype.

#4768. Are AI Design Visualizers Selling Us on Slop?

Can I interest you in an autonomous sauna rideshare? How about a conversation pit car? Or a Magic 8 Ball in the shape of Rick Rubin? How about a plate for a single almond or a toilet turntable?

Friends, do I even need to say it? These objects—or slopjects, as their creator calls them—are not real. Though they look convincing on the feed, they don’t exist in meatspace the way that you or I do. They are Dadaist fantasies, dreamed up and rendered digitally without the limitations of production budgets, market demand, or even those pesky things known as laws.

The slopject’s unsavory first cousin, the slopspace—a full-scale interior scheme, created through digital rendering, and now generative AI—is increasingly populating home-decor inspiration sites like this one, where a viewer can encounter improbable living scenarios like garage apartments with no ladders or stairs to reach the lofted bed.

With hyperrealistic renderings a mere prompt away (and disclosures of AI-generated content remaining spotty at best), it’s getting harder to tell what’s real. On platforms like Pinterest and Instagram, where homeowners often seek inspiration for their design projects, the speculative images that float through the digital ether can be particularly hard to detect. Entire subreddits are dedicated to sniffing them out.

And detection is just the beginning. Aside from struggling to detangle fact from fiction in stumbled-upon images, consumers are also using LLMs—or large language models, AI tools designed to work with human speech—to generate their own visions of their dream home, without always understanding what it takes to make those fantasies a reality. That dynamic is starting to have concrete consequences for the professionals charged with designing and building the rooms we live in, where dollars and cents, artisanal skill, and the laws of physics remain painfully real. (Just ask the guy who tried to exit the lofted bed without a ladder.)

“People are seeing or prompting more fantastical solutions that are not rooted in the reality of the built environment, and then they’re presenting those to us as something that can be executed,” says Kevin Greenberg, founder and principal of the AD PRO Directory–listed firm Space Exploration Design. “We do it diplomatically and we do it politely, but we will tell them, ‘Oh, you know, it’s really difficult to achieve a stone ceiling.’”

This change is happening fast. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index Report notes that more than half of the population has started using generative AI in the past three years—a swiftness that outpaces both personal computers and the internet itself. When Midjourney and other AI imaging tools first hit the market, Greenberg says, clients used them to test the limits of what was aesthetically possible. “The prompt was like, ‘tropical Tudor fantasy,’ and then we were left to clean up the mess,” he recalls. “The images we were seeing were just tacky, and we all got a really big belly laugh out of it.” No one’s laughing now, he says.

These days, homeowners are feeding designer-created collages, mood boards, and sketches into Claude to see what spaces might look like once they’re built. The results tend to be uncanny: surfaces gleam like the Las Vegas strip, proportions are wonky, and there’s an unsettling feeling of dead air. Cy and Genevieve Carter, the principals of the New York City–based interiors firm Carter Design, joke that the worst dig they can make on a space is to say it feels like standing inside of a rendering. In the world of AI images, “there’s not a simplicity of space,” says Genevieve, which often means that more subtle textures like plaster don’t properly register.

Jake Shapiro, the owner of Hudson Valley–based millwork studio Slabrock, compares the images produced through AI software to the bloodless cuisine now rendered on deli signs. “It looks like scrambled eggs, but it also looks like H.P. Lovecraft, and that’s just horrific,” he says. “The same thing exists in design.”

There’s treachery in these images, designers agree, in that they portray a space nearly—but not quite—photorealistically. While that theoretically might help a homeowner understand how a designer’s vision for a space maps onto the real thing, it also bakes in a false sense of exactness that can leave room for misunderstanding or even disappointment. Organic materials like wood, for instance, can be difficult to predict with precision in AI. Every tree is different, Shapiro points out.

Catherine Campbell Pearson, a set designer and stylist based in Brooklyn, is seeing AI-fantasy expectations infiltrate the environments she designs for photoshoots too. In the past she and her clients would work from a “comp,” or a Photoshopped portrayal of the imagined end shoot. With those more lo-fi pictures, there was an understanding that the finished product would look slightly different. That’s disappearing in the age of GenAI: “It’s such a cohesive version of their idea that there’s much more attachment to the finished product looking exactly like this AI image.”

This phenomenon has real consequences for designers, whose expertise is on the line when a rendering goes awry. When clients go off on their own and submit designers’ early proposals into AI platforms, “The rendering that it produces is really unsexy and clunky and ugly,” says Greenberg. “Then they’re looking at us like, ‘Well, you’re actually not that good at your job.’”

What these examples illustrate isn’t a new problem, exactly, but it is one that’s more apparent in the age of AI. Just as Pearson has relied on low-resolution comps to create environments in the past, designers often use tools like collage, drawings, and mood boards to gesture at vibe and design intent before progressing to a more dialed-in rendering. But most homeowners don’t have the language to communicate exactly what they want to a designer—and when they do, the language may not precisely match the listener’s interpretation. (One person’s “cozy” interior is another’s clutter-filled nightmare, just as one person’s “serene” oasis is another’s sterile dystopia.)

LLMs offer clients a way to articulate their ideas in a way they may not have been able to otherwise—but in doing so, they create a highly specific rendering for a space that will require negotiation with real materials, labor, and budget—the latter being a serious constraint where AI can cause problems, says Tyler Polich, cofounder of the Los Angeles–based firm Years Studio. He shares an example of a client fiddling with an image and generating an element fully clad in copper—an option he and his partner would have never presented because of the cost. “Maybe it makes for a compelling image,” he concedes, “but we know that Gemini just blew their budget immediately.”

In certain cases, these visualizations can simplify things for designers and clients. Lucca Zeray, the Berkshires-based maker of Lucca House modular shelving, has found the addition of an AI rendering tool—a “configurator” that can depict his brand’s color-edged units in the proportions they’re seeking and provide a cost estimate—to be a game changer in the ordering process. “It’s a way that we can be like, ‘Here, you draw it,’ and close the gap,” he says. Unlike the every-detail-on-the-table possibilities of a full interior design rendering, Zeray’s configurator is only manipulating a few straightforward options, which might be part of the reason for its success.

In the reality of a built design, image making is only a small piece of the puzzle. The real work is in executing—navigating the personal relationships, sourcing fabricators, and negotiating details with the give and take of material reality. “We don’t work just in ideas,” says Genevieve Carter. “We work in stuff and things, and people, and their expertise is still a dialogue.”

Beyond the making itself, the design still needs to be good. Before AI was widely adopted, the algorithm-fueled flattening of taste was already in the cultural crosshairs. Social platforms reward likeable, heavily publicized images, like Athena Calderone’s marble-wrapped Brooklyn kitchen—photos that have been shared again and again. The problem then becomes that everyone is asking for an Athena Calederone–style kitchen. (It’s worth noting that even Calderone herself seems to have moved on from this look, by the way—her most recent home tour features a much moodier, Art Deco–inflected interior.) In today’s technological climate, this dilemma is taking a new form, as visuals take shape based on all of the environments that have been photographed and put online. But, says Polich, there’s an inherent flaw in this system: “The vast amount of visual information is relatively mediocre.” Real estate websites, DIY blogs, e-commerce images—most of the internet doesn’t look like, well, AD. It’s designed to be crowd-pleasing and just fine, not necessarily something extraordinary or innovative.

To find freedom from the tethers of the algorithm, Space Exploration Design encourages clients to go analog in seeking inspiration: “Flip through old magazines, show us an image from Automotive Design, show us a watch, show us your favorite painting—show us something else that we can build from, or that we can respond to in an oblique way,” Greenberg says.

Years Studio similarly seeks to tease out its clients’ personalities—“something that is real and human and only exists in them,” as Polich puts it. That’s a vulnerable undertaking, but also one that AI cannot replicate when its foundation is built on remixing what’s already come before. Greenberg, the Carters, and Polich all recognize that there’s some element of a trust fall required on the client’s side. By the end of a project, a designer is often familiar with the most intimate details of their client’s life—even what they keep in their nightstand. (They see those specialty chargers, and they don’t judge.)

But in earning trust, ironically, AI is also occasionally lending designers an assist. For the Carters, an exacting client was reassured in the studio’s recommendation of a particular stone after she’d exhausted all of the other options herself in her AI engine of choice. Another time, they won over a prospect by tweaking his AI rendering, and suggesting color options the client hadn’t considered. Is it possible that Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini could remind homeowners why they hired a designer in the first place? Just ask the Rick Rubin Magic 8 ball: Signs point to yes.
