#4767. The Science Behind Mogging

Believe it or not, there is something happening in your brain.

AT SIX-FOOT-FOUR, I’m not accustomed to feeling physically dwarfed. Sure, I might not have bulging muscles—but I confess I occasionally survey the other men in the gym and entertain the idea that I might be the hottest guy in the room. Sometimes, though, a bigger, better looking dude walks in and starts lifting heavier weights than me. My confidence evaporates, along with, I imagine, the admiring glances of all the men and women (who, on reflection, might not actually have been paying me any mind).

Until recently, I didn’t have a name for this peculiar, perhaps Palaeolithic phenomenon. Mogging, derived from “alpha Male Of the Group,” describes the act of one man outshining another, through any combination of height, muscularity, facial attractiveness, status, or charisma (a.k.a. “aura”). On the receiving end, it’s the sudden, visceral realization that another man might be stronger or better-looking than you, and the cascade of feelings of inferiority that follow.

“To mog” entered the lexicon thanks to figures like Braden Peters, better known as Clavicular. The 20-year-old looksmaxxing influencer was spectacularly “frame-mogged” on his own livestream in a viral moment earlier this year. The curious phrasing captured online attention, and on November 3 “mogging” was crowned Collins Dictionary’s word of the year for 2026.

But this type of social scenario didn’t just emerge with the dawn of the internet. I was curious: Does this emasculating sensation stem from an ancient status instinct, an ego threat, a form of social comparison, or something else? And why are some men so sensitive to it?

THIS ISSUE OF mogging raises a question: Why should another man’s stature have such an immediate effect on my self-esteem? It’s a theme explored in the classics. In Homer’s Iliad, the ancient Greek epic, King Priam spots the enormous warrior Ajax, “whose head and shoulders tower above the rest.” Yet Homer also understood that size wasn't everything. Earlier in the same passage, Menelaus is described as broader-shouldered than Odysseus, the cunning hero played by Matt Damon in The Odyssey—but the shorter man’s extraordinary eloquence renders his stature irrelevant.

Modern researchers have also looked for answers. Human judgment “is by nature comparative” and social comparisons are “spontaneous, effortless, and unintentional reactions to the performance of others,” according to a 2014 review of the early indications on the brain mechanisms of social comparison and their influence on the reward system.

Meanwhile, other related research found that physically stronger men were perceived as having higher social status, partly because they were considered more capable leaders. But does this make the discomfort of being mogged inevitable?

Psychologists distinguish between dominance, in which status is secured through intimidation, and prestige, which is earned through the admiration of others. Research suggests that even if the strongest and most attractive may initially draw outsized attention, or mog, prestige is ultimately conferred upon those who benefit the group, rather than pursue aggressive self-interest.

For couples therapist Sarah Tilley, this dynamic reflects the tension between our instinctive deference to appearances and our recognition of its limitations. Snap judgments of competence from candidates’ faces predicted almost 69 percent of US senate races in 2004, according to a study in Science,

“There is a deference to beauty and we’re all culprits,” she says. “Beauty trumps intelligence, but only for a short amount of time. Smart people will know that, but it takes wisdom.” In other words, the actual effects of a mog could be fleeting if there is someone smarter in the room.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY happening when you feel the mog? Turns out, there are chemical responses behind those feelings of self-doubt.

“A review of more than 200 lab studies found that our cortisol is reliably spiked when we feel that others are judging us and when we can’t control the outcome,” says Dr Manesh Girn, a neuroscientist and men’s work facilitator.

“Envy toward someone who outranks you on something you care about also activates the anterior cingulate cortex, a region tied to processing pain and conflict,” he says, citing a study on the neural correlates of envy and schadenfreude (the feeling of satisfaction when someone faces consequences they deserve).

But the susceptibility to feeling mogged also depends on one’s values and sense of self-worth. “Shorter men are more sensitive than taller men to dominance cues in other men's faces and voices,” adds Girn. In the envy study, pain responses only arose when the other person’s perceived superiority was in a domain the participant particularly cared about.

Looksmaxxer-in-chief Peters admitted last month that he now simply removes himself from social settings when there’s a possibility he might be mogged. “It really has a soul-crushing effect,” he told podcaster Patrick Bet-David, recalling a recent weight room encounter. “We just felt the mog from all the way across the gym to the point where I just left. Why would I want that internal pressure?”

Such an extreme reaction suggests “a maladaptive mindset,” says Charlotte Markey, a professor of psychology at Rutgers University. “Social comparison is a very normal process, including in terms of our physical attributes.”

For some men in 2026, that drives an obsession to become the strongest of the pack. This can become genuinely debilitating.

“I've cared for young people who then go to the gym five plus hours a day, and it starts to detract from their quality of life,” says Jason Nagata, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco, who researches male body image. “The concern is when self-improvement becomes self-worth, because it becomes dependent on outperforming someone else.”

And while this might be driven by instinct, the experts caution against succumbing to our baser instincts. “It may be evolutionarily baked in,” says Markey, “but we want to be careful not to oversimplify here. We aren’t cavemen.”

HOWEVER, THE CAVEMAN is not quite dead. We form impressions of a face within a tenth of a second, and people can estimate a man’s upper body strength from his face alone. For our ancestors, misjudging who could beat them in a fight may have been a costly mistake. Some research suggests that our sensitivity to physical formidability reflects this ancient pressure, which may help explain why strength continues to influence perceptions of status.

Despite sometimes feeling the mog (and after injuries that prevent heavy lifting), I’m generally content to stick to lighter weights in the gym rather than packing on mass to stand out more in a room. Yet I wonder whether my own instinctive competitiveness has affected my relationships with other men. If I’m constantly assessing where I stand in some invisible hierarchy, like a dog jostling for position in its pack, surely it becomes more difficult to strike up friendships.

In a 2017 study of 100 physically active young men, researchers found that those at risk of muscle dysmorphia were less inclined to socialize than their peers, potentially due to social comparison tendencies. The pursuit of the perfect physique, it seems, can come at the expense of the very relationships it might be intended to improve.

SO WHY, AFTER millennia of social comparison, do we have this very modern understanding of the mogging dynamic? Social media has transformed what was once a largely local competition into a global one, exposing men to an endless parade of gorgeous bodies and faces against which to measure themselves (albeit at lower rates than women). “The Greeks didn’t compare themselves with the best, idealized versions of everyone in the world,” says Nagata.

Indeed, researchers effectively recreated the experience of being mogged in a study involving 300 men aged 18 to 30. They were randomly assigned to view images of bare-chested and muscular men alongside clothed photos and pictures of scenery. Exposure to the half-naked Chads resulted in significantly lower body satisfaction.

I would never flee a gym or a bar upon the entrance of a potentially more attractive man. But back in April—shortly after mogging entered my lexicon—I couldn’t help noticing how much attention a very handsome (and very muscular) longtime male friend was receiving. One woman I didn’t even know basically cat-called him on the street and complimented his outfit. Naturally I assessed my own. It wasn’t nearly as cool, I lamented.

Now, after years of feeling this mysterious, disempowering sensation in his company without entirely being able to place it, I had a name for my predicament: I’d been mogged. Still, I was able to keep it together. We enjoyed our lunch, and we remain friends.

Perhaps the instinct to compare ourselves is unavoidable. Sometimes I wonder whether the worst thing about discovering mogging is becoming conscious of a competition I never even realized I was in.

Mattha Busby is a journalist who covers drug policy, culture, and health.

#4765. The 6 Best Brooks Shoes for Walking, Tested By Style and Fitness Editors

The Adrenaline GTS 26 and the Ghost 18 topped our list.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ve been known to have questionable standards in some areas of life—like my preference for boxed wine post-grad or my ability to convince myself that cereal counts as dinner. But when it comes to what I put on my feet, the bar is high. I used to think a good walking shoe just meant something that didn’t give me blisters. Now, as a style writer with a pile of sneakers so high it rivals Everest, I expect a lot more. I’m talking support, tons of comfort, and yes, style. That’s exactly why Brooks has become my go-to. The brand’s secret sauce: a perfectly balanced, firm-yet-plush cushioning that makes long days on my feet feel like a walk in the park.

Brooks has been around for over 100 years, and the brand has perfected its walking (and running) shoes. It’s no wonder that Brooks sneakers also come highly recommended by our team of active editors and podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM. “Brooks has always been one of my go-to shoes, especially for walking,” says Schaeffer. That’s thanks to their ideal balance of comfort and support, extensive sizing, secure laces, and breathable, sturdy mesh uppers. You need a shoe specifically for walking because it offers the necessary cushion to take the impact off your joints and give your foot the support it needs to propel forward. These features help prevent aches and injuries.

There’s a seemingly endless amount of sneakers to choose from, but don’t stress: I’ve put in the work to try out the best Brooks shoes for walking. I log (at least) 10,000 steps per day between walking my energetic Jack Russell terrier all around Long Island and commuting into Manhattan for work. Our team of editors also tested every Brooks sneaker through power walking, long days at the office, and leisurely strolls. Our favorite shoe of the bunch is the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, but many others came close for their cushion and stability.

After testing dozens of shoes, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 26 takes the crown as my go-to for walking (and tbh, everything else). The latest Adrenaline GTS iteration still nails the balance between cushion and support, keeping my stride steady without feeling stiff or squished—which is exactly what I loved about the 25.

What really seals the deal? The firm-yet-cozy midsole hugs the foot just right, offering a secure, locked-in feel that still stays comfortable mile after mile. The 26 has about the same amount of cushioning as the previous version (maybeee a tinge more). It’s the perfect amount of cushion to keep feet comfy without sacrificing stability. The mesh upper got an upgrade too, with even more perforations to keep things cool even on the hottest days. I also love that Brooks kept the 10mm heel-to-toe drop (as opposed to the GTS 24's 12mm drop), which helps reduce the potential for strain in the hips and knees. I just snagged the 26 two weeks ago, but so far, I’ve racked up 15+ walking miles and 5 running miles, pain-free.

The previous Adrenaline iteration actually took home the top spot for walking shoes in our 2026 Fitness Awards for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. And so far, the Adrenaline GTS 26 is looking like a superb contender, keeping all of our favorite details of its younger sibling while improving breathability.

My favorite thing about both versions is the shoe’s GuideRails tech, which uses firm foam on either side of the heel to keep feet locked in. The foam is infused with nitrogen, making it super comfortable and lightweight without being overly plush. Bonus: The (did I mention breathable?) mesh upper keeps things comfy without too much stretch (key for stability while walking), Schaeffer says.

One heads-up: the Adrenaline GTS 26 is one of the heavier shoes on this list at 9.6 oz., so if you like a super lightweight shoe, you may want to consider the Glycerin Flex. However, I actually find this sneaker feels way lighter thanks to the mesh upper.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review

If versatility is your priority, the Brooks Ghost 18 delivers. With its nitrogen-fused cushioning, the latest version of the shoe packs in the same amount of plush padding that we loved in the Ghost 17 (it was a 2025 WH Sneaker Award winner for a reason!). Impressively, the moderately high stack height at the heel doesn’t feel too squishy or wobbly. It’s a great do-it-all shoe for long walks, standing all day, and running.

Upgrades from the previous version include a new sockliner that makes for a comfy, snug fit and a flat tongue (the old one was a more classic padded option). “It does a good job of hugging the shape of your ankle without rubbing or chafing,” says fitness writer and WH contributor Korin Miller. “I like the smooth, seamless feel it creates, but I noticed that the edges start to curl in with repeated use.” I’ve noticed the same, but it’s definitely not an issue once your foot is in the shoe—just something to double-check when you slide your foot in.

I’ve worn these for long walks with my pup, all-day errands, a Costco shopping spree (IYKYK), and a full day on my feet at a music festival—and my arches stayed happy through it all. The soft midsole offers that just-right level of give that absorbs impact without feeling too soft or marshmallowy. The knit mesh upper is even more breathable than in the last version, adding to the barely-there feel, as does the plush ankle collar, which doesn’t chafe or rub at all.

One of my only gripes about the Ghost 17 was the slightly narrow toe box, but thankfully, the Ghost 18 solved this issue for me. It’s much more spacious now, both in terms of width and height.

If you’re after a walking shoe that’s super cushy, the Brooks Glycerin 23 is it. I’ve tested these on nearly 10-mile walks through nature preserves and standing for hours at the DMV (ugh). I never once felt like my feet were sore or that I needed to rush to sit down—these things felt like walking on pillows.

But the cushioning isn’t the only win here. The Glycerin 23’s knit upper gives this shoe a sock-like feel that hugs your foot without squeezing. It’s smooth, stretchy, and breathable, making it one of the most comfortable shoes I’ve worn on long walks. The shoe has a mild heel drop that helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot and reduces foot fatigue, which I sometimes experience with other walking shoes. While I wouldn’t quite describe the shoe as sleek or minimalist, it balances its plush cushioning with a more understated silhouette (aka it doesn’t veer into chunky dad shoe territory).

I also appreciate how well this shoe performs on uneven surfaces thanks to its wide platform and ample traction. The durable outsole covers plenty of ground, and the traction has a complex, winding tread pattern. I never feel like I’m going to slip, even on slick pavement.

So far, the Glycerin 23 does a great job of keeping my feet locked in despite its super thick cushioning—but it’s not designed for max stability. Those with specific foot problems, like plantar fasciitis or issues with overpronation, may want to pick a slightly less cushioned, more supportive shoe, like the Adrenaline GTS 25.

Read More: The Best Shoes For Standing All Day

The Brooks Ghost Max 3 took home the top spot in our guide to the most comfortable sneakers for its perfect balance of maximum support and cushioning. It keeps my feet comfortably locked in, even after hours of wear, and my ankles never feel wobbly, which often happens with plush shoes like this one.

“Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!),” says style contributor Lily Wohlner. I agree. That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it almost feels like walking on a moving runway at the airport.

Even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s super stable thanks to its signature Guardrails tech (the same found in the Adrenaline GTS 25). The outsole also has a broad base, which reduces rolling of the foot inward and outward and cradles the foot in place without interfering with your stride. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton says these features are great for high arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel one ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options.

During testing, we did notice some wear and tear on the upper pretty early on (after a few months). While it was a bit of a bummer, the elite combo of cushion and support keeps this kick high on my list of Brooks sneakers.

Think of the Glyceric Flex as Glycerin 23’s lighter, more flexible counterpart. The upper and outsole are both made from super bendy materials that give the shoe an almost barefoot feel.

I’m a big fan of this shoe for walking, long periods of standing, running, and plyometric workouts. It's incredibly versatile, thanks to ample nitrogen-infused cushioning and a flexible midsole. The FlexZone technology—a strategically placed groove in the center of the shoe’s outsole—helps enhance the shoe’s flexibility and allows the foot to move naturally. Combined with the pods under the front of the foot (which reminds me of On’s signature CloudTec system you see on most of the brand’s outsoles), the shoe has a super bouncy feel without feeling wobbly.

Bonus: at only 8.0 ounces, it's the lightest shoe on this list, so your feet won’t feel bogged down. But it still falls in Schaeffer’s recommended weight range (eight to 10 ounces), so it's hefty enough to keep your foot locked in. Plus, the flat knit upper is super soft, breathable, and—yes—flexible, which adds to its airy feel.

But the shoe’s lighter weight means it offers less heft and a less supportive feel. If you need more structure or have specific stability needs, these might not be your best bet. But, if you’re into a flexible, responsive shoe that doesn’t weigh you down—this one’s tough to beat.

The Brooks Ghost Max L offers a super plush, easygoing stride. The high-stacked cushioning is next-level—soft but stable, like walking on a marshmallow. It has an outsole with a curved bottom, like a rocking chair, to help propel you forward so each step takes a bit less energy.

I didn’t expect to notice the rocker bottom that much, but I totally get the hype. Schaeffer says he actually prefers rocker-bottom shoes for walking, especially as we get older, because they help take pressure off joints. That said, the same rocker technology makes me feel a little off-balance when I try to run or power walk in them, so I keep these strictly for leisurely walks and casual wear.

Looks-wise, I’m team Ghost Max L all the way. Some might say the stacked foam gives grandma shoes, but I think it strikes that perfect balance of chunky and cool—especially when styled right. I like to wear mine with a wide-leg pant and a blazer on top. It’s got just the right amount of bulk to feel trendy without being clunky, and pairs well with everything from athleisure to workwear.

However, this shoe runs small. Definitely size up if you’re in between sizes or like a little wiggle room. I could have used a half size larger than what I wear in the rest of my Brooks shoes for a little more comfort, but I still get a lot of casual wear out of them regardless.

First things first, you want a good mix of comfort and stability in your walking shoe, says Schaeffer. He recommends looking for a pair that cups your heel in a way that isn’t too snug or too loose. This feature will keep your feet from wobbling with every step you take. That sort of stability keeps your foot aligned as you walk, which is key for overpronation (foot rolls in too much) or underpronation (foot rolls out), helping prevent strain on your joints and maintaining balance. You want a shoe that’s comfortable on your feet, but Shaeffer says to avoid any that are overly cushioned, and instead look for a shoe that is a bit sturdier to keep your feet in neutral alignment to avoid foot fatigue and prevent sprains or strains.

The front of your sneaker (aka toe box) should never be too snug because it can pinch the nerves and inflame the ball of your foot (aka metatarsalgia). One way to know if your toe box is wide enough? Make sure your foot lies one thumb width from the side of the shoe and one thumb width from the front of the shoe. Tip: If you have a longer second toe, a larger toe box is even more important, Schaeffer says.

Brooks is famous for its incredible arch support, which is exactly what Schaeffer says to look for in a walking shoe. However, if your arches need a little extra TLC, Schaeffer suggests getting insoles that cater to your specific foot needs. He recommends Dr. Scholl’s Multipurpose Insoles or custom orthotics. "The insoles help with alignment and keep you balanced," he says, which is especially important if you suffer from chronic pain, plantar fasciitis, or issues with your feet rolling inward or outward while you walk. If this sounds like you, we def recommend scheduling a visit with a podiatrist to make sure your feet get the care they need.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer says to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Schaeffer says most people love a lightweight shoe since it's nice to feel like there's nothing down there. Just make sure the shoe has a supportive feel, and it holds your foot with every step you take. "In this case, I'm okay with the shoe being light," he says. "But, if the shoe is too light (under four ounces), you sacrifice function and stability." All of the Brooks sneakers on this list are between eight and 10 ounces, so they're the perfect weight in Schaeffer's book.

Over the past two years, the Women’s Health team has undertaken a comprehensive approach to curating the ultimate guide to the best Brooks walking shoes by testing nearly every new pair as it drops. Along with insights from Brad Schaeffer, DPM, board-certified foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City, we’ve put more than 30 Brooks sneakers through their paces.

As the associate style and reviews editor, I led the testing process with support from fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi, NASM-CPT, associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, and fitness and reviews editor Charles Thorp, NASM. Our evaluation involved multiple phases, consulting runners and walkers on the Women's Health team, and most importantly, testing the shoes firsthand. We subjected each shoe to everything from fast walks to long travel days to leisurely strolls. The narrowed-down list above includes the six shoes we were most impressed by

#4762. Why Better Recovery Might Be the Missing Link in Your Workout Routine

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You work hard in the gym, nail your nutrition, and consistently try to challenge yourself with heavier weights or more reps. But no matter what you do lately, it seems as if your progress just won’t budge. So what’s going on?

A plateau can be incredibly frustrating, but there is some good news: It may not be your meticulously planned workouts that need tweaking. The solution for your stall in progress may lie in something a little simpler: recovery.

Many people think results happen during our sweat sessions, but in actuality, the gains we’re working toward happen afterward. Adapting to stress, building muscle, and getting stronger all happen when we take rest. So, before you fire your personal trainer or scour the internet for a new workout plan, try making a few simple tweaks to how you spend your downtime, if you’re even giving yourself any.

Read on for what the science and experts say about recovery—and how you can use yours to escape your fitness plateau.

Meet the experts: Donna Duffy, PhD, is an associate professor in the department of kinesiology at the University of North Carolina, Greensboro, and head of research at Collective X Health, a women's health intelligence and research platform co-founded by WH advisory board member Stacy Sims. Lisa Woodroffe, MD, is a sports medicine physician at the University of Iowa Health Care and team doctor for several of the Iowa Hawkeye women’s athletic teams. Asad Siddiqi, DO, is the chief of rehabilitation medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital.

Working out is only one piece of the equation when it comes to seeing results. In order to get all the benefits of training, your body needs time to rest and recover after a workout. “During rest, your body recovers using sleep, food, and downtime to repair the tissues you’ve stressed during training and prepare them to handle the next challenge,” says Donna Duffy, PhD, an associate professor in the department of kinesiology at the University of North Carolina, Greensboro.

There’s a lot that goes on in your body during rest: In addition to your muscles repairing and building back stronger, you experience a nervous system reset—as your heart rate decreases after a training session, your body shifts out of a stressed state and begins to calm down, Duffy explains. Then there is increased blood flow during and after exercise, which helps flush out things like lactic acid and delivers fresh oxygen and nutrients to stressed parts of the body.

That is, assuming you’re giving your body enough time to do all that. “If you continually pile more workouts on top of fatigue without giving your body enough time and resources to recover, that fatigue can start to interfere with your overall performance in and out of the gym,” Duffy says.

When a person fails to recover adequately, a weight that seemed doable on Monday feels heavier on Wednesday, and an easy run becomes a hard one. All of this can be incredibly frustrating, and may make people think they just need to work harder, but experts say sometimes the opposite is true. “Your body may not need more training,” says Duffy. “Instead, it may need more opportunity to recover from the training you're already doing.”

Your body may be sending you signals that you’re not as well recovered as you think. According to Duffy, some common signs that your body has not recovered well include:

Showing signs of poor recovery? Start by making these tweaks.

When deciding if your body needs a rest, consider factors like workout duration, intensity, and fatigue, says Asad Siddiqi, DO, chief of rehabilitation medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital. Soreness or fatigue that stays below a 3 to 4 out of 10 during or immediately after training and does not last beyond 24 to 36 hours is the upper limit of “acceptable” exercise-induced discomfort, and a day in between loading is probably fine. Meanwhile, if you go above a 5, Dr. Siddiqi recommends taking an extra day beyond that to monitor how you’re recovering before doing the same workout again. Typically, a two-day break will allow people enough time to recover, but the most important barometer is how you feel, he says. If you’re still super sore and think your form will be compromised, you need more time off.

Bob and Brad A7 Pro Massage Gun with Heat and Cold Therapy

TriggerPoint Grid Multi-Density Foam Roller

This doesn’t mean you need to be completely inactive during those days off, particularly if you’re doing circuit training. If you hit arms really hard on Monday and need to give them some extra time to recover, you can still do legs the next day. But, if you are doing intense and fatiguing full-body workouts, try alternating resistance training with low-impact aerobic or mobility exercises like yoga.

Even if you’re doing circuit training, at a minimum, most people should have at least one full rest day per week, says Lisa Woodroffe, MD, a sports medicine physician at the University of Iowa Health Care and team doctor for several of the Iowa Hawkeye women’s athletic teams. And, if you’re someone who has been feeling consistently sore, unusually fatigued, or seeing a dip in performance, it’s time to up your number of rest days.

For a variety of reasons, many active people are just simply not eating enough, says Dr. Woodroffe. “They are either underestimating how much energy they are expending in exercise, or overestimating what they are eating, or with busy schedules running out of time in their day to get everything they need.” It’s also worth mentioning that some people may be exercising with the explicit goal of losing weight—which can result in underfueling for their workouts, she says.

Eating enough is critical for recovery. “We know that insufficient fueling patterns have cascading and multiplying effects on the body’s ability to respond to training load and recovery,” Dr. Woodroffe says. “All cells of the body need adequate energy to maintain optimal function. When there is not enough energy to go around, there will be effects not only at the cellular level but eventually also at the organ system level.” We’re talking effects on muscle recovery, bone density, cardiovascular function, and cognitive performance.

That’s why experts recommend having a plan in place for getting all the fuel you need. “Emphasizing a routine of three to five meals a day that includes carbs for energy, protein for muscle building, and fresh vegetables and fruits for minerals and gut health is the baseline,” says Dr. Siddiqi. You don’t need to count calories if that’s not your thing—but you should have a goal of at least three meals supplemented by additional snacks every day that hit all of the macros (carbs, protein, and fats).

Protein is particularly important for active people, but no macro should be ignored. Dr. Woodroffe always notes that no food groups should be restricted unless otherwise directed by a medical professional. If you need any help with your fueling strategy, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor or dietitian who can give you personalized recommendations.

One overall, simple way to make sure you’re eating enough? Feeling full. You should eat to be satiated and not feel constantly hungry. When it comes to snacking, it’s recommended that you eat easily digestible carbs (Think: fruit, bagels, toast) 30 to 60 minutes before a workout, and then a combination of carbs, protein, and fluids within 60 minutes following. It’s one reason dietitians love chocolate milk as a post-workout drink.

Your training program is a balancing act. “A plateau can happen either due to not enough training, or not enough recovery,” Dr. Woodroffe says. But how can we actually tell which one is happening? What are the clues that someone needs to pull back versus increase the challenge?

“Overall, training should be a positive experience that challenges the body and mind but doesn’t put you out of commission,” Dr. Siddiqi says. You want to be sore after a workout, but not so much that you can’t move. If you’re experiencing the symptoms above that are signs you’re not recovering properly, you’re probably overloading and should pull back. Start by taking two full rest days to give your body a real chance to recover, and then consider implementing one additional rest day per week compared to your old schedule or adjusting your training plan to allow for less intensity.

On the flip side, if you’re plateauing and not feeling drained at all, then it may be because you need to challenge yourself more. If that’s the case, Dr. Siddiqi recommends a steady increase in load by roughly 10 percent week over week. “The definition of ‘load’ in this situation is variable, and so this could mean 10 percent more intense based on your perceived exertion, 10 percent greater distance, 10 percent greater duration, or however else you think could be meaningful,” he says. The key, though, is to have a steady increase on your way to your goal, avoiding any major spikes.

So how do you know when symptoms are more than just poor recovery after a challenging workout versus a health issue that needs a professional follow-up? “Sometimes fatigue, soreness, or a dip in performance really can be a sign that you need more recovery, but it's also important not to assume that every change is caused by your training,” says Duffy. “If symptoms are persistent, getting worse, or affecting your ability to function normally, there may be something else going on.”

Duffy suggests seeing a health care professional if:

Whatever you may be experiencing—a regular old case of doing too much or something more serious—consider this your sign to take a second, check in with yourself, and don’t hesitate to ask for support. You’ll be out there moving again (and even better) before you know it.

I also found the LED backlight makes it super easy to read in low-light conditions, especially during a late-night jog. Other practical elements include a full auto-calendar, an energy-saving feature to keep the battery going strong, and a design that delivers durability and performance in one.

When it comes to field watches, the Hamilton Khaki Field is the gold standard—simple, robust, and packed with style. The Bremont Terra Nova is the kind of watch that effortlessly blends rugged practicality with standout style. The cushion-shaped case? As for the automatic movement, it features a Glucydur balance wheel (enhances its precision by maintaining consistent oscillations), an Anachron balance spring (offers excellent resistance to magnetic fields), and a Nivaflex mainspring (stores 38 hours of energy to power the watch).

What really makes it a go-to for adventurers and aviators is the oversized Super-LumiNova numerals. The Tudor Black Bay isn’t just any watch—it’s the perfect blend of timeless style, top-notch craftsmanship, and everyday usability. Let’s start with that 41mm steel case. So whether you’re checking the time in a dimly lit bar or on an overnight hike, it’s always easy to read. If you’re ready for any action-packed adventure—007 style—the Omega Seamaster Diver 300m is the watch you want. Plus, it even has a Helium escape valve—a small pressure-release system that lets tiny built-up gas particles flee to prevent the crystal from popping off.

During our testing, we noticed the titanium bracelet feels incredibly light on the wrist, which makes a big difference for all-day comfort. It has a smooth, almost silky texture but isn't as glossy. Another bonus: Titanium is hypoallergenic, so it won't irritate the skin for people with metal sensitivities.

This watch is a serious upgrade and, yeah, it’s the priciest one on the list, but here’s why it’s worth the investment: It’s a timeless classic with next-level features that will last a lifetime. It’s powered by the Chronometer 8806 movement, so it’s super accurate, and it comes with a 5-year warranty, just in case. In all honesty, it's the kind of watch that'll make you look like a million bucks at an upscale gala or extravagant dinner party. Pair it with a tailored suit and some slick dress shoes for a look that means business.

The movement is the engine of the watch—it's what keeps it ticking. Below, we've broken down the main three types and their benefits.

Powered by a battery and known for being super accurate, quartz movement is low maintenance, lightweight, and affordable. It's a great option if you just want a reliable watch without the fuss. Quartz watches will only require the replacement of the battery every few years, which is a simple task and costs fairly little.

Backed by the motion of your wrist—no battery required. The gears that make up the movement wind themselves when the watch moves. Automatic watches feel a little more special, sometimes like high-end brands Rolex or Omega, but they'll need to be worn regularly or placed in a watch winder to stay powered. They'll also require consistent maintenance and servicing to keep them optimally running. Automatic watches typically cost more than most quartz watches, but there are many great options that are affordable these days.

You wind it yourself, usually every couple days. Instead of the movement rotating automatically with motion, the gears need hand-winding to keep the movement running. These watches require attention and typically harken back to the era of vintage, throwback timepieces like pocket watches. Manual watches usually cost more than quartz watches and are on par in price with some automatic watches. They tend to be a little less affordable though.

Think of the case as the body of the watch—it's the shell that houses everything important, like the movement (the engine that makes it tick) and the dial (the thing with the numbers and hands). Cases come in different shapes, sizes, and materials. Below, we break down the most common materials used for cases.

Durable, versatile, and scratch-resistant. It's the most common and works for everyday wear.

Lighter than steel but just as strong, making it perfect for sports watches.

Scratch-proof and sleek but can be a bit pricey. It has a modern, luxurious feel.

A strap is any flexible band—made of leather, rubber, nylon, or fabric—that secures the watch to your wrist. Straps can change the entire vibe of the watch. A bracelet, on the other hand, is made of metal—stainless steel, titanium, or sometimes gold—linked together. Bracelets usually feel sturdier and add a bit of weight to the watch, giving a more premium, polished look. The good thing is many watches allow you to swap between a strap and a bracelet, so you can switch up the style depending on the occasion.

Classic, comfortable, and stylish. Perfect for dress watches but less durable for heavy-duty activities.

Stainless steel or titanium bracelets are durable and versatile for both casual and formal occasions.

Great for sports and water activities—comfortable and easy to clean.

When shopping for the best men's watch, features and complications can make all the difference in terms of functionality and style. Ultimately, these details should match your lifestyle. We've broken down some important specs to keep an eye out for, but these are by no means an exhaustive list of everything you could find in some complex watches.

This is the ring around the watch face, and when it rotates, it actually serves a purpose (beyond looking cool). On dive watches, for example, the bezel is used to track elapsed time—turn it to line up with the minute hand before you dive, and you'll know how long you're underwater. Some bezels work for other things, like GMT watches, where they help track a second time zone. But in everyday life, most people just fidget with them because it's oddly satisfying with a ratcheting sound.

Water resistance tells you how well your watch can handle moisture. There are two equivalent measurements you will typically find when it comes to this rating. Meters (as in depth) is the first and atmosphere (designated as ATM and measures the pressure of every 10 meters. So the first rating is 30m, which is rated at 3 ATM. This is splash-proof, which means your watch can handle occasional hand-washing or light rain, but don't submerge it. 50m (5 ATM) is good for shallow water activities like light swimming, but no diving. 100m (10 ATM) can handle swimming, snorkeling, and most water sports. 200m+ (20 ATM) is built for diving and serious water activities. Watches like the Omega Seamaster are built specifically for this sort of pressure.

A chronograph is a type of complication added to the watch movement that essentially gives the watch a stopwatch functionality. It's great for timing events, workouts, or even laps around a track. You'll typically see sub dials for seconds, minutes, and sometimes hours. While it adds functionality, it also gives the watch a sporty, complex look. The most famous example of a chronograph is the Rolex Daytona, made famous by watch icon Paul Newman.

A date window adds convenience—you won't have to check your phone or calendar to know the date. It's a small but handy detail, especially for busy schedules. Watches such as the Seiko 5 or Tudor Black Bay makes this feature feel seamless by blending it into the design.

Luminous markers or hands are a must if you plan on wearing the watch in low-light situations, like at night or in darker environments. Watches with Super-LumiNova or tritium tubes glow brightly and for extended periods and make the dial easier to read when overhead light is sparse.

Pay attention to case diameter and thickness. Case diameter is the main number you'll see alongside watches. Generally speaking, around 38-42mm diameter is ideal for most wrists, but larger or smaller watches can suit personal taste. The diameter of cases tends to ebb and flow with watch trends. For the first part of this century, case sizes gravitated over 40mm for lots of watch makers. But in 2026, smaller watches (even down to 32 and 34mm) are en vogue. We like to find a happy medium and suggest trying on different sizes to see what's most comfortable for your wrist.

If you’re rough on your gear or are looking for an everyday wear, opt for a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal (the transparent covering that protects the dial), shock resistance, or robust designs for long-lasting wear.

Our style team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, continually tests almost every watch known to man and put them through their paces for everything they’re designed to handle: marathon training, cycling, traveling, hiking, sleep tracking, daily fitness routines, and dressy occasions. To identify the most ubiquitous watches, we relied on our previous experience testing and owning various models, as well as prior expert coverage on Men’s Health.

We considered features such as case material, comfort, battery life, accuracy, dial design and aesthetics, water resistance, and magnetic resistance. Bonus points were given for unique specs that added functionality like a date window or sub dials. Our picks aren't just utilitarian though—they're seriously stylish, making them the perfect accessory for everything from the gym to date nights. In the end, we narrowed it down to 7 standout watches that tick all the right boxes and can provide a timepiece for any type of guy.

#4757. I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

Plus, the expert-backed reason a few minutes of mobility can add up over time.

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, says Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

“Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance issues, and injury,” says Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”

That’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

Mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” says Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”

And just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he says.

My routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

During the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

From the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

Heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

By the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

The routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

That said, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

Consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

However, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

According to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”

Kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

Following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

Mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

While there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

Alexa’s work has appeared in Business Insider, Parade, Men's Journal, Apartment Therapy, Men’s Fitness, Allrecipes, Family Handyman, Eat This, Not That!, Body Network, Everyday Health, SheBuysTravel, Tasting Table, Elite Daily, and more. When she’s not writing, you’ll likely find her at Pilates, hiking, designing her next tablescape, or jetting off on a getaway.

#4755. How to Do the Walking Lunge for Lower Body Gains

Build stronger quads, hamstrings, and glutes one step at a time.

YOUR LEGS ARE built for movement, whether you’re running, walking, or jumping. So why do most go-to leg exercises have you planting your feet in one spot?

Enter the walking lunge, a truly dynamic lower-body exercise that’s a perfect complement to exercises like heavy squats and Romanian deadlifts. (A bonus: It’s a unilateral exercise that isn’t the dreaded Bulgarian split squat.) The walking lunge is one of the few strength moves that truly gets you moving. And in doing so, it exposes muscle imbalances, trains balance and coordination, and challenges your core and upper body more than you might expect—all while attacking every muscle in your legs.

Walking lunges might appear deceptively simple at first, especially if you have done standard reverse lunges before. And in truth, they can be simple. Here, Men’s Health fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. walks you through the steps to take so that you’re not dragging your feet but making gains toward powerful legs.

FORM IS EVERYTHING with this move. You’ll want to stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, squeeze your glutes and shoulder blades while keeping your gaze at a neutral spot straight ahead of you.

Once you’re comfortable with this slow and controlled movement, you can add weights to build extra muscle and strength. You can hold them at your sides, hold them by your shoulders in what’s called a front rack position, or grab one heavy dumbbell and hold it to your chest in a goblet position. “Regardless of how you hold the load, make sure to keep your upper-body tight,” says Samuel. “Grip the dumbbells like you mean it, squeeze your shoulder blades, and tighten your abs, too.”

Don’t obsess over keeping your torso too upright, though, says Samuel. “Especially as you work with heavier loads, don’t be afraid to lean forward slightly,” he says. “That can help you capitalize on your glutes, one of your strongest muscle groups, with each stride.”

When you’re starting out, says Samuel, aim to take a step that keeps your front shin perpendicular to the ground when you lower your torso into the lunge. But as you grow more experienced, you can play with the length of your stride to chase different goals. “If you take very small steps forward,” says Samuel, “you’ll attack your quads more. Larger steps can help you build hip mobility and knee health. If you take larger steps, go lighter with the load.”

“The greatest benefits of the walking lunge come from how it challenges us while in motion,” says Samuel. “In addition to building strength and muscle, every step forward challenges your front leg (primarily tibailis and quad muscles) to decelerate your body in space, and then quickly work to accelerate into the next step. That’s building coordination and balance, in addition to training almost every lower-body muscle and building serious strength.”

You’ll work a number of major leg muscles when you do walking lunges, including your calves, hamstrings, quads, and glutes.

SMALL MISTAKES IN your walking lunge technique can turn the lower body exercise into a potential knee-wrecking disaster.

You want to land on the heel of your foot first to provide a strong base for the rest of your lunge position. When you get started with walking lunges, aim for a vertical shin as you lower down to the ground to stay at a 90-degree angle in your front and back legs.

You also don’t want to think of taking a step forward, but stepping out a couple inches by slightly turning your glute. Another adjustment to protect your knee is to shift your knee slightly outward instead of toward the midline. (If you still feel any knee pain during lunges, try a reverse lunge instead).

Keep your torso straight and avoid dipping forward, which you may be more inclined to do if you’re carrying heavy weights for this exercise. Your chest should be aligned with the back of your thigh the entire time. As you get up from the lunge, you want to avoid using momentum. That means no shoulder or torso rocking.

THE WALKING LUNGE is a great way to sneak in some movement on leg day if most of your lower-body exercises have both feet anchored to the ground. Load up some weights, and try to aim for 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg, 1 to 2 times a week. You can alternate each leg or finish up all your reps on one leg before switching to the other. Samuel says that will keep more tension and gives you an opportunity to really focus on the muscle.

An advantage of this move is its versatility, allowing you to do it anytime, anywhere. If you’re crunched for time or in a hotel room, try bodyweight walking lunges. Do it for 45 seconds with a 15 second rest for 5 minutes to break a sweat and build muscle.

Jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., is the fitness director of Men's Health and a certified trainer with more than 10 years of training experience. He's logged training time with NFL athletes and track athletes and his current training regimen includes weight training, HIIT conditioning, and yoga. Before joining Men's Health, he served as a sports columnist and tech columnist for the New York Daily News.

These storage bed picks include sleek, streamlined designs with completely concealed side storage, queen- and king-size beds with pullouts at the footboard, and more. A storage bed frame need not be ugly, even if function is the whole point of buying one. To truly give these recommendations on the best storage beds, I featured options that include a variety of price points, storage features, designs, and more to guide you on your own shopping journey. Read more on the key factors other writers and I kept in mind below:

Delivery and Assembly: The last thing you want is to wait months for your bed frame to help you organize (and elevate) your space. We selected options that offer reasonable shipping windows (usually within one month from placing your order to its arrival at your home) as well as white glove delivery to help set up the storage bed in your desired room, or a frame simple enough to assemble yourself.

Design: A big passion of ours at AD is finding furniture that is not only functional but is also not an eyesore. We skipped clunky bed frames and included pieces that can sit comfortably anywhere in modern and minimalist bedrooms and beyond.

Size: Our editors tested a mix of queen and king sizes, and prices in this story reflect queens. We looked for picks that come in a range of sizes to accommodate any space. Keep in mind that storage beds often have features like pull-out drawers and lift-up bases, so be sure to measure your space and compare it to your desired storage bed's dimensions to ensure the bed can open properly in your bedroom.

Storage Features: The storage bed you select should align with your space. If you're tight on floor space, consider a storage bed that lifts up. If you have low ceilings, consider a storage bed that has drawers underneath.

Durability: We tested storage beds by sleeping on them night after night, taking notice of any factors like creakiness or wobbliness. We also looked for options with high-quality materials like fine upholstery and solid wood that are designed to last.

Price: Storage beds run from a few hundred dollars to well over $2,000, and our picks span that whole range. While the price isn't always the biggest indicator of quality, materials like bouclé and solid wood are usually found in more high-end storage beds.

What Are the Different Types of Storage Beds?

Lift-up beds: Also called an "ottoman bed," this is a model where the mattress base lifts up with the aid of gas struts (pressurized cylinders that do most of the lifting for you), which retailers often call hydraulic lifts. This typically offers the most room out of the storage bed options.

Drawer beds: Fairly self-explanatory: drawers (either under, alongside, or at the foot of the bed) are this frame’s storage approach.

Headboard storage beds: A headboard storage bed draws from mid-century styles, where built-in shelves or nightstands create storage opportunities. This is a good option if what you need to store is also aesthetically pleasing.

Cubby beds: Instead of drawers, these cubbies are open shelving solutions underneath the bed frame, particularly suitable for holding books if you’re looking for a stylish way to create a bedroom library.

What’s a “Hydraulic Lift” in a Storage Bed?

When your storage bed has interior storage (in other words, when you lift the mattress base upward to access its storage), it needs a lift mechanism to make it possible for you to lift the bed without breaking your back, and to keep the slatted frame upright while you lift your items in and out. Most use gas struts, though you'll often see them sold as hydraulic. If your storage bed has interior storage and no lift, you will collapse yourself and ultimately be pancaked by your own sleep-and-store investment.

What Features Should I Look for in the Best Storage Beds?

A good storage bed, in our opinion, doesn't look like a storage bed. It looks like a regular bed. It's crafted from, ideally, kiln-dried hardwood, it has a slatted base so you don't need to bother with a box spring, and it has non-sticky drawers (thank you, Thuma) or a lift mechanism to help with the lifting of interior storage (thank you, Saatva). Look for a solid wood base, linen upholstery, and invest in some vacuum-sealed bags. I live by these.

You're primarily searching for durability and space in storage bed models. Look for frames made from solid wood since this type of material is typically sturdy and long-lasting. A lift mechanism makes storage more accessible without back-breaking exercises. While upholstered beds are a popular favorite, make sure what lies beneath the textile is also going to stand the test of time.

#4753. Get the Women’s Health Beginner Workout Plan: 4-Week Strength Training and Cardio Program

It’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately. My feed is full of people hitting the weights for the first time ever or setting big goals like getting their first pull-up. And let me just say: It’s awesome!

So, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party. When you’re starting to work out, it can be hard to sift through all the options and find a program that’s actually accessible for a true beginner (or, someone restarting after quite some time). That is, until now.

The Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey. This comprehensive program guides you through strength and cardio workouts that only take between 20 and 45 minutes. And, of course, it answers every burning question you could have about starting a fitness routine.

No matter your age or experience, starting an exercise routine has many benefits, says Kristen McParland, CPT, your coach for the next four weeks. Building muscle increases total-body strength; your bones, ligaments, and tendons get healthier; and even your blood pressure and immunity may improve. So lace up those sneakers and we’ll see you at the gym now, too.

Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan

Over the next four weeks, you’ll follow a specific plan each day, focusing either on strength training, optional cardio, active recovery, or rest (more on these, below). Each strength workout includes a warm-up and a cooldown (which you can use on cardio days, too). More info on each below.

Simply follow the instructions of each full-body strength training workout in the Women's Health+ Beginner Workout Plan. You can find detailed how-to instructions for each exercise in the Exercise Guide section of the PDF.

Equipment Needed: Dumbbells, kettlebells, a step or box, and a slam ball. Don’t have access to a kettlebell or slam ball? Don't worry—you can still do those exercises with a dumbbell.

Cardio is important for everyone, regardless of fitness level or routine. That’s because when you’re lifting heavy, your heart needs to be able to take on that stress. Training cardio—through running, cycling, or brisk walking—will help improve your heart strength.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Complete 20 to 30 minutes of running, biking, cycling, rowing, or using the elliptical or stair climber (whatever you enjoy). No matter which form of cardio you choose, start with interval training: exert yourself for 30 seconds, then go at a light pace for 1 to 2 minutes, alternating the pattern for a total of 20 minutes. The goal is to “get your heart rate up, but then pull it back and recover,” McParland says. Eventually, you’ll be able to decrease the rest time and maintain that higher-intensity movement for 15 to 20 minutes without a break.

Your activity on this day is up to you. The goal is to do some kind of low-intensity movement lasting 20 minutes. Some ideas: outdoor walk or hike, bike ride, incline treadmill walk, yoga, or Pilates class.

Take this day to relax so your muscles have time to repair. Still, if your body is craving some type of activity for recovery, you could stretch, go for a walk, or even try a treatment like a massage, sauna, or cold-plunge session.

Here’s how things will progress each week.

Complete the five programmed workouts when it’s convenient for you. Focus on your form and take your two rest days when you need to recover.

If you completed all the workouts in Week 1, repeat them during Week 2, adjusting one variable in your routine, McParland says: the number of reps or sets, the weight, the speed of the moves (slower is harder). If you missed a workout, don’t stress. Refocus on completing all of the Week 1 workouts before making any of the changes above.

You’ve officially done two full weeks of this workout plan—nice job! During this third week, repeat the workouts from Week 2 in exactly the same way or adjust one variable again (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, and rest periods). If you feel you’re crushing it and are ready to level up, try the third full-body strength workout.

Still going strong? Thought so! Hit all six workouts and adjust one variable per workout for an extra challenge (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, rest time). You can also ramp up your cardio time (to 30 to 40 minutes) or speed, shorten rest intervals (for interval training), or raise your step goal by 10 percent (e.g., if your daily step goal was 5,000 a day, make it 5,500).

Ready to become your strongest self? Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan now.

When you’re just beginning to work out, do a minimum of two full-body strength training days each week, McParland recommends. During both of those days, you should hit at least one exercise from each category of the foundational movement patterns. This will give you enough of a challenge to stimulate muscle growth, she says.

During the first two weeks of this plan, you will have two strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will 20 to 30 minutes), one day of active rest (a stint of low-intensity movement lasting at least 20 minutes), and two recovery days, for a total of five workouts per week.

After those two weeks, see how your body feels and if your body is craving a third day of full-body training. If so, progress to the next phase of this plan. That weekly schedule consists of three strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will run 20 to 30 minutes), one active rest day (lasting at least 20 minutes), and one recovery day, for a total of six workouts per week. If your body isn’t ready for three strength-training days yet, wait another two weeks. Once you’ve completed the full four weeks of this plan, consider adding in the third day.

Start with medium weights that will challenge you for 10 to 12 reps, says Sariya. Essentially, you’ll want to feel you’ve reached 70 to 80 percent of your rate of perceived exertion (i.e., your fatigue level is at a 7 or 8 out of 10) by the time you’re doing your final reps in a set. When you feel you can do more than 12 reps, it’s time to increase your weight, but keep the same number of reps. This way, you’re always working toward your goal of building strength.

As for how much to increase by: a good rule of thumb is 2.5 to 5 pounds for an upper-body exercise and 5 to 10 pounds for a lower-body move.

What if I need to rest in the middle of a set?

Resting during a workout is important—if you don’t take enough time to recover between exercises, you won’t have enough energy in your body for the next one. With this plan, you’ll rest between moves in a superset or tri-set for 20 to 30 seconds, or however long it takes to transition between exercises. Between supersets and tri-sets, you’ll rest for one minute.

If you get fatigued in the middle of a set, push through if you feel safe doing so, Sariya says. However, if you feel dizzy or fear you might drop a weight on yourself, put it down and take time to recover. When you’re feeling better, you can start again. If you’re in any sort of pain, stop the workout entirely.

Cardio is a great supplement to strength training, McParland says. Plus, it has a slew of benefits, such as better endurance in strength training, better blood pressure regulation, and higher VO2 max, she says.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Pick any form of cardio you enjoy, whether that’s brisk walking, running, cycling, or swimming, and sprinkle it in two or three days a week for 20 to 30 minutes, McParland recommends.

On an active rest day, you’ll still exercise a bit through low-intensity movement, like a leisurely bike ride or hike. On a recovery day, you’ll do just that: recover. After all, you need to give your muscles time to rebuild and repair, Sariya says. But to maximize the recovery aspect, you can also opt to stretch, go for a gentle walk, or even get a self-care body treatment like a massage.

Once you’ve got the WH+ Beginner Workout Plan under your belt, you’re ready to take things to another level. One way to do that is by simply restarting the program—and completing the moves with heavier weights this time. (This is called progressive overload, and it’s another foundational concept in strength training. The idea is that over time, you will keep increasing the stimulus to your muscles to continuously challenge them and make them stronger.)

Picking the right weight is an art as much as it is a science, but for a general rule of thumb, for upper-body moves, increase your weights by 2.5 to 5 pounds and see how that feels. For lower-body ones, try adding 5 to 10. You should feel like you’re ending each set two to three reps away from failure (where your form starts to break down). You can tell you’re close if your range of motion starts to shorten or your reps are slowing down. That’s how you know you’re successfully challenging yourself. And, if you don’t happen to have a lot of different-sized weights at your disposal, you can always just increase the number of reps you do instead.

But, if you’re looking for something new, WH+ has a bunch of other trainer-created programs to help you grow your knowledge and confidence in the gym and attack other fitness goals.

A TRUE NECESSITY for any real home gym, a great weight bench opens the door to a ton of exercise possibilities. The best weight benches are sturdy and reliable, allowing you access to a whole range of exercises, and the ability to target nearly every muscle in your body.

The best weight benches can be used for way more than just the classics that bear its name, like the bench press. "They're good for everything from chest presses, dumbbell bench presses, incline bench supersets, skull crushers, glute bridges, incline rows to hit your back, ab moves, quad and leg moves like split squats, and more biceps moves than you can imagine," explains Men's Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS Neither flat nor adjustable weight benches occupy as much room as bulkier equipment, such as a hefty power rack, either. And for those that are adjustable, you can easily change the angle on your presses.

Whether you prefer to do your weight work with barbells or dumbbells (or even adjustable dumbbells), the best weight benches are compatible. Plus, many of the best weight benches include attachments and hidden features that allow for an even wider range of workouts, like a leg developer or squat rack.

We've gathered a selection of top-notch weight benches after rigorous testing and research to elevate your training and home gym experience. Keep reading, because you can't go wrong with any of these eight benches.

This model from Hammer Strength was originally introduced in 2016 exclusively for athletics and clubs, and was designed to be a versatile bench with an Olympic rack system. We're such a fan of this brand, we've got quite a few pieces in our own Men's Health gym. It's American-made and sold around the world due to its high-quality, durable construction.

With seven different back pad positions (from −10 degrees for decline lifts and up to 75 degrees for overhead presses), it packs more multi-functionality than most benches out there. Plus, it has built-in wheels, making it great for home gym spaces that require moving a bench around during workouts to accommodate space.

From Samuel's point of view, this is one of the sturdiest benches he's ever used. "Its tough surface lets me create a great base for bench presses," he says. An underrated thing he loves: the comfort of the seat portion of the bench, which allows for locking in a good position during overhead presses and incline curls.

It's more expensive than other options in this guide, but if you're looking for a bench that can keep up with your biggest reps and hardest lifts, this pick has got your back.

REP Fitness nailed it with this piece. This is the bench that I choose to lift with at home. The assembly is as easy as you could hope for with a heavy-duty bench like this. A few separate parts connect with screws and an Allen key. Everything was put together and ready for my workout in less than half an hour (just enough time for you to feel accomplished but not tired).

This bench shines in that it is as comfortable as it is durable. Few benches combine sturdiness, comfort, and versatility like this one from REP Fitness. It offers six different incline angles and a three-post design that anchors it to the floor no matter the exercise. It can also support up to 1,000 pounds, making it a solid option for novice to intermediate lifters.

"The backrest feels way more cushioned than other benches in its class, yet still manages to deliver rigidity when I drive my shoulder blades down for a set of bench presses," explains Samuel. This bench has only a minimal gap between the seat and back, which has never interfered with any of our lifts. It's also not ridiculously heavy (less than 100 pounds), so it's easy to move around my home gym when needed.

It's also a total breeze to adjust from fully flat up to a 90-degree incline. I've never had an issue with either of the two adjustment mechanisms getting stuck. Three seat positions add to its versatility, too. And the roller pads help secure your lower body with decline sit-ups and decline presses.

Bowflex's flagship 5.1S Collapsible Bench is a good mid-range weight bench for small spaces and beginners. What we love most about this bench is its stowable design—when not in use, it can be stored vertically to reduce its footprint by more than 50 percent. For those who only use a bench at home from time to time and aren't pushing hundreds of pounds per exercise, this transformable option is a great choice.

"This bench is rated to support up to 600 pounds, but keep in mind that it's considerably lightweight," says Samuel. "Meaning if you line up on there for, say, incline rows or preacher curls, it may slip. I find it works best for me for bench presses and seated exercises like press, biceps curls, etc."
