#4715. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4714. BYD and Geely approached FIA about a 12th F1 team, says Ben Sulayem

BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem named the two Chinese automakers while speaking at the New Economy Forum in Madrid, as first reported by Grande Prêmio.

But there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal. The FIA is also pushing F1 toward the kind of engine an EV maker has the least reason to build.

“One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem said of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.

He said he suggested that BYD buy an existing team instead of starting a new one. BYD wasn’t interested in that route. It wants its own team, so Ben Sulayem told the company to come back with a “serious proposal” that shows the project can work.

He also made it clear that Chinese manufacturers won’t get special treatment. Any bid would go through the same process as other prospective entrants, and the rules won’t be rewritten to suit them. Right now, there’s no expansion process at all: the FIA isn’t actively looking for a 12th team.

Still, Ben Sulayem repeated that he’d like F1’s next newcomer to come from China, pointing to the country’s EV technology and the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.

This isn’t new for BYD. Back in March, we reported that BYD was exploring a Formula 1 entry, either by buying a team or building one from scratch.

In April, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD had met F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali in Shanghai and that an entry was “something we’re discussing.” By July, the tone had cooled. Li said “the dream is always there, but we don’t have a concrete agenda,” and special advisor Alfredo Altavilla set a clear condition: “We will never participate in Formula 1 just to put a sticker on the side of a car.”

Altavilla said BYD would only consider F1 to the extent its technology can serve the sport.

Geely is the new name here. The group sold 3.02 million vehicles last year and owns Volvo, Polestar, and Lotus, a brand with decades of F1 history. It’s also heading into Canada next year as Chinese automakers push hard into new markets.

The last newcomer, Cadillac, took a long road. The FIA opened an expression-of-interest process in 2023, and GM’s team only joined the grid as the 11th team this season, running Ferrari power until its own power unit arrives. Audi got in the other way, by taking over Sauber.

Here’s where it gets awkward for an EV maker. The 2026 F1 power units split output roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and electric power, with the MGU-K jumping to 350 kW.

The FIA is already walking that back. In June, it agreed to shift the split to 60-40 in favor of combustion for 2027 and 2028. And Ben Sulayem has been pushing for V8 engines running on sustainable fuel with “minor electrification” for the next rules cycle, starting in 2031 at the latest, possibly 2030. Domenicali says F1 should have a package ready to discuss by the end of this year.

So the FIA president wants a Chinese EV maker on the grid, while pushing a rulebook that makes their main strength less relevant.

We like the idea of BYD or Geely in F1. Chinese automakers have the money and the engineers, and they badly need brand prestige outside China. BYD in particular has been on a performance push with Yangwang, and F1 would be the loudest possible way to tell Europe it’s not just a cheap car brand.

they look for visibility/recognition on the world stage, regardless EVs. And in some (primitive) markets they market themselves as hybrids automakers, not as EV automakers.

They will make a hybrid power unit (which they already make anyway) to comply with the backward F1 regulations.

But Ben Sulayem’s comments don’t move things much. There’s no entry process, BYD has already turned down his main suggestion, and Geely’s interest is a name dropped at a conference, not a bid.

A Chinese would likely be good for F1 as well. Motorsports are on the rise in China, and that would be the cherry on top in helping popularize the sport in the world’s largest market.

The bigger issue is the engine. Altavilla was clear that BYD isn’t interested in slapping a logo on a car. It wants F1 to showcase its technology, and BYD’s technology is batteries and electric drive. The FIA’s V8 push goes the other way. It’s hard to sell an EV giant on a sport that’s reducing the electric part of the powertrain.

#4713. These Fragrances Double As Skincare Products

We’re often told that certain scent ingredients can cause sensitivity and irritation. The latest innovations aim to do the exact opposite, nurturing your outer layer with next-generation formulas.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom. In the middle of her pink-tiled bathroom was a small alcove with a skirted makeup table. Perched on top were probably a dozen, maybe more, intricately detailed glass perfume bottles and coordinating scented powders. The fragranced dusting powders were applied with oversized, almost-feathery puffs to absorb oil from the skin and leave it smelling fresh and clean, while the perfume itself acted like a topper, locking in the coordinating scent.

I was transfixed by the ritual of it. Scent has always had an emotional lure of sorts. Whether it transports you back in time or conjures a mood, the connections that fragrances evoke are personal and emotional. All that unfolds once a fragrance makes contact with the skin. As the notes dance and bloom, the scent really takes hold. But what if the skin-scent connection went one step further? Could a fragrance improve the tone, texture, quality, and health of our skin?

It’s no longer a theoretical—it’s reality.

Dual-purpose beauty products used to be a one-off. Nowadays, it’s expected that a product will tackle two issues at once. “We’ve already seen growing interest in functional fragrances, scents formulated with sensitive skin in mind, and alternative fragrance formats like hair mists and body oils, so it’s not surprising to see brands exploring ways to incorporate skincare ingredients into traditional fragrance formats,” says Darryl Do, a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. The idea of perfume that offers skincare benefits is fitting, and, quite honestly, maybe even a little late to the game. “It feels relevant as consumers become more conscious of the ingredients in their beauty products and what they intend to deliver,” Do continues.

Meet the experts: Darryl Do is a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. Jenna Queller, MD, is a dermatologist and founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton. Charlene Valledor is a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. Farah K. Ahmed is president and CEO of the fragrance creators association (FCA).

As skincare and scent merges into a brand-new category, some are wondering what took so long. “Scent has long been part of wellness rituals,” says Farah K. Ahmed, President & CEO Fragrance Creators Association (FCA). “What’s different today is that we have science showing that functional fragrances actually work.” We spoke with scent experts and a cosmetic chemist for the backstory on the trend and how to make the most of fragrances infused with skincare so you can reap the benefits.

Skin and scent have a long-standing connection. “In the fragrance industry, the term “skin scent” describes fragrances that are close to the natural scent of skin in order to complement it rather than overpower it,” says Do. But how a scent wears on the skin varies.

It’s all comes down to body chemistry, which includes pH, how much natural oil is produced by your skin, moisture and perspiration levels, and natural odor, explains Charlene Valledor, a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. That’s why the very same perfume can smell wildly different from one person to the next. Someone with a skin pH of 5.75, more sebum, or who eats a spicy diet, for example, will provide a different environment than someone with a skin pH of 4.75, drier skin, and eats virtually no spicy foods.

But it doesn’t stop there: What you apply to your skin before perfume also influences how a fragrance takes hold. By the time most people finish their morning routine, they’ve already created a fragrance profile and applying perfume introduces another layer on top of that existing baseline, Do says.

Unfortunately, your skin doesn’t always play nicely with certain scents. The ingredients in the bottle themselves, which includes everything from the concentration of alcohol to the presence of essential oils can cause itching, redness, and general irritation. “Fragrance can directly disrupt skin’s protective barrier or trigger an outright allergic reaction,” explains board-certified dermatologist Jenna Queller, MD, founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton, FL. “Irritation can happen to anyone, particularly when the skin is already dry or compromised. An allergy is different: the immune system has become sensitized to a specific ingredient.”

Dr. Queller says that while certain compounds like cinnamal, eugenol, isoeugenol, and geraniol are well-known contact allergens and can damage or irritate the outer layer of skin and weaken the protective barrier, others, such as limonene and linalool, which are commonly found in citrus, floral, and herbal fragrances, can become more allergenic after exposure to air. “A higher concentrations can increase the risk of irritation,” she says. “However, no single concentration guarantees a product is safe for everyone. If you develop a true allergy, even a small amount can trigger a reaction.”

Deciphering how much allergen is in a perfume—even in a natural or organic scent or essential oil, which isn’t necessarily a safe option for sensitive skin—is difficult. “You can’t judge a fragrance by how strong it smells,” Dr. Queller suggests. “Subtle scents can contain allergens, which is why the ingredient list matters more than the intensity.” If your skin is sensitive or dry, or you are rosacea- or eczema-prone, a fragrance intolerance or allergy, which often manifests as redness, itching, dryness, burning, and even swelling, hives, or blisters, is likely to form more easily, especially since she says the skin barrier may already be impaired.

So, what’s the best way to wear a fragrance while also safeguarding your skin’s health, especially if one of the trendier skincare-infused fragrances may not be a good fit? Dr. Queller suggests applying the scent to clothing rather than directly to the skin, although she says it’s not a guarantee because fragrance can transfer to the skin. Of course, each scents’ chemical composition can vary so naturally, a bit of trial and error may be involved to determine which irritate you specifically.

The latest fragrance technology is innovative because it not only helps you avoid irritant reactions, it promises to care for a nurture skin directly. In fact, it seems we’re moving toward a world in which dual-purpose fragrances can leave you smelling good and feeling soft. It makes sense when you learn that keratinocytes—the primary cells in your epidermis—contain olfactory receptors that respond to certain fragrances, says Dr. Queller. “Skin has its own sensory biology,” she says, “and research suggests scent may influence important cellular functions, including skin regeneration and wound healing.” In fact, one study showed that Sandalore, a sandalwood note, activates a receptor that speeds up cell growth and migration to help close cuts and sores. Another research paper found that the same pathway prolonged the growth phase of cultured human hair follicles.

It’s a welcome development. We all live extremely busy, over-scheduled lives and most of us want beauty products that do more than one thing. The new Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume captures this ethos brilliantly. It combines plant-derived exosomes, thought to boost collagen, reduce inflammation, and support healthier-looking skin, with one of two scents: a warm blend of vanilla, amber, and almond or an oceanic mix of sheer musk, sea air notes, and driftwood. Similarly, Bella Hadid’s alcohol-free, essential oil-powered Orebella collection promises to hydrate skin with a bi-phase formula that simultaneously moisturizes while delivering a long-lasting scent. Another offering worth noting is Salt + Stone’s Body Mist. In six intoxicating scents, each light-as-air-mist is infused with glycerin and red algae for smooth, touchable skin. The idea of all of these is that rather than leaving your outer layer dehydrated and more susceptible to aging—a common complaint with scents formulated with alcohol—these products support dry skin and enhance its moisture levels.

Future Society’s unscented Base Scent follows a similar path in a different way. It works with the skin’s natural microbiome to help the body smell better. It relies on aspergillus ferment, zinc, and arginine, and you can wear it on its own or layer it over perfume to create a more neutral body scent over time. The microbiome also factors significantly into Argentum’s Les Perfumes Infinis collection. Water-based and free of potentially drying alcohol, each of the twelve scents is formulated in such a way as to not disrupt the delicate balance of bacteria naturally found on your outer layer.

Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume

This fragrance, proven to last up to twelve hours, harnesses the power of plant-derived exosomes and an advanced hydration complex to hydrate skin and strengthen its barrier.

All of Orebella’s scents, including this brand-new blend of creamy milk, woody amber, and fresh bergamot features a base of hydrating snow mushroom and the brand’s signature five-oil blend.

Salt & Stone Bergamot & Hinoki Body and Hair Fragrance Mist

Salt + Stone’s body products have rightfully gained a cult following and their hair & body mists are no different. What does make them different is that they contain humectant glycerin to help skin hang onto moisture and red algae to promote smoothness. This bergamot and hinoki blend is one of their latest.

A scent with no scent? Yup. This one is formulated with prebiotics that work with your skin’s natural microbiome to keep your natural scent more consistent and balanced.

ARgENTUM Les Parfums Infinis LOVER Eau de Parfum

Each of these alcohol- and solvent-free fragrances is gentle on skin and blended based upon one of the main elements (Earth, Air, Water). Lover, for example, is a mix of geranium, rose, and berries meant to evoke a garden after a rainfall.

So, can a few spritzes of a skin-boosting fragrance achieve the same goals as a watery serum or thicker moisturizer? Potentially, but as Dr. Queller shares, it really comes down to the formulation. “A fragrance that incorporates ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, or nourishing emollients can help improve skin hydration and support the skin barrier.” Her advice? Look beyond the label and marketing claims. “A beautifully formulated fragrance can offer skincare benefits, but that doesn’t automatically make it suitable for sensitive skin.”

What is undoubtedly true is that the skin-scent connection remains strong, perhaps stronger than ever, and this new fragrance category may provide more options for those who may not have been able to wear scent before. These next-generation fragrances go one step further than functional fragrances, which can boost your mood, productivity, and wellness, to focus on skin health in a way that was never tackled before. So go ahead and douse yourself in one of these new skin health-boosting fragrances and wait for everyone to ask, “What perfume are you wearing?”

#4712. Watch BYD’s robotic charging arm plug itself in and charge EVs in 5 minutes [Video]

BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes. Now, BYD is taking things a step further with integrated solar power and a robotic arm that plugs itself in. See how it all works in action.

After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its new ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.

The Chinese automaker launched a new integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.

In 2006, BYD president and CEO Wang Chuanfu revealed his vision of “Three Green Dreams,” including harnessing solar power to generate renewable energy, storing that energy in batteries, and replacing gas-powered vehicles with electric ones that run on clean energy.

The new charging system is the “world’s first,” according to BYD, to integrate solar power generation, energy storage, Flash Charging, and robotic charging together in one solution.

BYD’s Flash Charging tech enables a vehicle’s battery to charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, essentially the same time it takes to fill up at a gas station. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

The new robotic charging arm automatically locates the vehicle’s charging port, opens its cover, plugs in, and then removes it once the session is over.

By combining robotic charging with its Automated Valet Parking, BYD said the new tech goes beyond automated driving and parking to the charging process itself.

Once the vehicle is parked, the robotic charging arm automatically takes over and connects it to Flash Charging without the driver even touching the cable.

A post shared by Michael Martinez (@mmichael_martinez)

Michaël Martinez, head of marketing at BYD France, posted a video (shown above) showcasing the new charging tech in action.

The integrated solution is built around BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging (SSC) system, fusing solar energy generation, battery storage, and its 5-minute Flash Charging tech. Together, the setup captures energy from the sun, stores it, and distributes it as needed.

If they could tie this into a smart summon type of capability, where the vehicle communicates with the charger and moves the vehicle into the proper location for charging and then moves to a parking spot once charging is complete. Rental car fleets would benefit and so would those in shopping centers. There are so many possibilities and this looks far more mature that the old snake charging Tesla demoed.

BYD has over 16 years of experience in the solar industry with a portfolio that includes solar cells, modules, and systems.

Its solar division, BYD Solar, does business in over 100 countries and regions. By using solar power, BYD said, the SCC system can operate independently off-the-grid.

The new technology is part of BYD’s wider Flash Charging rollout. By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy 6,000 Flash Charging stations globally.

BACK PAIN DOESN'T care about your big plans to sail through life in comfort, making it hard to do everything from getting in a workout to sitting at your computer. Relief can come in many forms, including regularly stretching and strengthening the surrounding muscles, but sometimes, it can also involve using one of the best inversion tables to ease pressure on your back.

“An inversion table is a device that allows you to hang at an angle, or even upside down, with your feet secured,” explains Max Shlykov, MD, an orthopedic spine surgeon at the Maryland Spine Center. “This position stretches and decompresses the spine and surrounding muscles.”

It’s important to get this out of the way now: An inversion table won’t magically cure your back pain or fix the underlying cause of it. But it can temporarily ease your pain and the tension that’s contributing to it. Inversion tables tend to be especially helpful for people with chronic back issues like herniated discs, sciatica, degenerative disc disease, muscle spasms, or general stiffness, according to Shayan Ghadamabadi, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University Health Care Physical & Occupational Therapy.

The best inversion tables are sturdy enough to support your height and weight, with adjustable hanging angles, Dr. Shlykov says. “Models that are more lightweight may be easier on your back to use and set up,” he adds.

You’re not born knowing how to pick an inversion table, making it important to choose wisely. Here’s what to consider when looking for one of these pain-relieving tools, plus sturdy options to try. You’ll also get access to a free personal training app with a library of video and audio guides for on and off the inversion table, Dr. Verma says. The only qualm? It may be difficult or time-consuming to assemble.

The Innova ITX9900 Heavy Duty Inversion Therapy Table is a budget-friendly option that doesn’t compromise on quality, according to Dr. Wallace. It offers a six-position adjustable pin system for safety locking and consistent inversion, a large, padded backrest, and soft-touch foam handlebars for easy access to getting in and out of position, he says. This table is great for anyone, but it’s particularly good for beginners thanks to its ease of use and adjustable headrest, height, and footrest.

This inversion table also features a True Balance System, which helps users find their center of gravity for smooth, seamless inversion. Not only will this maximize tension release, but it can also improve spinal decompression. Another pro: The headrest is adjustable, too.

When it comes to getting a full, comfortable stretch, the EP-560 is a safe bet. It features patented wrap-around ankle supports, an ergonomic T-grip ankle lock, and an easy-dial foot platform for a more comfortable, secure fit. The backrest is also a game-changer. Most inversion tables use a simple foam material; the EP-560 ComforTrak backrest is designed to reduce friction and enhance spinal stretch and decompression. We also love that it’s pretty customizable. It comes with built-in tools for easy adjustability, including a Lumbar Bridge for deeper traction on the lower back and Acupressure Nodes that target muscle tension.

The device is made out of an ultra-durable, heat-treated steel, adding an extra layer of strength and support. If you’re a little closer to the 300-lb range, this is a solid option.

It’s on the pricier side, but the Harison Electric Inversion Table is a top pick for both Dr. Mesiwala and Dr. Verma thanks to its adjustable footbed, memory-foam backrest, and heavy-duty build. The device is made with seamless welding and a steel frame to support up to 350 pounds, and the ergonomic ankle lock design is supportive without feeling too tight or restrictive. Security is also a top priority, and the table includes a high-quality safety belt that allows you to strap in while inverted (on top of the secure ankle holders).

The table is heavier than other options on this list, but it’s foldable for easy storage. It also includes a 30-day trial and replacement of spare parts within one year for no extra cost.

Read More: The Best Massage Guns, Tested By Us

If you’re looking for an inversion table that doubles as a massager, here’s your pick. The vertical massage pad covers the entire spine with a contoured lumbar pad for a close-up massage and vibrating sensation, and the in-unit heating pad provides warmth to the lower back. There are also multiple mode settings to suit your massage and heat preferences, and the included user manual provides all necessary instructions and details.

This model has a new, improved ankle-holding system to reduce pressure on the ankles when inverted, while still ensuring a secure, protective fit. There’s also a six-position pin system on the side of the machine that lets you adjust the angle without dismounting the device.

Each inversion table accommodates different heights, so it's important to read the fine print. The Teclor Inversion Table adjusts to fit people up to 6'8", making it a good option for taller users. It also can support up to 350 pounds, one of the largest weight capacities you’ll find.

This is a relatively simple inversion table, and the low price supports that. But you’ll still get a comfortably padded back, cushioned handles, and an easy-to-reach handle for adjustability. The ankle-holding system is thickly padded, too. A double-locking system helps to ensure your device is firmly in place when it’s in use. When you’re done inverting, it folds up small enough to stash in a closet.

Read More: The 6 Best Compression Boots to Support Muscle Recovery

Consider the Teeter FitSpine LX9 the slightly more luxurious version of our top pick, the X3. This has all the elements users love about the X3, including that durable heat-treated steel frame and padded back, but in a slightly sleeker, user-friendly design. The LX9 has an eight-point floating suspension system for a large range of motion, along with reinforced padded handles for a comfortable grip.

Enjoy eight acupressure nodes to help relieve muscle tension while you hang. The included lumbar bridge is adjustable and works to tweak your hip alignment. The LX9 has a step-through design with a specialized boarding platform to make it easy to get on and off. There’s even a built-in storage caddy to hold your gear while you invert.

Using an inversion table isn’t as simple as diving into a new set of dumbbells. These devices require you to move your body upside-down, making it important to know what you’re doing and how to ease into the process.

It’s important to start with a “modest” angle vs. going into a full-out inversion when you’re starting out, according to Raymond Agostino, DPT, owner of Agostino Athletics in Fort Myers, Florida. “The goal is to introduce your body to the position and create a gentle traction effect without overwhelming your system,” he says.

Agostino suggests starting with a gentle recline, like 20 to 25 degrees for 30 to 45 seconds and see how you feel. “If you feel comfortable and don't experience dizziness, increased pain, or other symptoms, you can gradually increase the time or angle over future sessions,” he says. Agostino recommends only changing one variable at a time—angle and inversion time—to ease yourself in. “You don't need to go farther upside down and stay there longer all at once,” he says.

When you’re inverted, you may feel a pressure sensation in your head or a mild “head rush,” Agostino says. “When your head is positioned below your heart, blood pressure and pressure within the eyes can increase, which is one reason inversion feels very different from simply lying flat,” he explains. You might also feel a feeling of fullness in your head or facial pressure. “Those sensations should remain mild and should resolve when you return upright,” according to Agostino.

Agostino points out that you don’t get a trophy for going completely upside down. “If a smaller angle provides the stretch or relief you're looking for, there may be no reason to progress to a full inversion,” he says.

Safety is paramount when shopping for an inversion table. "It’s ideal to find a product with comfortable ankle straps and safety locks to keep you secure and in place," says Kushagra Verma, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center. You also want to make sure the table can be controlled and manipulated by the user if you plan to use the device alone. Inversion tables should be used with caution, especially if you’re a beginner, says Rahul Shah, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine and neck surgeon at Premier Orthopaedic Associates. Additionally, older adults and those who have chronic dizziness, high blood pressure, glaucoma, inner ear problems, heart disease, and/or severe injuries should avoid inversion tables without talking to their doctor first, he says. Keep this in mind, too, per Agostino: “A little pressure may be expected. Feeling like something is wrong is not something you need to train yourself to tolerate.” If it feels like your back pain is worsening, or if you develop new numbness, tingling, weakness, or radiating pain, Agostino recommends that you stop using the inversion tale.

Sturdiness and durability are crucial for preventing accidents or instability while you’re upside down, Dr. Verma says. He recommends always looking for a product made with high-quality materials, such as stainless steel, to provide better support and longevity. Be sure to read customer reviews and seek expert opinions on the machine's sturdiness when shopping. Of course, all the selections on our list have been vetted in this way.

In addition to safety features, all experts agree that it’s crucial to consider how much weight an inversion table can safely hold. (The machine should clearly state this in the product description.) Because the machine puts you in a rather compromising position, maximum weight capacity is key for keeping you safe and at ease, Dr. Shah says. Going over the weight capacity raises the odds that the table will break or flip while you’re on it, potentially injuring you in the process, Agostino says.

It’s important to consider the table's length to ensure it accommodates your size and height, says Ali Mesiwala, MD, a neurosurgeon and complex spine expert at DISC Sports and Spine Center. Most inversion tables are adjustable for a customized fit, but it’s best to ensure the maximum height is within your range for effective use. The width of the table is another key factor, as a wider table can offer more stability during inversion, particularly if you’re on the taller or heavier side, says Brian Wallace, DC, a chiropractor at Pinewood Family Care. As a general rule of thumb, the width of the table should be wide enough for your core to conformably fit and not fall to either side, Dr. Shah adds.

Depending on your needs, different inversion tables include add-on features like lumbar spine support, heat, memory foam, or massage elements, Dr. Wallace says. These extra features are not a necessity, but they can be beneficial if you’re looking for added comfort and therapeutic benefits, he says. Just remember: extra add-ons should be considered second to the table's fundamental stability, comfort, and safety.

An inversion table isn’t the cheapest tool you’ll use to reduce your back pain, but there is a range to consider. Most tables will run you anywhere from $150 to $450, with higher-priced models having additional features like heat, memory foam, and massage.

To track down the best inversion tables, Men’s Health editors, including contributor Korin Miller, consulted three orthopedic surgeons, a neurosurgeon, a chiropractor, and two physical therapists to learn more about the important features to look for in an inversion table. From there, we looked at the most popular inversion tables on the market and narrowed the field based on our experts’ requirements. Each inversion table was ranked based on factors such as size, weight capacity, and safety features. This story was first published in August, and was updated in November to reflect the most recent products on the market, along with advice on how to use these machines.

Extended inversion can cause excessive blood flow to the head and lead to nausea, vomiting, and dizziness, so Dr. Mesiwala recommends using an inversion table for a maximum of five minutes at a time, up to twice a day. If you’re a beginner, he suggests only inverting for 30 seconds once a day as you get your bearings.

The best time to use an inversion table is typically when your muscles are relaxed, such as after a workout at the end of the day, says Dr. Wallace. Remember: You should not be inverted for long periods, and it’s best to start slowly and work your way up to time and frequency.

This is ultimately up to you. Some people feel comfortable with their arms by their sides or crossed over their chest, while others prefer to stretch them overhead. You can also put your arms on the support bars. Essentially, you should do whatever feels comfortable to you.

#4710. Tesla Cybertruck had its best month in over a year. It’s still going away

New EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.

Across all new vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.

EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October. That’s up from 10.3% a year earlier and well above October’s industrywide average of 6.8%.

Tesla’s average selling price fell from September to $54,194, but it was still up 1.2% year over year. The Cybertruck helped push that average higher. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 1,914 Cybertrucks in October, its best month in more than a year, at an average price of $92,380.

The sad thing is that there likely is a market for an affordable electric pickup truck in the U.S. to compete with Ford’s F150 and others. The Ford Fathom may be the best fit for that market, now.

That sales bump comes as Tesla prepares to end Cybertruck production at its Austin factory in mid-2027. Elon Musk said Tesla will dismantle the assembly line around June or July to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis.

#4709. The Best Hoka Walking Shoes In 2026, Tested By Podiatrists and Editors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There are many perks of being a Women’s Health style writer, and testing comfortable sneakers for work ranks very high on the list. My days are basically a rotation of steps—commutes, errands, long walks in the name of journalism—which means I’ve become extremely picky about what earns a spot on my feet. But time after time, I keep coming back to Hoka, aka the King of Cushion.

Since the brand launched in 2009, Hoka has perfected the balance between support and comfort (the number one feature in a walking shoe), says podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City.

Hoka has not only asserted itself as a top contender in the sneaker scene, but the brand has also become a style statement, too, making ortho-looking shoes look cool with their plush cushioning. The brand churns out a bunch of styles for all sorts of activities, from running shoes to hiking boots, but Hoka’s walking shoes are some of my favorites. I get that combing through all the specs can get overwhelming, so luckily, I’ve done the legwork for you by testing and walking in Hoka sneaks for the past two years. Plus, I enlisted the help of Schaeffer and other WH editors to get the scoop on the right shoes for you.

After testing nearly every Hoka model, the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning that gives me a spring in my step.

The first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly more narrow, too, but I actually preferred the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

Despite its lighter weight, it has an ample stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

I also found that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

So far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the new Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review

Technically, the Mach 7 is a running shoe—but don’t let that marketing label fool you. The previous iteration, the Mach 6, took home our 2025 Fitness Award for top walking shoe thanks to its blend of responsive cushioning, breathability, and lightweight construction—and the Mach 7 has built on that winning formula with an updated outer and grippier bottom. I’ve walked more than 150 miles in the ultra-light, ridiculously comfortable sneaker, and not once have I felt even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

The midsole is stiff yet flexible, while the cushioning is relatively low-key compared to its popular sibling, the Bondi 9. But, its slimness is an illusion. In fact, it’s just as supportive as most Hoka models and still offers a spring-like sensation after your foot hits the ground for a comfortable stride. This style doesn’t offer any special stability features for people whose feet tend to roll while walking, but I found it still does a decent job of keeping my feet in a neutral position, despite my high arches and tendency to underpronate (or land on the outer edge of my feet).

I wear the standard size and haven’t had any issues, but Accardi prefers the wide sizing, which she finds more suitable for her bunions and ability to spread her toes. If you have similar foot concerns or just like more wiggle room, we definitely recommend the wide fit.

While our one complaint with the Mach 6 was its lack of traction, I thankfully found that the Mach 7 features a more durable rubber at the heel and a stickier rubber up front, which makes a noticeable difference in grip.

Thanks to its incredible support and cushioning, the Gaviota 6 keeps my feet pain-free even after miles of wear. The shoe is designed with Hoka’s signature H-frame, which is a firm, dense foam in the midsole that provides a stable base to really lock your feet in place. I recently discovered that I have high arches, causing my ankles to roll inward when I walk, so this shoe has been a game-changer for me and my recent foot woes.

While the Gaviota 6 is geared toward flat arches on paper, I’m currently contending with a bit of foot fatigue from my new 1-mile-per-day (at least!) running goal, and the Gaviota 6 has given my dogs the TLC they need. That’s likely due to the combo of plush cushioning and stability tech. After weeks in the Gaviota 6, my gait naturally shifted from a heel strike to a midfoot strike—exactly what Schaeffer recommends for pain-free walking.

Other super supportive sneakers I’ve tried tend to have a stiff midsole. Not so with this shoe. It has a hefty EVA foam for a plush feel, like I’m walking on marshmallows. Plus, I found this foam also does a bang-up job of absorbing impact from my strides. In other words, it’s super easy on my joints. Bonus points: its fabric doesn’t rub at all, even when I’m wearing thin socks, which is a must-have when I’m clocking hundreds of miles in it.Weighing in at under nine ounces, the Gaviota 6 actually sheds half an ounce from the already lightweight Gaviota 5. I love that it feels lighter than it looks, but it still has a bulky look that may not vibe with everyone. FWIW, I love the chunky aesthetic and wear it with hiking gear, wide-leg trousers, and even casual dresses.

Plantar fasciitis (that painful inflammation under your arch) demands serious support, and the Hoka Bondi 9 delivers. It’s the brand’s plushest model, with cushioning that feels soft yet springy like you’re walking on clouds.

“I’ve been struggling with plantar fasciitis after months of half-marathon training, and this shoe—along with daily leg stretches—got me through long-haul walks pain-free,” says Accardi. That’s thanks to the Bondi’s plush underfoot cushioning and generous stack height. Schaeffer also recommends this shoe to his clients with plantar fasciitis, and says it provides a nice mix of cushion and stability. I also supinate and found that the Bondi 9’s premium foam midsole keeps my feet in a neutral position.

Contributor Lily Wohlner is also a mega-fan of this shoe. She's logged 15 miles walking in it and even wore it to the office to see how it holds up during long days on her feet. The verdict? It's the most comfortable shoe she owns, and she can wear it all day long without an ounce of foot pain.

Compared to the last iteration, this pair looks less bulky and feels lighter, and our style team found that this streamlined aesthetic plays nicer with most casual fits. However, be aware the shoe runs a tad narrow. Ritchey says she doesn’t have particularly wide feet, but that the toe box is a bit too small. She walked over 17 miles in this shoe recently and started to blister slightly in her pinky toes.

“The Arahi 8 has become my absolute companion running and walking shoe ever since I started bouncing back from my stress fracture,” Accardi says. “My podiatrist said I needed something firm and supportive—too much squish and flex could cause my feet to roll and exacerbate my injury—and the Arahi delivered.” Don’t let the sturdy midsole fool you: It’s relatively comfy for a stability shoe, with just enough give to keep things feeling smooth. Compared to the Arahi 7, this version hugs the foot better and offers noticeably more bounce-back with every step. It’s got that sweet spot of stability and responsiveness.

Fitness editor Cori Ritchey is a huge fan of the shoe’s “well-balanced cushioning,” saying that it feels plush underfoot but didn’t affect her stability while walking long distances or running. She loves that the toe box on the Arahi 8 is a bit wider than the Bondi 9, giving her plenty of room to spread her toes. But, if you are into plush, cloud-like cushioning, you may want to stick with the Bondi’s. The Arahi doesn’t have that marshmallow-like softness—it’s much firmer.

One of its standout features is the integrated H-frame support system: Strategically placed firmer foam that wraps around the sides of your foot to guide your stride and keep your foot in a neutral position. You can definitely feel the structure working, but the payoff in stability is huge, especially if you’re recovering, need extra support, or just want something you can rely on to keep your form in check.

As someone who never reties her shoe laces (I always slip my sneakers on), the Hoka Transport originally caught my eye with its toggle lace system that eliminates the hassle of tying and untying.

It reminds me of my favorite Salomon XT-6 shoes and has a cool granola-girl vibe—which makes sense, since it is technically a hiking shoe. However, I will admit that while the Transport 2 looks very similar to the original, I prefer the sleeker look of the previous iteration. This version is also slightly heavier, but it’s barely noticeable while walking, and I chalk it up to the slight increase in cushioning.

This shoe has quite a bit of cushion, but I found the midsole to be a bit on the stiffer side, meaning you just might want to plan for a longer break-in period before wearing it on long walks right off the bat. On the flip side, the firmness makes for a stable stride. It’s also great for neutral arches since it's not designed with any specific stability features in mind. But even with my slightly high arches, I felt locked in with every step.

Thanks to the high-traction, chunky outsole, I feel stable during trail walks across gravel, sandy paths, and uneven terrain. I also like that the outer shell material is Cordura, a water and abrasion-resistant mesh that’s built to prevent scuffs and withstand wear and tear.

One thing to note: I went with the standard width, and the fit is a bit snug, especially with thicker socks. If you have wider feet, consider sizing up or opting for the wide version.

Hoka is known for its incredibly cushioned sneakers, but extreme cushioning is not always the best for keeping feet stable. In recent years, Hoka has leveled up their offering with more stability options, but the right pick depends on how your foot moves. If your stride is balanced, go for a neutral shoe like the Clifton or Bondi. These models provide cushioning and support without changing your natural gait.

If your foot tends to roll inward (aka overpronation) or outwards (supination), a stability Hoka shoe like the Arahi or Gaviota features extra structure along the arch and heel to keep your feet aligned and locked in. This lowers your risk of aches and injury.

A popular Hoka sneaker, like the Bondi or Clifton, has super-thick cushioning made of EVA foam that is rubber-like and incredibly durable. With each step, it compresses and provides a snappy bounce. Despite the Hokas’ bulky look, they’re all relatively lightweight at under 10 ounces—hefty enough to keep your foot locked in, but light enough not to bog you down. Plus, several Hoka styles feature a "rocker bottom," which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to the base of a rocking chair. That shape helps you to walk from heel to toe, which means you exert less energy to propel your strides.

Some Hoka sneakers are designed for specific arch types: flat, neutral, and high. For example, the Gaviota is designed with flat feet in mind; the Clifton is designed for neutral arches; and the Bondi is suitable for high arches. If you’re unsure of your arch type, a simple test is to dip your foot into water and step onto a piece of paper. If you see your entire foot, it’s flat, while seeing half means it’s neutral. Seeing barely anything means you have a high arch.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer says to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

With their cloud-like cushioning, springy soles, and ample support, Hoka sneakers absorb impact from every step and keep feet locked in a neutral position. That makes them ideal for hot girl walks, a 12-3-30 walking workout, and taking your pup for a leisurely stroll.

Topping the list is the Hoka Clifton 11. I love the super supportive, plush midsole that keeps my feet from rolling and feels ultra-flexible. A close second is the Hoka Mach 7, our runner-up that’s technically a running shoe but totally crushes it for walking, too. It’s light, bouncy, and built for those who like to switch up their stride

Over the past two years, I’ve been testing Hoka sneakers alongside my team for a comprehensive approach to the best walking shoes for every foot type and stride. Women’s Health editors have been testing Hoka sneakers since the brand launched in 2009. For this update, I tested the updated models alongside WH fitness editor Cori Ritchey and fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi. Along with Schaeffer’s insights, I evaluated each for its cushioning, stability, and arch type.

#4708. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

THE SECRET TO training your abs is out—and it entails more than situps and planks, more than just targeting your rectus abdominis, the ballyhooed band of muscle between your chest and your hips. If you want true core strength (and, yes, that six-pack), a growing group of experts will tell you that you need to carry heavy weights and walk. This forces your core to constantly microcorrect and rebalance as you move, explains Aaron Horschig, C.S.C.S., D.P.T., a St. Louis–based physical therapist. You also need to twist and turn, challenging your oblique muscles and back extensors.

“While there’s nothing wrong with training the abs for show, training for stability—which encompasses all of the muscles that surround the spine and hips—is essential training for everyone,” says Horschig. His new book, Rebuilding Milo, includes a variety of exercises, many of which challenge your entire core—think lower back extensors, glutes, and obliques, which all team up with your abs to stabilize and bolster your back, lending postural support.

Unlike body parts that handle just one or two tasks (like your biceps, which are most heavily utilized to bend your elbows), all those core muscles have a host of responsibilities. They work together to flex your spine (as happens during a classic situp), and they help rotate your shoulders so you can turn to look at a friend. They also prevent excessive rounding of the lower back (known as anti-flexion), a key tactic in the battle to stop back pain. The ideal abs regimen trains all these functions, protecting you against injuries and readying your core (and spine) for anything life can throw at you. Horschig says people finally get that. “More and more people are starting to understand the true role of core,” he says.

The end result of all this work? A lower back that’s armor-plated against persistent pain, and the ability to move athletically and fluidly. And along the way, you’ll build those six-pack abs, too.

HOW TO DO IT:An underrated plank upgrade, this move challenges your abs and obliques (and your glutes, too!). Start in pushup position, feet wide. Lift your left hand and touch it to your right shoulder. Keep your hips square as you do. Repeat on the other side.

REPS & SETS:Work for time, not reps, doing three 40-second sets.

HOW TO DO IT:Stand in a split stance, left shoulder next to the high pulley of a cable machine, both hands grasping the handle, then bend at the knees until your left thigh is nearly parallel to the floor. Keep your hips square to the front as you pull the cable across your body, then return it to the start.

REPS & SETS:Do 10 to 12 reps per side. Do 3 sets.

HOW TO DO IT:Stand holding kettlebells in both hands, the left bell at your chest, the right bell at your hip. Walk forward (or march in place) for 10 to 15 steps per leg. Move slowly, working to keep your hips square.

REPS & SETS:Do 2 sets per side, challenging your abs and lower-back muscles to keep you upright against the heavy load.

TRAIN YOUR ABS EVERYDAY. Some muscle groups require several days to recover, but your core muscles are built to be resilient. That means you can train them nearly every day. Consider doing 3 or 4 sets of core work in every work- out, rotating in new and different ab exercises to continually challenge your rectus abdominis, oblique muscles, and lower-back spinal erectors.

NEVER GOING HEAVY. Bodyweight planks and situps are a solid starting point for your ab training. But just like any other muscle, core muscles are meant to be loaded and overloaded. Add resistance to your core training, and don’t be afraid to challenge yourself, especially on moves like the mixed-rack carry above. “You have to do that sometimes,” says the popular bodybuilder and trainer known as Ulisses Jr. “I’d be lying if I told you I didn’t load my abs.”

#4705. The Best Our Legacy Camion Boot Alternatives, According to Style Editors

AHEAD OF THE fall, I knew I was going to need a sickening boot that could just fall in line with my entire wardrobe. I don’t spend much on clothes, because, well, I wear-test them for a living, but when it comes to shopping for footwear I’ve been guilty of dropping more bread than I’d like to admit. There are times I don’t mind dishing out a little cash for a well-made shoe, especially if that means I’ll have it for years to come. One style that was calling my name that I couldn’t resist was Our Legacy’s Camion Boot.

If you’ve spent any time scrolling through men’s fashion content on Instagram or TikTok, chances are you’ve come across it. Even actor Paul Mescal has been spotted wearing the boot during a press tour for “Hamnet” in London. The sleek leather ankle-high boot has become something of a cult favorite among stylish guys, thanks to its distinctive square toe and minimalist design, which helps make any simple outfit look 10 times cooler. Whether I’m wearing baggy jeans or relaxed trousers, The Camion Boot adds a certain je ne sais quoi that my cowboy or lace-up boots can’t replicate. And by no means does the boot feel squishy like your favorite pair of sneakers, but the Vibram rubber outsole keeps my feet comfortable on days when I'm standing and walking around for hours.

For those unfamiliar, Our Legacy is a Swedish fashion label founded in Stockholm in 2005. Over the past two decades, the brand has built a loyal following for taking menswear staples and remixing them with unique proportions, fabrics, and details. The Camion Boot is one of its most recognizable designs, decorated with an inside zip closure and a metal branded tab. It feels timeless without looking boring. Even though it’s easy on the eyes, its $700-plus price tag is tough on the wallet. Luckily, you don’t have to cough up designer money to get the look. Below, I’ve gathered a list of affordable alternatives that deliver the same vibe for a fraction of the price.

If you’re looking for a boot that captures the sleek appeal of Our Legacy’s Camion without spending a small fortune, Florsheim’s Medford is a strong contender. The leather upper has a subtle burnished finish that delivers a slightly worn-in look, as the clean silhouette makes it easy to dress up or down. I’d pair the brown version with black denim and a chunky sweater for dinner followed by a night out. It also looks sharp with dressy pants and tailored trousers, so you can get plenty of mileage out of it at the office.

Inside, there’s a fully cushioned, removable footbed made with OrthoLite rebound foam, which helps absorb impact and provides a little extra bounce underfoot. This comes in handy if you’re spending hours on your feet. The leather is also designed to feel comfortable from the jump, so you shouldn’t have to suffer through a lengthy break-in period. And while I wouldn’t treat these like rain boots, the leather construction makes them a practical choice for everyday wear, especially with proper care. You don’t have to settle for a black colorway either—it comes in a few different brown shades as well.

Zara offers a squared-off toe that is unapologetically bold, giving the boot that exaggerated, fashion-forward shape that makes Our Legacy’s Camion so recognizable. I’d argue the toe is even more pronounced here, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing if you want your footwear to stand out more. I’d style these with relaxed jeans that fall just over the shaft or wide-leg trousers to really lean into the silhouette.

The biggest difference comes down to the material. Unlike the Camion, Zara’s version is made from polyurethane, a synthetic material that mimics the appearance of leather, so it’s a budget-friendly pick. It’s generally easy to wipe clean, but it won’t develop the same natural patina as genuine leather and can eventually peel or crack with repeated wear.

Steve Madden’s Ronco might be the closest style to the Camion boot as far as design is concerned. It nailed the features from the stitched detailing across the upper right down to the substantial rubber sole. The latter is worth pointing out because it gives the boot a similar sturdy, grounded appearance, while the 1.5-inch heel adds just enough height without going overboard. Sure, the rounded toe isn’t quite as boxy as the Camion’s signature square shape, but the overall silhouette comes pretty darn close. And at a fraction of the price, it’s hard not to appreciate the resemblance.

I’m especially drawn to the brown leather version, which has a rich, burnished finish that shifts between lighter and darker shades, giving it a slightly weathered, vintage effect. It has a lot more depth than your standard brown boot. I’d pair these with relaxed denim and a chunky sweater for an easy apple-picking look, or throw them on with tailored trousers and a leather jacket for something a little sharper. There’s also a black option if you prefer to keep things simple.

Banana Republic takes a different approach with this Italian leather Chelsea-style boot. The silhouette is sleek and understated, but what really caught my attention is the leather’s distressed finish. It has that subtly weathered, almost cracked appearance you’d normally expect from a well-loved pair of boots, except the detail is already built into the design. It gives the shoe a vintage feel without looking like something that’s been sitting in the back of your closet for a decade. I also appreciate that this pair doesn’t try too hard to replicate the Camion. Instead, it offers a more classic interpretation that feels right at home with the rest of my wardrobe. I’d wear it with pleated trousers and a button-down for the office, then swap in straight-leg jeans and a crewneck for a day of shopping.

Camper has a knack for taking classic footwear and giving it a slightly unexpected twist, which perfectly describes the Dean Boot. The black-and-burgundy color combination immediately caught my attention because it’s subtle enough to wear with anything, but there’s also a richness to the pebbled leather texture that makes it more interesting than your standard black ankle boot. I’d pair these with relaxed black trousers or dark denim and let the boots bring a little personality to the outfit.

The upper combines calfskin leather with recycled PET, which is plastic recycled from materials like water bottles, and latex for added flexibility. Underfoot, there’s a removable OrthoLite footbed for cushioning and an XL Extralight EVA outsole, a lightweight foam-based material designed to absorb impact without weighing you down. I also appreciate the pull tab, which makes slipping them on a little easier, especially since there’s no traditional side zipper. Plus, the defined heel and outsole design offer some stability for walking, though actual traction will depend on the surface.

I’ve owned my Frye boots for about a year now, and they’ve more than earned their place in my footwear rotation. They’re so versatile, I can wear them with a suit one day and jeans, a T-shirt, and leather jacket the next. The design is minimal with a premium leather upper and stitching around the edge that adds to the sturdy construction. Comfort-wise, I didn’t have to deal with that annoying break-in period that often comes with leather boots.

After a year of wear, the leather has started developing some natural creases, but I look at it like it adds character. There’s enough wiggle room in the toe box that my feet don’t feel cramped. The inner side zipper is another detail I’ve come to appreciate, especially when I’m taking them off after a long day. I’ve put these through their paces on city streets and even worn them in the rain. I found the leather has dried quickly after getting wet, and the grip has felt secure underfoot. Sure, they’re not cheap, but considering how well they’ve held up and how often I wear them, I’d say I’ve already gotten my money’s worth.

If you’re a guy who gets suited up more often than not, Suitsupply’s leather boot deserves a spot on your radar. It’s the dressiest option on this list, with a smooth, semi-matte leather, which catches just enough light to look sharp without being overly shiny. It also has a fine, tight grain, which gives the surface a supple finish. I’d wear these with a charcoal suit or tailored black trousers and a crisp button-down, for a holiday party. But I would also style them with dark denim and a cashmere sweater. The side zipper makes getting dressed a little less of a production in the morning. The leather sole adds to that dress-shoe appeal, although I’d be a little more cautious wearing these on slick pavement.

Now, these are the most expensive boots on this list, but because they’re made in Italy using Blake-stitched construction, a technique that stitches the upper directly to the sole for a slimmer, more flexible profile than you’d typically get with bulkier boot construction. You can expect some natural creasing after a few wears, particularly where your foot bends, but that doesn’t mean the leather is cracking.

To keep it from drying out, Suitsupply recommends applying shoe polish at least once a month, or more frequently if you’re wearing them daily. This helps maintain the color and adds some protection against moisture. I’d also work in a leather conditioner whenever the material starts feeling dry to help prevent actual cracking. It’s a little extra maintenance, sure, but worthwhile if you’re investing this much in a pair of boots.
