#4665. Ray Nicholson Is Smiling Through It All

At 34, the ascending actor has finally found his own lane—and learned to (maybe) stop comparing himself to his famous father.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

This article was featured in MH Flex, our monthly newsletter recommending the one in-depth interview you need to flex your pop culture knowledge. Sign up here to get it first.

“I’M RUNNING PURELY off of fumes and caffeine,” Ray Nicholson says, with a glimmer in his eye and the end of his mouth curled into a slight grin. He points to a half-finished iced coffee sitting in front of him and nods his head. “It’s good.”

That grin, it turns out, is a weapon. It’s a smile that, somehow, employs both his dimples and furrowed brow just as much as his mouth and teeth. It’s the kind of smile that stops you in your tracks when he flashes it in the middle of a sentence. It’s also got a kill count on-screen, evoking something different in each context. Whether he’s cutting the tension in a war drama, like in his latest movie, Netflix’s The Mosquito Bowl; or making single frames into nightmares, as in Smile 2; or playing an unhinged stalker in Borderline or an unstable boyfriend in I Love You Forever—it’s clear Nicholson knows what he’s doing with that thing.

It’s also a familiar grin, because it’s virtually identical to a rather iconic one: that of his father, Jack Nicholson, whose smile has been on display in timeless performances in movies like The Shining and One Flew over the Cuckoo’s Nest. You know the smile I’m talking about.

And today? Nicholson the younger is putting that grin to a new use: namely, masking whatever else is going on inside as he glugs away at that coffee and tries to make it through a couple of grueling days of press, press, press. “It’s somewhere between hypnosis, interrogation, and a Miss America pageant,” he says with a laugh, as the smile flashes again.

The Mosquito Bowl, which comes from director Peter Berg (Friday Night Lights, Lone Survivor), follows a group of soldiers whose college football rivalries evolve into a close-knit brotherhood on the World War II battlefield. It’s based on the true story of a football game (the titular Mosquito Bowl) that was actually played. The film is based on a book of the same name by Friday Night Lights author Buzz Bissinger.

If Nicholson is tired, one would never know. It’s not just the smile, though of course that doesn’t hurt. To me, he seems excited, unafraid of diving into stories about filming The Mosquito Bowl in Australia and bonding with costars Bill Skarsgård, Nicholas Galitzine, and Tom Francis over hours of daily football and military drill training.

This all feels like a natural fit for Nicholson, who played football in high school and planned to play at Boston College until a run-in with MRSA cut that dream short. His performance and his relationship with his costars make the movie. But there’s more than that. In his career thus far—and in our conversation—Nicholson has proved himself as someone who’s got a certain type of charisma that pops off the screen, an inherently watchable face, a screen presence that simply can’t be taught. It’s almost as if it’s in his genes.

MEN’S HEALTH: You have a penchant for playing very intense roles. Why do you think that is?

RAY NICHOLSON: It’s interesting. As a young actor… It’s sort of what you get. You know what I mean? I guess I have an intense face. I guess I’m intense. But ultimately, the challenge of becoming an artist is learning how to put 100 percent of your heart and soul into something and not leave anything behind. That’s the only way I feel comfortable on camera, and that’s the joy of doing it. I find fulfillment in that hole in the soul when I have that intensity. The mundane is more difficult for me; I’m trying to learn how to enjoy that.

MH: Your character, Tony, in The Mosquito Bowl, is a normal guy, more or less, but he’s in this extraordinary situation. Did it feel like a bit of fresh air to get to take on that kind of role compared to something like Smile 2, for example?

RN: Yeah. On Smile 2, I was very much a day player. But it never really shifts. Ultimately, I’m there to be of service. Especially in Smile 2, Naomi [Scott] is acting her ass off all day, and they might have three seconds for one shot I’m doing all day, and I might have been there for 14 hours, but it doesn’t matter. I’m there for a day, and just to be there and be good vibes.

But this, we were there every single day. I’m glad I learned so much from Pete and Bill. As an artist, as a human being, I learned how to have grace with the cards I was dealt. I was dealt very beautiful cards, but you can play a good hand very poorly. I think I’ve finally found grace with my circumstance.

MH: Did shooting on location in Australia help you feel immersed?

RN: For sure. We were all away from family—all we had was each other. Which was really beautiful and a challenge, but exactly what it needed. And when you get a script like that, all that brotherhood is baked in and then all you need is buy-in. And we fell in love with each other. Me, Tom, and Bill, we’ve traveled the world. We went to the African World Cup final. They’re my best friends. I think about them every day. It’s amazing to think I didn’t know them before this, and now they’re people I think of every single day. We shot all outdoors, all sequentially, in order.

RN: Insanely rare. It’s insanely rare, because it makes it so much easier. I know how I felt, because I did it yesterday.

MH: Can you tell me about your relationship with football? Obviously, it makes sense with this movie.

RN: The first sport I played was basketball. I grew up a really chubby kid. I was not cool. And my sister was the most popular, beautiful girl in elementary school, and I was the fat nerdy brother that liked Yu-Gi-Oh! and whatever.

RN: Yu-Gi-Oh! was sick, objectively. And I played Pokémon. When I was about 9 years old, I was really overweight, so I found AAU basketball. I remember my first practice, I was jogging around and I literally tripped over half court and these guys picked me up. That was the first time I felt something like that. Then, when I got a little bit older, I played Pop Warner. And, once again, I was a bit chubbier, but I was fast and I had a good arm. I wanted to play quarterback, they wanted me to play offensive line. And then I became this chubby Michael Vick, trucking other kids [Laughs]. Kind of a beast. And that was the first time I felt confident.

RN: I’m confident between these lines. And I could be angry. My anger was always so self-directed. I had so much shame. That was the first place I was like, “Ah, I can express this.” That’s a really important thing for kids.

I was very happy, a reporter in one of my Zoom interviews was like, “You averaged 8.94 yards a carry. You want to tell them what that means?” I was like, “That means I was fucking good!” [Laughs]

RN: It was the first thing that gave me confidence, and you have that feeling of family. And you have that tough love. You have this love through discipline and through pain, but that’s the love between men. That was so important to me, and that saved my life. It came into my life exactly when I needed it, and I really struggled when I lost it. I got a staph infection that turned into MRSA. My arm was so inflamed, they drew a line on my arm and were like, “If the infection gets past here [points to biceps], we’re cutting your arm off.” I lost 50 pounds in a week.

RN: My senior year of high school. I thought I was going to go to Boston College and play football. Not on scholarship, but I went to the camp and they were like, “You could be a deferred walk-on,” or whatever. I thought I was going to be like Jerry Maguire—that’s what I wanted to do. I came out of this semi-comatose thing and I was like, “I want to be an actor. I’m just so scared. I’m just so fucking scared.” And then I just slowly dipped my toe in. I’m glad everything’s happening now, because I have the head on my shoulders to handle it.

MH: You went through something really tough.

RN: Yeah. If I was a kid, I don’t even know if I would be alive, to be honest with you. I’m so grateful that it happened on a bigger plan than on mine. A lot of the things I was originally attracted to would coil like a flame hat now. It’s all a big blessing.

MH: What was it like working with Peter Berg?

RN: Bill and I are used to growing up with eccentric men, you know what I mean? We kind of understand it. It’s one of those things where, with eccentric men, it requires you to butt heads and be like, “I didn't like that, but I like you.” You know what I mean? Bill’s always like, “You’re Pete’s favorite son. You guys fight, but he loves you the most.” We really had this familial thing. Bill was the older brother, Nick and I were the middle brothers, and Tom was the little brother.

We all worked so hard, and we wanted to fight for what was best. I really respect Pete. I love him as a filmmaker. I love him as a man. I really respect him as a leader, because you’re going to meet him exactly where he’s at. And I respect that. I think conflict is where art is made. We’re too conflict averse, and I really admire Pete for his style and his honesty.

MH: When you’ve gone through this kind of experience, how do you come down afterward when it’s time to go home?

RN: There’s this mourning process. The last week of filming, we were all crying. The cast was crying, the crew was crying, makeup was crying. It was really intense. And we fell in love with the experience and we fell in love with each other. Before Bill met us, he went to Okinawa. And he actually took a charcoal etching of the gravestones of Tony Butkovich, Bob Bauman, and Dave Schreiner, and he gave them to us on the last day. And we all were tearing up and we wrote a letter to each other and to the men that we played. I think part of it was you have to let go.

It took me a while to go home—I didn’t go straight home. Me and Tom went to Sydney and just hung out at the beach with some friends we had made there. We went to go see Oasis.

RN: For sure. But also, it’s like you have this fear of do we really love each other or were we just working on this project? It’s been really cool in the months since we started shooting to see how our relationships have developed. We’ll always have The Mosquito Bowl.

RN: It just took a while for me to get home. I really relish being alone. I really needed time to reset. I went through a breakup right when I got home. I almost took six months off, not even looking for a job. I finished writing the script I wanted to do, but I really just took some time. I always have to take time to be like, “What am I if I’m not acting?” And that’s a hard thing.

MH: What was your wake-up point of, like, “Okay, time to get back to it”?

RN: I finished that script and I was like, “Well, I’m not a writer!” I’m really proud of what I did, but I think it was just like, “Oh.” We were getting closer to press, and I was like, “Oh, geez.” Like, “Oh god, should I have done a job already?”

MH: And what’s it like at this stage in the process?

RN: Going into press, Bill and I were like, “We’re not going to see the final cut. We’re promoting purely on good vibes. We’ve fucking got this.” And we watched it during the premiere, and I cried. I was so happy. I was so proud of how it turned out.

We were talking about feeling like frauds. I think if someone handed me a script and was like, “Here, you play Ray Nicholson,” I’d be like, “You could probably find somebody better.” There’s always that fraudulent thing, and we all feel it, and that’s the beauty of it. It comes and goes. Now I feel a little bit better about what’s coming next, because I feel really proud of this movie.

RN: I look forward to more opportunities with more filmmakers I love and respect. I also operate from a place of faith that the right thing will come.My dad’s my hero. I think he’s magic. I love him more than anything. When I was first doing a Meisner exercise and you’re knocking, coming through the door, I was comparing myself to, Is that worthy of three Oscars and a 50-year career? So much of my practice has just been learning to be present. And so now I have less moments when I’m in my car driving, crying, thinking about I’m getting an Oscar, and my dad... And that’s a good thing. I’ve just gotten way more present about it.

I’m also open to the idea that this might not be right for me. The world might take me in another direction. I was really closed off to that before. Because I thought that if I didn’t do something, I was unworthy of my life. I think a lot of that is just therapy. And I’m finding the real joy in it.

I lost football and I was really lost in my life, and I didn’t know what to do. Acting has slowly become the thing that saves my life. It’s not only what gives me a purpose, but it’s the tool I meet myself with. I don’t know who the hell I am. I don’t really remember anything from my life. And then somehow, when I read a script, I’m like, “Oh, that is you.” When I first started, I didn’t really have those kind of goals. I don’t want to say because it’s bullshit, but that’s the industry. That’s beautiful, and I love the industry, but I’m more focused on how I approach every day.

RN: That was the key thing, and that’s all personal life stuff. But the key is being of service, and I believe that ultimately, I’m in the service industry. When I think about my dad, he makes me smile every time I see him on-screen. I want some kid somewhere to smile every time he sees me.

MH: Last question. Do you have a favorite or most rewatched movie of your dad’s?

RN: It’s tough. I’m a sucker. It’s like every PTA or Kubrick movie you watch, you’re like, “That’s my favorite.” I didn’t watch my dad’s movies until I was 18. I love Cuckoo’s Nest. I love The Shining. I always come back to The Last Detail. For some reason, I really fucking love that movie. I think it’s because he loves it so much and he’s like, “It’s underappreciated.” So I’m like, “But I love it, Dad!” I love watching his movies. It’s a cool thing, and I want my kid to watch my movies someday.

RN: I just want to make people happy and smile. And break their hearts a little bit.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#4664. 7 Running Shorts for Women That WH Editors Love

Editor-tested picks built for comfort, pockets, and sweat control.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s nothing more humiliating than having a huge sweat stain on your butt after strenuous mile repeats—been there, done that. A good run is supposed to lift your mood, not bring you down, so finding the best running shorts to keep the endorphins flowing (and your butt dry) is essential.

Not all workout shorts are made the same. Some offer more compression, while others are less restrictive and have convenient features like pockets—the holy grail! “You need a place to carry all your resources—pockets are a non-negotiable for running gels, electrolytes, phone, wallet, and keys,” says New York-based running coach and personal trainer Amanda Katz, NASM-CPT.

While many athletic shorts can be used for different purposes, running shorts usually have a built-in interior liner, sweat-wicking material, and a nonconstrictive design to keep you cool and comfortable as you rack up mileage in your sleek running shoes.

I researched and gathered the best running shorts from a running coach and editors who’ve personally tested them. Whether you’re training for a marathon or are a hobby jogger, all the shorts I picked are from trusted activewear and athleisure brands that will benefit you in the long run (literally). Ready to find out more about the best running shorts for women? Keep scrolling.

After testing countless pairs of running shorts over the years, the Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short from Lululemon is my fave for its sweat-wicking fabric and comfortable fit. The polyester blend wicks away sweat, prevents cling, and promotes airflow while running. The loose, flowy fit keeps me cool, while a built-in interior liner adds lightweight coverage and support without bulk.

The side pockets are small, but hold small essentials like a credit card, key, or energy gels for long runs. The leg openings are spacious, allowing for a full range of motion, and an adjustable drawstring secures the waistband for a customizable fit. Want to hit the road at the crack of dawn or at night? No sweat; reflective detailing improves visibility in dark or dim light, making early morning or evening runs safer.

I appreciate the 4-inch length, given I prefer more coverage, but a 2.5-inch length is available if you prefer a shorter fit. WH associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, is also a fan of the fit and vast color palette. “They never ride up or move around, which is hard to find in a running short,” she says. With tons of colors and sizes to choose from, you can't go wrong.

New Balance is a top brand in the running world, and the RC Short is one of my faves. It runs slightly big, but I love the extra breathing room during a sweat session.

The lightweight, flowy construction uses the brand’s quick-drying tech fabric (a polyester and spandex blend) to wick moisture from the skin. The breathable design promotes tons of airflow, creating a cooling effect while I run—especially ideal during scorching hot summer runs.

The seamless, interior lining reduces chafing and irritation, while the waistband features an adjustable drawstring to customize the fit. It’s also not too tight—some liners can feel like you’re wearing a diaper (hate). As for storage, there’s a back pocket for securing small running essentials and even tiny snacks like a granola bar when you’re on the move.

A pair of high cut shorts, such as the Alo Match Point Short, is a running staple. The high-cut at the thighs keeps things perfectly airy and flowy for optimal coolness when I get overheated, more so than the Lululemon Hotty Hot Short.

This construction, paired with its moisture-wicking polyester fabric, creates the perfect breathable running shorts. While it’s a bit short at just over two inches, there’s still great coverage with a built-in brief, and I find it doesn’t show too much skin.

WH style contributor Lily Wolhner also appreciates this loose style for various workouts. “My favorite part about this short is that it’s never clingy, so it doesn’t ride up the thigh or need constant re-adjusting while you’re working out,” Wolhner says. “I’ve worn it for months and recently tested it during a 45-minute strength and HIIT workout, as well as an hour-long cross-training workout—I never felt over-exposed or uncomfortable in it.”

By the looks of the elastic waistband, I expected it to dig into my skin—wrong. It felt comfortable, although it’s important to note this short does run big, so I suggest sizing down.

We love a two-for-one, and this short from Brooks is ideal for both trail running and running at the gym. It has light compression with a built-in tight liner that doesn’t sacrifice mobility.

The mega-durable polyester fabric resists tears and moisture, which makes it ideal for trail running in tough terrain. “I love the high waist, the zipper pocket to carry my keys, and the tight shorts under a looser short aesthetic,” Katz says.

Two waistband pockets are impressively large and can even fit a water flask, so you can always stay hydrated during your jogs.

I personally don’t love compression-lined shorts because I like to feel totally free, but if you prefer extra coverage and double layers, this short is ideal.

If you want a no-frills pair of shorts at an affordable price point that will stand the test of time, the Under Armour Play Up 3.0 belongs in your running gear collection. I’ve owned multiple pairs for years in eye-catching colors, and they’re still in good condition with no pills—even after dozens of runs and wash cycles.

The lightweight knit fabric made from smooth polyester has an anti-pill finish for extra durability, and is impressively comfy. Plus, it hides embarrassing sweat stains post-run, despite the slightly thicker material.

The waistband uses a wide elastic band that provides a secure fit without any adjustable features. However, I find it still fits roomy and allows for a full range of motion.

It includes deep side pockets but no enclosure, so I don’t recommend stashing anything super important besides fuel, like energy gels. I wear it the most for shorter, mid-distance runs and whenever I want to add a pop of color—it has 21 color options!

I usually don’t gravitate toward compression shorts since I don’t like feeling constricted, but the Athleta Salutation Stash 5-Inch Short offers the perfect amount of tightness. It hugs my thighs with gentle compression, while the high-rise waistband distributes pressure evenly for a secure fit without digging in. Plus, the two deep side pockets offer convenient storage for longer runs.

The smooth, double-knit fabric is buttery-soft and offers great coverage. While on the thicker side, it conceals sweat stains well—a huge win during long-haul runs. I wouldn’t say it feels the most breathable compared to other shorts in this guide, but the nylon and lycra blend wicks away sweat and dries fast.

Another huge selling point? The fabric’s UPF 50 protection, which prevents UV radiation from scorching your thighs. This is my favorite feature as someone fair-skinned and prone to nasty sunburns (IYKYK). Aside from its fabric, I love that it has a matching jacket for a coordinated workout set.

Tracksmith’s Van Cortlandt Shorts combine retro styling with a performance-driven design that makes them a winner both on and off the track. It’s made from a lightweight mesh fabric to maximize airflow, paired with an antimicrobial finish to help combat odor by wicking away sweat and limiting bacteria buildup during intense runs.

After summer runs when I’m dripping with sweat, I noticed zero smell—and that the short dries at the speed of light.

Like our best overall, it’s quite short at 2.5 inches, so if you prefer a longer style, you should look to other styles in this guide. On the flip side, it doesn’t disrupt my range of motion during speed work or long runs. As for fit, I found it runs true to size, but make sure to consult the size chart as always.

Running shorts with sweat-wicking fabric are the way to go, Katz says. Most shorts use a blend of polyester, spandex, and/or nylon, which lifts moisture from the skin while staying flexible during movement. Based on testing, it’s best to avoid cotton since it doesn’t dry nearly as fast and clings to the skin when wet.

It’s important to determine what kind of rise and inseam you desire. High-waisted running shorts offer more coverage and tummy control, while a mid-rise waist sits right at the hips. Ultimately, what you find most flattering for your body type is the best option.

The inseam is the length from the crotch to the bottom. A longer length will show less skin but may disrupt the range of motion, while some running shorts favorites, like the Lululemon Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short, offer a 2.5-inch option if you like a mini fit.

As for an interior liner or compression, this will make running shorts fit more snugly. “Compression is a matter of preference, but the goal in this material is to boost recovery,” says Katz. If you want a less constrictive fit, it’s probably best to avoid that feature.

In addition to my own testing, Women’s Health associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT also extensively tested tons of running shorts to determine whether or not they’re the real deal. Each pair was worn during training runs or races for anywhere from three weeks to even three years to see how they performed and held up.

Essential features considered were materials, inseam, pockets, durability, and adjustability. Additionally, I asked a running coach for their go-to running shorts and guidance on how they should fit.

Nicolette Accardi is the Fitness Commerce Editor at Women’s Health with a specialty in running content and athleisure. She likes to chase her next best time by testing out shoes and other running gear, and styling her workout clothes as streetwear. She’s also a certified personal trainer through the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM). Nicolette studied journalism and health sociology at Rutgers University. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. #4661. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4660. The Best Fall Skincare Routine, According to Dermatologists

Your cold-weather glow starts with these expert-approved tweaks.

Aveeno has solved for that here, adding a calming concoction of niacinamide and the brand’s famed oat complex,” says beauty director Brian Underwood.

We’ve previously named this the best overall hyaluronic acid serum and Dr. Nazarian agrees. She appreciates that it boasts multiple forms of hyaluronic acid to enhance hydration, adding that it’s a great serum for layering with other products in your routine.

You can slather this budget-friendly moisturizer on your face and body. It earned snaps from Dr. Gohara, who points to the combination of glycerin to attract water and ceramides to support the skin barrier.

Pro tip from Dr. Gohara: Whether you use a lotion or a face cream, apply it to slightly damp skin.

For extra dryness, layer SkinMedica Barrier Calming Cream on top, advises Dr. Gohara. “Just as you double up on clothes, you can double up on moisturizer. Hydration first, a protective outer layer second,” she says. And that’s exactly what the Barrier Calming Cream does. It contains a nourishing blend of moisturizing glycerin, niacinamide to minimize skin inflammation, and calming oat kernel extract.

The experts I chatted with say eye cream is a totally optional step. You can technically get away with just using a plain face moisturizer under your eyes, says Dr. Nazarian. However, since the undereye skin is thinner and prone to dryness during colder months, a separate eye cream can be helpful for dealing with dryness, fine lines, or crepiness.

Lock in hydration with this lightweight face serum that doesn’t feel overly tacky on your skin.

Both Dr. Garshick and Dr. Nazarian suggest humectants such as glycerin and hyaluronic acid to attract water, plus skin barrier-supporting ingredients such as ceramides. You might also benefit from slathering on a richer cream packed with fatty acids, shea butter, or squalane if your skin is very dry.

That means you should wear a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher on your exposed skin, including your ears, neck, and hands. #4659. Kia just made history at Germany’s most prestigious auto awards

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

The award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

The judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

It’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, launched in May, outperformed the new Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

#4658. Is Yeti’s New Performance Outdoor Clothing Any Good? I Put It to the Test to Find Out.

Sizing up the new apparel drop from the cooler and drinkware giant.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IN A SURPRISE move not many saw, Yeti recently launched a performance outdoor clothing line. It’s a deviation, sure, but perhaps a sensible one given the brand’s commitment to outdoor gear and all things insulation. As frequent testers of new products in this ever-expanding category, we could not resist the chance to throw them on and put them through the paces in the elements.

We put three signature garments from the latest five-piece line to test: The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket, the Tilloo Hooded Rain Jacket, and the Sansaba Fleece 260 Full-Zip. For context, the other two pieces are the Caprock Merino Quarter-Zip and the Heuco 310 Full-Zip, essentially siblings of the fleece we tried out. To the brand’s credit, no PFAs are used in the line and all items come with a three-year warranty.

Before even testing, there’s plenty to be intrigued by. The pieces show some clear restraint from a brand that tends toward boldness and large logos (you know, like the beloved coolers). You’d barely even know these were Yeti tops, as you really have to hunt for the brand stamp. And there’s a less-is-more approach in the design here, clearly made with active lifestyles and packability in mind (even color-wise, there are only two options max per item, a somewhat refreshing factoid).

I tried all three pieces over a couple of weeks in the dead of fall in the Pacific Northwest. Translation? They were subjected to downpours, foggy night jogs, chilly mornings, and windy afternoons. I wore them on long walks with the dog, bike commutes in the rain, adventures on muddy trails, and to evening soccer games. I even brought them to the coast during a storm that stirred up high surf and sideways precipitation. Here’s what I think after all the initial testing.

The Tensleep Hooded Hybrid Jacket looks good, there’s no denying as much. The sleek, trim fit works for even the most active functions and we found it never overheated in testing. Lightweight and packable, it’s somewhat nimble thanks to two-way stretch fabric but not as much so as the other two items tested.

The water resistance is also impressive. I walked the dog through a downpour in this jacket for about 30 minutes and came back with just a few moisture spots on my layer beneath. Not bad for a jacket that certainly doesn’t claim to be waterproof (though does sport a water-repellant finish). In drizzle and light rain, you’re just fine in this puffer jacket. In fact, the water would bead up with the same intensity even after many wears, meaning that exterior was done right.

While I liked the felt-lined pockets, I think they could be even warmer. The blend of Expedry Down and traceable European Lavalan Wool insulation is perhaps the jacket’s strongest feature. Going with a hybrid blend affords an ability to tightrope walk that fine-line between breathability and protection from the elements—and the proof was in the performance.

At $400 though, this is not a cheap item by any stretch of the imagination.

This was my favorite piece of the trio, and arguably the most straightforward. From the superior YKK Aquaguard zipper to the extremely packable nature of the jacket, the Tilloo is a genuine winner. Like a big boss in your favorite video game, so many jackets in the category have a weak spot hidden somewhere. It usually translates to water seeping in from a cuff or finding its way in through an average zipper. Not here—this jacket is watertight yet breathable.

One of the coolest features is just how quiet this jacket is. As somebody born and raised in the Pacific Northwest, I’ve worn a fair number of waterproof shells. Many of them swish loudly as you move (not unlike Jim Carrey in Dumb and Dumber as he’s pretending to run while driving). This less crinkly option is quite quiet, a bonus you perhaps never knew you desired (but once you have it, it’s hard to go back).

If you’re like me, you like to get outdoors to get away from all the noise. A loud jacket can disrupt an adventure, whether you’re birding in a marsh or scanning for wildlife on a hike. This jacket is not silent but it’s noticeably more hushed than most others, even during animated motions and heavy exercise. The Velcro cuffs create nice clasps over base layers (or just above a smartwatch during a run) while the liner itself is fairly soft to the touch, unlike the less appealing, membrane-like feel you get from so many options. The hood is adjustable and offers a nice panorama without hampering much of your view. And the way it pulls rain off is impressive, meaning you never have to shake off pooling areas like you might with a lesser jacket or umbrella.

It has become my go-to for offseason excursions. While $350 is an undeniable expense, the jacket is worth the price.

Straight on, the Sansaba Fleece 260 is incredibly soft (like, you’re gonna want to nuzzle it). The proprietary PrimaLoft Bio Fleece is a sensory joy, with a lovely feel and a density level that seems to hit the Goldilocks spot. Best, it’s a composite of 100% post-consumer recycled materials. These shorter fibers are densely distributed, creating what Yeti classifies as a midweight garment. We’d argue that it performs on the higher end of the spectrum, at least in terms of insulation and warmth. No, it wouldn’t quite cut it on its own for significant stretches in below-freezing conditions, but it does just find in the kind of cold we’re normally subjected to.

The fleece also breathes quite well. I found that it paired nicely with a brisk mountain hike or even a sweaty workout in damp conditions. However, playing under anything more than a light drizzle requires a proper shell to fend off precipitation. We liked the length of the collar, stylish yet still big enough to hide under during chilly gusts of wind.

Billed as a fleece made for movement and strenuous activities, the Sansaba fared pretty well. I really put it to the sword one day, zipping it up for a four-mile run in light rain. Normally, I’d wear a long-sleeve moisture-wicking shirt beneath, but I wanted to see how the fleece would fare atop a regular cotton T-shirt. While it did well at fending off light moisture and pulling some of the sweat from my arms, I was pretty soaked in sweat at the end. A pretty easy fix with a better undershirt, sure, but it indicates that perhaps the fleece can’t quite do the most strenuous activities without an unwanted side effect (props for drying so quickly after the fact, however).

Additional cons? The interior of the pockets could use some work. The plain mesh is boring and doesn’t do much to warm the paws. But the fleece is so warm and welcoming throughout the top that you can just rest your hands elsewhere for a quick warm-up. The collar also hugs the neck nicely. This is bittersweet, as it really cradles the area and keeps it warm; however, if you like to duck your chin and mouth (and a little nose) beneath this part of a top during a wind gust, it’s harder to do as it’s fairly snug. For $180, this is a pretty good deal, but not necessarily superior to several other fleeces at a similar price point.

While you don’t need the whole set, you might want a few of these pieces to bolster your outdoor apparel game. I recommend them all, but with some caveats. The rain jacket is the best item for the price and is very much on par with others in the category.

The puffer is nice but I don’t find it a whole lot better than, say, this one from Wren that I’ve been wearing for a couple of years now (the Columbia Terwilliger Treail Heat Seal Jacket is another fine option). The neat, textured, and non-glossy (per so, so many) look is hard to beat, but it’s a significant chunk of change even give its merits.

The fleece is also an attractive piece of outerwear with some high-performance capabilities, but perhaps not at the same level as some of its counterparts at its decidedly high price point. I tends toward options like the Patagonia Better Jacket and the Trailmade from REI, a bargain-and-a-half. But the Sansaba is an undoubtedly good-looking option with a lot going for it.

Yeti is clearly on to something here and has turned heads with a combination of clean fits, useful tech, and designs with mobility in mind (not to mention some environmentally conscious moves too). But this writer would suggest splurging on perhaps just one of the items depending on your adventuring angles and lifestyle.

#4657. Your Guide to Running on the Treadmill This Winter

Here’s why it feels harder to run indoors—and how to hack it to make it more enjoyable.

There’s almost no other cardio machine that brings up as many feelings as the treadmill. For the first few years of my running career, I’d do just about everything I could to avoid hopping on one, even if that meant running in freezing temps or heavy rain.

Then, last winter happened. There was more snow and ice on the ground in New York City than I had seen in a long time, but I had a half-marathon to train for. It left me no choice: I had to move my workouts to the treadmill unless I wanted to end up like that meme where the woman says snow is the perfect texture for running just to wipe out on live television a few seconds later.

But, as any treadmill hater knows, moving a run indoors isn’t as simple as it sounds. A lot changes on a tread—form, mental stimulation, pace—and it can totally mess with your head. Once you understand why, though, it’s a lot easier to work with the treadmill instead of against it; here’s how.

Because it is! For starters, your form changes. “Many people shorten their stride on the treadmill—me included,” says Amy Woods, a USAT-certified run coach and ISSA-certified strength and conditioning coach. “We also tend to run a little more upright.”

There’s a simple reason behind it. When you’re running outside, your legs have all the space they need for each stride, but on a treadmill, you’re contained to the length and width of the belt. Plus, most people tend to stick too close to the front of the tread, making their space even smaller, says Morgan Mowers, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and V.02-certified run coach.

Between a shortened stride and the fact that it’s a bit easier to propel yourself forward when you’ve got the help of the moving belt, you end up using different muscles on a treadmill compared to outdoors. “We see a decrease in activation of hamstrings and glutes, those bigger propellers that push you forward,” Mowers says. Instead, you’re seeing more activation in your hip flexors, quads, calves, and knees.

On paper, a lot of these differences should actually make treadmill running easier than running outside. Another example? A treadmill provides a consistent surface. Outside, terrain and incline can vary with each step, so you call on more stabilizing muscles in your ankles and calves, Mowers says. “With every step, there's a little bit of a change when you're running outside versus on a treadmill,” she says. “Even if you are changing up the incline, it's the same exact surface over and over again.” You also don’t have to deal with the same environmental challenges—like heat and wind resistance—that come with running outside. There’s even a famous 1996 study that claims runners should set their incline to 1 percent to accommodate for the difference.

Even with all these easier-sounding differences, running on a treadmill often feels anything but. For many people, myself included, slowing down on a treadmill is the norm. One possible reason: You may just not be used to it, Woods says. Running safely on a treadmill, especially at higher speeds, takes practice. “It's definitely a different feeling when you're running on a treadmill,” Woods says. “You have to be more aware of your foot placement, your arm swing, and where your eyes are looking.” Even if you’re not consciously aware of it, your proprioception (your ability to sense your body’s position in space) could be affected.

Plus, when you’re on the treadmill, you’re stuck at one pace unless you change it, Mowers points out. “That consistency that your body is feeling on a treadmill can make it feel harder, and also may result in you going at an overall slower pace,” she says. When you hop on a treadmill, you start yourself at a pace and settle in until you physically change it. Over the course of a mile outdoors, in comparison, you may start at an 11:00 pace, then speed up to a 10:45 pace for most of it, and end up cruising at a 10:30 pace—all without really noticing. Even though your effort feels the same, your outdoor mile ends up faster.

Then there’s the mental side of things. Outside, you’ve got much more stimulation, says Rachelle Reed, PhD, an exercise physiologist. Your surroundings can offer the perfect distraction, and the natural variations in scenery, incline, terrain, and pace can help keep your brain more engaged too. This can have an impact on your rate of perceived exertion (RPE), Reed says. In fact, a 2019 meta-analysis found that at faster speeds, runners rated their effort as harder on a treadmill compared to outdoors. Basically, it’s harder to go hard on the tread. And because running on a treadmill is technically easier than running outdoors because you have less variation, wind resistance, and environmental factors to navigate at any given moment, that higher RPE really speaks to the mental effects of being inside, Reed says.

The good news? All these differences between treadmill and outdoor running only really matter if you’re training for a race. That’s because come race day, you’ll want your muscles fully prepped to accommodate your outdoor stride, along with the ability to run across inconsistent terrain and in various elements, Mowers says. Meanwhile, if you’re just looking to do cardio, you can take your pick between the two.

If you are in fact training for a race, how should a treadmill fit into your training? In this case, going outside tends to be superior to staying in, our experts agree. Don’t move your run to the tread at just any sign of inconvenience—running in the rain, cold, and (reasonable) heat all make you a better runner, and you never know if those conditions will pop up on race day, so you’ll be glad to have the practice.

Still, there are definitely situations where it’s not a good idea to go outside. Mowers draws the line when it comes to safety: If the ground is icy, snowy, or slippery in any way, she’ll stay inside to avoid potential injury. If temps are dangerously hot, she’ll run on the treadmill. If there’s risk from serious weather, like thunder and lightning or flooding, she’ll also stay safe indoors. And, she’ll stick to her tread in the event of poor air quality (anything that’s an air quality index over 101).

It’s always worth considering personal safety, too. If your only window to run is late at night and you feel more comfortable staying indoors, do that.

How hot is too hot? This is going to vary down to the person and place. Anything above 85 degrees can be dangerous, Woods says, and you also need to factor in dew point, humidity, and the effort of your run. (Harder efforts are more risky than easier ones.) If temps are higher and you decide to run outdoors, make sure you bring plenty of hydration and fuel, go slower than normal, and pay attention to signs of overheating.

There’s also the convenience factor. You may need to do a run on the treadmill because it’s more accommodating to your schedule or childcare needs. That’s totally okay too. Ideally, the majority of your runs (we’re talking about 80 percent, and especially your long runs) will be outside, but if you’re someone who finds themselves needing to do the bulk of their running indoors, a run coach can help you make sure you’re prepped for race day. (Woods works with athletes who do the bulk of their training on treads—it’s possible!) The treadmill exists for a reason, and your training will not be affected by the occasional indoor run.

First and foremost, don’t be too hard on yourself about pace. “I always disconnect from pace on the treadmill,” Woods says. Instead, she focuses on her time and RPE. It’s really about thinking about the “spirit of the workout,” she says. For example, you can pay attention to what heart rate zone or effort level you’re supposed to get to and match that—even if that looks slower and feels harder indoors.

And, no, you don’t need to set your incline to 1 percent to compensate for bringing your workout indoors, our experts agree. The biggest reason? The study that established the idea was very small (it had just nine participants) and done only in men. That said, the incline buttons will become useful depending on the kind of run you have on deck for the day.

Finally, give yourself a good warm-up on the treadmill, Mowers says. “Just the act of getting on a treadmill is going to increase our heart rate a little bit because we're a hamster on a wheel; we're trying not to fall off of this thing, and we're so aware of the fact that we're running,” she says. You may need at least 10 to 15 minutes to settle in before getting started with the rest of your workout.

Here’s how to approach different kinds of runs indoors.

Nothing really has to change, Woods says. It may take you a little longer to run a 5K on your treadmill, but try to stick to the appropriate lower heart rate zones and RPE that you’d normally achieve on these kinds of runs outdoors.

You can play with incline if you’d like—but it’s not a requirement if this is a one-off run you’re doing inside. Running for one day on a completely flat surface won’t affect your training. One reason you may want to try changing the incline may simply be because it adds some variety and stimulation, Woods says. If you’re someone who struggles because the treadmill feels boring, try increasing the incline anywhere from 1 to 4 percent for anywhere from 30 seconds to a few minutes every so often.

Another hack: Every 10 minutes, increase your speed slightly. That should give you enough time to warm up a little each time and settle into the pace, so you shouldn’t see much of a jump in demand on your heart rate or effort.

This one gets a bit trickier, Woods says. Going at all-out speeds on a treadmill can be much tougher—and not feel super safe. This is a time when you’ll want to think about the spirit of the workout. If you have intervals where you’re supposed to get to max heart rate efforts, instead of turning up the speed super high, you can increase the incline in addition to adjusting the speed slightly, Woods says. That should still get you to your zone 4 or 5, all while allowing you to stay slower and feel more in control. This is much easier to accomplish in a tempo run (where you’re holding the pace for longer chunks of time) compared to intervals, so you could also swap an interval run for tempo too.

You also have the option to skip a speed workout, Woods says. Missing one session won’t have an impact on your training, and if you’d rather not do it on the treadmill, you also have the option to switch it with another run for the week.

Now, here’s a workout that translates pretty well to the treadmill: All you have to do is up your incline for the duration marked in your workout. Woods recommends sticking between 1 and 4 percent as a good rule of thumb, but you can always bump up to 5 to 8 as long as you can keep good run form.

Ideally, you can move your long run to another day when you can run outside. But, if not, go by time—not mileage. Woods doesn’t recommend running on a treadmill for longer than two hours unless you are very experienced on one because of how it affects your form.

You also have the option to break up your run and do 90 minutes in the morning and 90 minutes in the afternoon. “This will help with form deterioration which is more noticeable and can be more dangerous on a tread,” Woods says.

While you’re on your long run, you’ll also want to incorporate moments of incline running and even some pace variation—both for improving your running and also giving yourself a mental reset. Woods also loves to sprinkle in 15- to 30-second walking breaks every mile or so to reset her form and hydrate.

Then the world is really your oyster on the treadmill, but all the same ideas apply: Focus on time and effort, not pace. And, feel free to sprinkle in different inclines and speeds to work different heart rate zones and find moments of mental reset.

#4656. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4655. BYD shows what its new ‘Cloud Carriage’ intelligent body control system can really do

BYD’s new EV may be about the size of a Toyota Camry, but it’s playing in a whole different league when it comes to technology.

BYD launched the second-generation Seal 07 last week, calling it “the new choice for a class-leading luxury experience.”

It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry.

Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology.

The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes.

The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its new Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System.

The setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System.

Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above.

BYD said the system provides ultra-fast response times down to the millisecond. The advanced suspension system adjusts damping force across a wide range of 100 to 10,000 Nm.

It’s equipped on the all-electric Flagship Seal 07 variant, while lower-priced versions have the Disus-C intelligent body control system. The top-spec EV model with the Disus-M setup starts at 172,900 yuan ($26,000). Still, not too bad for what you get.

Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s new interior design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.

BYD added a few premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio.

Quite impressive for sure. What's more impressive is that GM/Cadillac first offered magnetic ride control back in 2002 (a full 24 years ago!!). It may not have been quite as advanced as this system in 2026, but still one of the most advanced suspension systems offered to date for a line of vehicles.

I really want this car!! I truly hope BYD will be able to sell this in the USA soon.

The Seal 07 also debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that lets drivers interact with the vehicle and manage functions remotely.

Higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super trade-in price” special, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.
