#4654. The 29 Best Pieces of Camping Gear, According to Outdoor Editors

Our favorite, must-pack picks for backpacking, car camping, and everything in between.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WINTER IS QUICKLY approaching. But whether you’re a front-country weekend warrior or a hardcore backcountry camper, you still should have a few camping trips lined up for the year (leaf-peeping fall road trip, anyone?). And it’s never too late to take stock of your gear closet to see what’s missing, what’s busted, and what needs an upgrade.

We cover all the latest and greatest outdoor gear every year in the Men’s Health Outdoor Awards. But, in this guide, we’re covering just the greatest. To offer a wide breadth of options (since there are all different sorts of camping), we’ve broken this guide into categories of tents, sleep systems, kitchen, and general camping gear. Whether it’s all new for 2026 or it’s been around for years, these are our favorite camping and outdoor gear picks for backpacking, car camping, and everything in between—the gear that we love and pack for every trip.

This entry-level tent strikes a good balance of pack weight, affordability, and reliability. It’s roomy enough to sleep two with a dash of gear and sets up faster than most at this price point (even with the included rainfly) for easy-breezy camping in almost any season. Bonus: A limited lifetime warranty.

Nemo’s Aurora 3 ticks all our must-have boxes for a midrange, midsize tent. It sleeps three (tightly) or two who appreciate spreading out with more gear. A generously sized interior, plus oversized doors and vestibules, provides a much more livable space. We love that the hubbed pole design makes for a dead-simple setup and teardown. Plus, Nemo’s commitment to more eco-friendly gear means a bluesign-approved recycled tent floor and PFAS-free rainfly.

Redesigned for 2026, Sea to Summit upgrades its already fantastic Telos Evo tent line to be even more livable and weatherproof. A dedicated roof vent (with storm flap) promotes better airflow and reduces condensation. The versatile design also offers multiple pitch options, including hangout and stargaze modes. So it’s not only a reliable backcountry sleep space, but a day/night lounge when you need it.

The Lunar Solo is a budgversatility for extra gear or your dog. Plus, it’s durable and breathable with solid ventilation. It’s not the single best in any one category, but the price makes it a great all-arounder for weight-conscious backpackers and thru-hikers on a budget. Our main gripes are the tricky setup process and the fact that it requires seam sealing before use—neither of which is a deal breaker at this price point though.

Marmot sought to reinvent the wheel, er, sleeping bag with its all-new Wraptor. The clever design swaps traditional zippers for overlapping flips and magnetic snaps, ensuring a more versatile camp sleep setup. Shed the layers in warmer weather or bundle up when the temperature drops—it’s flexible in every temperature. This same adjustability caters to sleepers who appreciate a “swaddled like a baby” mummy bag and hybrid campers looking for more room to spread out on their stomachs and sides. Also available in a 15-degree option.

Exped’s midrange Terra line is our go-to bag for anyone looking for real, 650-fill-power duck down that’s affordable. The 15-degree temp rating makes this a solid three-season option that’s capable of most four-season camping in all but the coldest weather. It’s comfy enough for car camping, and with a roughly 3-pound pack weight, compact enough for backpacking overnighters. The glow-in-the-dark zipper pull and internal pocket are nifty features, too.

With the Cot One, Helinox creates an instant sleep surface that’s flat, level, comfortable, and off the ground. Fully set up, it’s the perfect front-country camp bed that supports more than 300 pounds. It packs down surprisingly small into the included zip case and weighs less than five pounds. Optional leg extensions are available to lift the cot up to 15 inches off the ground for maximum comfort.

This entry-level model from Wise Owl Outfitters is a great starter option for anyone looking to get into hammock camping or as a budget-friendly “just in case” hammock. The lightweight design weighs less than two pounds for the hammock, straps, carabiners, and stuff sack. It’s surprisingly durable and supports up to 500 pounds. Bonus: It’s available in more than a dozen colors, too.

You typically get what you pay for in the world of inflatable air pads, but Klymit’s Static V Base is something of a unicorn. It’s plenty comfy for front-country camp setups, but it really shines in the backcountry with a compact, featherweight construction that’s surprisingly durable to survive rock punctures and uneven ground. Most impressive? It’s typically available for less than $50.

We’ll take a proper foam pillow over an inflatable any day. Therm-a-Rest’s fan-favorite compressible relies on an upcycled foam fill and a plush polyester cover for serious front- and backcountry sleep comfort that’s the closest thing to your home bedroom setup. The cinch adjuster (hence the name) allows campers to tweak the pillow’s firmness to their liking. Plus, it packs down to about half its size for easy travel.

For front-country campers with access to electricity (or even a portable power station), Nestout’s Outdoor Cooker adds serious versatility to your outdoor kitchen. The modest 500-watt capability is plenty powerful for cooking rice, boiling, steaming, or whipping up everything from soup to oatmeal. At less than two pounds, it’s compact and lightweight enough to stash in the back of your rig until you need it.

Yeti’s newest cast-iron skillet is also the largest in its lineup. The 14-inch size makes it ideal as an all-in-one pan for car campers looking to pack less cookware. The oversized design comes polished and pre-seasoned, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. An additional grab handle and dual pour spouts make it safer and ultra-versatile for cooking up just about anything.

This portable fridge from BougeRV is the perfect accompaniment to your existing cooler. Stash the temperature critical foods (meat, eggs, bacon, etc.) in the former and everything else in the latter. It’s small enough to fit in the footwell of most passenger vehicles, and the included 240Wh detachable battery keeps it cold for more than a full day. What’s more: It’s more affordable than most premium midsize coolers.

Gerber elevates the lowly spork with the ComplEAT Multi-Fork. It’s the same multipurpose utensil we all know and love, including a deep-basin spoon, a tined fork end, and dual cut/scrape edges. But this premium take adds a six-function multi-tool that clips to the back. So, you also get a serrated package opener, a can opener, a bottle opener, twin flathead drivers, and a pry bar. A clever kickstand feature also keeps the business end up off of dirty rocks and ground.

For campers who value weight and packability above all else, BioLite’s CampStove 2+ is a game-changer. The clever design runs on pretty much any organic material (twigs, pine cones, leaves, wood) to keep it stoked off-grid almost indefinitely. The dual-purpose output charges your phone, GPS, headlamp, and other small devices (at up to three watts) in the backcountry, and it doubles as a stove at mealtime.

I’m willing to dump a lot of things from my pack to save weight, but coffee isn’t one of them. Sea to Summit’s Frontier Ultralight Collapsible Pour Over is as dead-simple and packable as a camp coffeemaker can get, so you’re guaranteed your morning Joe anywhere. It weighs just two ounces and folds down almost completely flat so you’ll practically forget it’s in your backpack. But it pops open to reveal a legit pour-over coffeemaker that works with most camp and travel mugs.

For serious front-country campers, Jetboil’s Genesis Basecamp is near perfect. The dual-burner system allows for more elaborate meal preparation than single-burner alternatives with up to 10,000 BTU output and maximum flame control. A 5-liter pot and 10-inch ceramic-coated nonstick fry pan are included, so you can prep just about anything for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, even for larger groups.

The all-new Daytrip 20L combines Yeti’s legendary all-day, keep-cold insulation with the portability of a traditional backpack cooler. It’s roomy enough for a six-pack, two lunches, snacks, and an ice pack, making it perfect for day-hike lunch breaks or even as add-on cold storage for weekend trips. A large top opening provides easy access, while external pockets add extra storage for keeping smaller essentials within easy reach.

For long weekends at the campsite or off-grid, we love this oversized cooler from RTIC. The 78-can capacity offers plenty of cold storage for a family getaway, and RTIC’s premium insulation ensures it stays chilled for up to five days. The lightweight design is easier to carry, and all-terrain, puncture-proof wheels make it easy to wheel from the car to the campsite, too.

Car camping is dirty business—literally. That’s why we love simple, versatile adventure storage that just works. Upgrade your existing loadout with this gear box from Gregory. It’s waterproof/dustproof, and the translucent lid makes organization infinitely easier than with traditional opaque storage totes. Plus, the clever hinged lid opens either way for easy access.

Solo Stove has long been a perennial favorite for us here at Men’s Health. Its latest Basecamp fire pit combines a just-right size that’s roomy enough for four adults to enjoy yet compact enough to easily transport from the backyard to the backseat for car camping. And, of course, it still features the same smokeless design and maximum burn efficiency that the brand is known for.

Leatherman’s Signal has been my multitool of choice since I can remember. The just-right tool selection includes everything you need for a day in the backcountry or your own backyard: Pliers, drivers, cutters, a saw, a micro hammer, bottle and can openers, wrenches, and a 420 HC combo knife. Plus, there’s a whistle and ferro rod if you need ‘em. It’s all packed into one compact tool that stuffs neatly in the available sheath or clips to your pack with the brand that invented the ultra-packable camp chair sought to make it even better. With an extended backrest, it’s now more comfortable and supportive than ever, with all the same backpacking-friendly packability as before. The shock-corded pole structure makes for easy setup, and the 100% recycled polyester seat fabric is a nice, eco-friendly touch.

The brand that invented the ultra-packable camp chair sought to make it even better. With an extended backrest, it’s now more comfortable and supportive than ever, with all the same backpacking-friendly packability as before. The shock-corded pole structure makes for easy setup, and the 100% recycled polyester seat fabric is a nice, eco-friendly touch.

The aptly named GigaPower Folding Torch is the single best way to start a campfire in any conditions. It uses the same small disposable fuel canisters that you’re probably already packing. Yet it’s powerful enough for starting large fires while car camping and compact enough to stash in a backpack if you’re planning to backcountry camp. Plus, it’s just so damn fun to use.

Our go-to camp table balances weight and durability, with a dead-simple design that makes setup and breakdown easy. The nearly flat silhouette slots neatly into the laptop sleeve of a backpack or soft cooler, too.

Bluetti’s Elite 100 V2 is the portable power station to buy if you only want to buy one. It’s relatively lightweight and compact enough to stash in the footwell of most vehicles. But the 1800-watt peak output can power everything from smartphones and laptops to rice cookers and blenders. It’s surprisingly affordable, too, especially compared to the competition. Just add a 100-watt folding solar panel for virtually limitless off-grid power.

Simple touches can elevate any car camping setup. Rumpl’s aptly named Everywhere Mat combines a great-looking microsuede topside that’s stain- and water-resistant with a durable waterproof bottom. So, you get the added livability of a true outdoor rug, including a softer place to walk and for your kids/pets to rest, and a way to protect your gear from stains, wet ground, and errant sticks and rocks.

Another solid storage option, Thule’s new Chasm 55L (and Chasm 80L) is plenty durable for outdoor use, with a molded EVA waterproof base. The semi-rigid structure stays upright when you need it, and the included movable panel lets you customize the interior layout to fit your setup. A zippered lid cleverly folds open and secures magnetically, so you can use it in either the full-open or half-open position.

While Black Diamond’s Spot 400-R is a bit of a gold standard when it comes to headlamps, you might need something a little stronger in certain outdoor situations. In comes the new Storm Headlamp, which can generate 550 lumens up to a distance of 137 meters. It also incorporates RGB lighting options and offers rechargeability via USB-C. While the 70 hours of runtime on low (4 on high and 30 on medium) is a tad short, this headlamp is going to go anywhere and do anything you need it to.

There is no one way to camp, especially these days. Here’s a quick rundown on the different camping styles.

The key isn't just packing more gear, but packing high-quality items that are durable, versatile, and work for your style of camping. That last bit is the most important. Focus on the things that actually make your experience better. For me, that means an ultra-comfortable sleep setup (with a luxurious portable mattress and a legit camp pillow) that's almost as good as my bed at home, and a solid camp kitchen (with a portable fridge and premium cookware set) because I love to cook. But that changes from the frontcountry to the backcountry.

Depending on how remote you’re going, you should figure out your own preferences for your style of camping. Weight savings is always more crucial when you step up from car camping and into more involved situations in the backcountry.

Weather and climate are always a factor when camping. Not just for what to pack and bring, but for the type of gear you invest in. Are you just a summer camper? Then you can probably get away with three-season camping gear. If you do want to do winter camping, then having two sets of gear (one for warmer and one for colder) might make sense or opting for four-season gear might be the way to go.

There are solo campers all the way to big group camping excursions, and everything in between. Making sure you have the right size tent for the people you tend to camp with is a first start. Maybe you like solo camping often, but you do a group trip every summer as well. You’ll probably need two tents then, or at least making sure that someone in the group has more of a three-person and up tent. The same thinking should go into your camp kitchen setup.

As an avid camper and adventure travel writer for more than two decades, I've tested countless outdoor products from all of the world's most recognized brands. Whether that’s a weeklong car camping trip or backpacking throughout Utah’s national parks, I’ve assessed outdoor gear in countless different scenarios and climates. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and some of his own personal testing.

While testing camping gear, we've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, ease of packing, weight, durability, functionality, performance, and necessity. The best camping gear is the gear you actually use, as overpacking can make things a bit tricky. Prioritize what’s best for your style of camping.

#4653. The 8 Best Standing Desks for Walking Pads, Tested and Reviewed

From budget picks to tricked-out options for a better WFH space.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, though, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even issues with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

“Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” says Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.)

But proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” says Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

To find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

While everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

Martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

At over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

During testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that important feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

While some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she says, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

This electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she says. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

Her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

This walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

Not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is important because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you plan to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.)

At the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

It’s important to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

We should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

I consulted with Bach and Darmofal to help identify what to look for in standing desks for walking pads. From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces. Our testers included Cori Ritchey, Lindsay Geller, Taryn Colbert, and Deanna Martin, who evaluated the desks for build quality, ease of assembly, adjustability, size, and overall functionality. Testing periods ranged from one week to over a month, with editors using their desks while sitting, standing, or walking on an under-desk treadmill. We also considered how stable each setup felt, how easily it fit into a home office, and any drawbacks our testers encountered.
